However, it decided the wider project would not have a significant environmental impact because restoration work was planned elsewhere in the park.
According to the agency's project outline, the $36 million investment will pay for new roofs, windows and shopfront repairs along Commercial Row. The work will also include structural repairs and new electrical wiring at three historic homes, new water and wastewater treatment plants, and a retaining wall in front of the Thurmond train depot. The Town of Thurmond and the New River Gorge Historical Society argue that restoring other landmarks does not give the Park Service permission to ignore the legal rules covering the 12 buildings. With the demolition contractor expected to arrive on 30 November, the two groups are waiting for the federal court in Charleston to decide whether to issue an emergency order stopping the work.

title: Meet Yash Patil, Indian-origin entrepreneur who took leave from Stanford to work with Open AI, founded his own startup and then sold it for $4.5 billion
text:
A 23-year-old Indian-origin entrepreneur who left Stanford University, joined OpenAI and later founded an artificial intelligence startup has struck a $4.5-billion acquisition deal barely 18 months after launching his company. Yash Patil, co-founder and chief executive of Applied Compute, has agreed to sell the startup to cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks in an all-stock transaction valued at $4.5 billion (around Rs 40,000 crore). The deal values the company at roughly $250 million for every month since it was founded.
Patil founded Applied Compute in May 2025 with fellow former OpenAI employees Rhythm Garg and Linden Li. The startup helps companies customize, train and deploy artificial intelligence models using their own data, allowing businesses to build AI systems tailored to their needs rather than relying entirely on third-party models.
The acquisition is expected to be completed in the third quarter of Palo Alto Networks' fiscal 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.
Following the acquisition, Patil is expected to become co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks, alongside the Applied Compute team.
From Stanford to OpenAI
Patil grew up in Austin, Texas, in a family of Indian immigrants. He attended the Liberal Arts and Science Academy before studying computer science at Stanford University. 
His journey into AI reportedly began after a chance meeting with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman at a dinner hosted for Stanford engineering students.
Following the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, Patil emailed Altman expressing interest in working on the chatbot. Altman encouraged him to apply for OpenAI's residency programme.
Patil joined OpenAI in 2023 at the age of 20, taking a leave of absence from Stanford. He later worked as a technical staff member on post-training infrastructure, reasoning models and technology associated with Codex, OpenAI's AI coding assistant.
At OpenAI, he met fellow Stanford alumni Rhythm Garg and Linden Li, who would later become his co-founders.
The trio left OpenAI in 2025 to build Applied Compute, betting that companies would increasingly want to develop and operate their own AI systems using proprietary data.
How Applied Compute became a billion-dollar startup
The idea for Applied Compute began taking shape in January 2025, around the time Chinese AI company DeepSeek released its R1 reasoning model, demonstrating the potential of powerful open-weight AI systems. The founders believed businesses would want to customize these models to suit their operations, train them using proprietary data and deploy them securely.
The startup attracted major investors as it rapidly scaled.
In June 2025, it raised $20 million in seed funding led by Benchmark, reportedly valuing the company at around $100 million. Another funding round brought in another $60 million, taking its valuation to approximately $500 million.By April 2026, Applied Compute had achieved unicorn status after raising $80 million at a $1.3-billion valuation in a funding round led by Kleiner Perkins.
Earlier in November 2026, it raised $350 million at a valuation of $3.25 billion, in a round led by investor Elad Gil.
The company said it had grown from zero revenue to more than $100 million in annualized revenue run-rate in just over 18 months, with a team of only a few dozen people.
Its customers reportedly include Microsoft, Nvidia, DoorDash, Shopify, Harvey, Cognition, Mercor, Clay and Decagon.
Why Palo Alto Networks is buying the startup
Palo Alto Networks, one of the world's largest cybersecurity companies, has been expanding its AI capabilities as businesses increasingly deploy artificial intelligence in sensitive operations. Applied Compute's technology could help enterprises train and run customised AI models while incorporating security measures to protect data, systems and models against cyber threats. The acquisition is part of Palo Alto Networks' broader strategy to become a central player in the AI economy.
CEO Nikesh Arora has said the company wants to position itself at the centre of AI adoption, particularly as enterprises increasingly require security infrastructure to support AI-powered operations. The $4.5-billion acquisition will bring Applied Compute's research team and platform into Palo Alto Networks, expanding its ability to help businesses deploy AI securely.

title: High-profile Colorado attorney who set own house on fire and apologized to wife and children for domestic violence dies of accidental drug overdose
text:
A Colorado attorney who was accused of setting fire to his own home has died from an accidental drug overdose, months after pleading guilty to misdemeanor charges involving his wife. The fire incident took place in 2025 and grabbed headlines as the attorney at that time was dealing with a high-profile case from which he had to step away.
Robert Werking, 60, died in October from an accidental overdose involving fentanyl, cocaine and methamphetamine, according to the Douglas County Coroner's Office.
Werking had attracted attention in July 2025 after first responders found him sitting on the front porch of his burning home in Centennial, Colorado. At the time, he was part of the legal team representing Aurora dentist James Craig, who was accused of poisoning his wife, Angela Craig, to death.
The attorney's death came months after he pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm while under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance and harassing his wife, Lisa Fine Moses, in an incident involving domestic violence.
On June 28, 2025, when firefighters responded to a blaze at his home, they found him sitting on the porch while flames engulfed the house behind him. 
Investigators found evidence that an accelerant had been used to start the fire.
Werking was arrested and charged with felony arson. He withdrew from Craig's defence shortly afterwards, just days before the high-profile murder trial was scheduled to begin. His wife Fine Moses was also representing the dentist. Craig was eventually convicted of first-degree murder in July 2025 and sentenced to life in prison for killing his wife.
Pleaded guilty to firearm and harassment charges
Werking's legal troubles also involved a separate incident involving his wife. On March 5, 2026, he pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm while under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance and harassing Fine Moses in an act of domestic violence on June 14, 2025. The felony arson charges relating to the June 28 fire were dismissed in the interests of justice.
During the sentencing hearing, Werking's attorney, David Beller, said his client had experienced mental health problems that were either undiagnosed or self-medicated. Beller said Werking had entered an inpatient treatment facility immediately after his release from jail and had made progress. Werking's law licence was also inactive because of disability. Senior Judge Dinsmore Tuttle sentenced him to one year of probation, requiring him to undergo mental health and substance-use treatment and complete 40 hours of community service.
During the sentencing hearing, Werking delivered an emotional statement apologising to his family for his actions. He described Fine Moses as a "saint" and said he hoped to make things right through community service. "My actions in this case devastated my family," he said. "I hurt our family, our children so badly... I am very sorry. My actions were selfish; my actions were terrible. ...I am ashamed and I will carry this guilt and shame for the rest of my life."

title: Sydney medical student identifies 5 relatives in forgotten 1965 film after social media appeal
text:
A forgotten film shot in Melbourne in 1965 has helped reunite a Sydney medical student with relatives he did not know were in the video. The find solved a mystery for a British television director who had been looking for the family. The discovery happened after the unknown people appeared in a clip shared on social media. The student spotted five members of his own family in the video.
Sydney medical student solves mystery of 1965 Melbourne family film
A forgotten film shot in Melbourne in 1965 has helped reunite a Sydney medical student with relatives he did not know were in the video. The find solved a mystery for a British television director who had been looking for the family. Zac de Boeck spotted five members of his family after his mother sent him a short video shared by ABC Melbourne on social media. The clip had sat among old film reels for decades. It showed three generations of his relatives outside their home in the Melbourne suburb of Mitcham.
The find ended a global search led by British television director Karen Walsh. She had been trying to find out who the strangers were after her late father, Arthur Howes, filmed them during a trip to Australia in 1965. According to ABC News, Howes filmed the family while travelling around Australia as he thought about moving there with his young family. 
He later went back to England with film of Melbourne, Sydney and Perth, and never moved to Australia for good. More than 60 years later, his daughter found the unknown family in one of the old recordings and set out to learn who they were.
A forgotten film sparks an international search
Walsh found the clip while sorting through her father's old film reels. The video lasted less than a minute and showed a family outside a red-brick house in suburban Melbourne. Children played in the driveway while adults watched close by. An older woman, thought to be the grandmother, stood on the garden path as the family went about their day. Walsh liked the scene, but she had no idea who the people were or where the house stood. She told ABC News that the film was too special to throw away.
"It is an absolutely charming little piece of video," she said.
She also explained why she wanted to find the people in the film.
"I just feel like I'm the curator of the footage. I don't feel I own it.
"I think the footage really belongs to the family who were being filmed."
Walsh lives in Bristol and works as a television director in the UK. She had worked in radio before and knew a local talkback show could help reach people who might know the family or the house. She contacted 774 ABC Melbourne and asked the station to help identify the people in the clip. The station shared her call for help on its breakfast show and told listeners to watch the video online. The search was also discussed on ABC Melbourne's breakfast show, where hosts asked listeners to help name the family. The old clip had been shot on an 8mm camera, which was a common way to make home movies at the time.
Clues in the house and driveway
Once the appeal aired, people began looking closely at details in the short clip for clues. The look of the brick house and a green-striped garage door drew notice, as viewers tried to figure out which Melbourne suburb it might be. The green van parked in the driveway also became a key clue in the search. Chris Scane, a historian with the Volkswagen Club of Victoria, said it was a standard split-window 1962 Kombi built in Clayton, Victoria.
"We'll be chasing all our members to dig in their files and see if they can find this car," he said.
Some viewers thought two boys jumping off the letterbox might be wearing uniforms from Xavier College. However, the school's archivist checked its records and ruled that out. The van's number plates seemed like another way to find the owners. But VicRoads could not share details about the vehicle because of privacy laws. Even with these clues, the family stayed unknown until the video reached someone who knew the people in it.
Medical student recognises five relatives
The big break came when de Boeck's mother sent him the ABC Melbourne video while he was looking at social media. She wanted to know if he knew anyone in the clip. De Boeck, a Palawa man studying medicine in Sydney, quickly spotted five people. He then contacted the ABC talkback show to tell them the video showed members of his own family. The broadcaster later confirmed that the film captured three generations of his relatives. They included his grandmother, great-uncle, great-grandparents and great-great-grandmother. The family lived in Mitcham during the 1960s, while the younger children playing in the driveway are thought to be extended family members. The first person de Boeck spotted was his great-grandmother, Dorothy Vanner.
"As I opened the video, I initially spotted my great-grandmother, Dorothy Vanner," he said.
Dorothy, a Palawa woman, died 10 years ago. She would have turned 101 in 2026. In the 1965 clip, she appears with her husband, Ron Vanner, when both were in their 40s, along with their two children. For de Boeck, seeing his great-grandmother so much younger was hard to process. He said he had only known her as an old woman because she was 70 when he was born.
"When I was born, great-grandma was 70, so in my brain, I only know her as an old lady," he said.
"Seeing her only 10 years older than I am now, it was just mind-boggling."
A rare glimpse of family history
The clip also gave de Boeck's grandmother, Kathryn Holland, a surprise chance to see her family as they looked more than 60 years ago. Holland is the older girl standing near her parents in the driveway. She does not remember the day the film was shot or the visitor behind the camera, Arthur Howes. Even though she has many family photos, she had never seen moving video of her childhood. The old film let her watch her late mother, father and grandmother in a way that still photos could not show.
"I've got lots of photos, but I haven't seen them on film. It was quite a surprise," she said.
"I look so young!"
Holland was also amazed that Walsh, a stranger living in another country, had taken the time to track down the family and return the clip to them.
"I just think she's extra special, going to all this trouble to find out who it belongs to," she said of Walsh.
"It's fabulous."
For Walsh, finding the family was something she had not expected when she first called the radio station. She admitted she had almost thrown the old film away while going through her father's things.
"I had no faith," she said.
"You know, I was so close to putting the film in the bin when I was going through the footage.
"Something made me stop and go, 'You know what, let's just see if we can find who this is.'"
The search took about 10 days from the first radio appeal to the discovery, according to ABC Melbourne's radio coverage.

title: Sofia Hernandez Mejia's arrest by ICE from Seattle airport: Husband says he feels useless as a US citizen
text:
The husband of Sofia Hernandez Mejia, the Mexican woman who was detained by ICE officers while boarding an Alaska Airlines flight along with her father, broke his silence about the entire incident and said he felt helpless as he was also there. Jose Castillo, a US citizen, said he felt helpless as masked immigration officers arrested his wife and her father, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, on Saturday while the family was preparing to board a flight from Seattle to Los Angeles. Recalling the incident in an interview with CBS News on Monday, Castillo said the situation unfolded so quickly that he struggled to understand what was happening.
"You black out. You don't even know what's going on. You don't even know what's happening. Everything is moving so fast. Trying to protect your wife and they're taking your father-in-law," he said. "As a US citizen, you feel useless," he added.
Castillo also expressed anger over the way the arrests were carried out, saying he was disgusted by the officers' actions. "How can you sit with yourself and strip somebody away like that in broad daylight, in front of families?" he said.
What happened during the Alaska Airlines flight arrest?
The incident took place on November 21 as passengers were boarding Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. 
The flight was scheduled to travel to Los Angeles. Videos of the confrontation circulated widely on social media, showing masked federal agents struggling with a person on the airport jet bridge as other passengers watched. Hernandez Mejia could be heard crying and telling officers that they were taking her father. She also said that the family had work authorization.
According to Castillo, he was travelling with his wife and father-in-law to attend a family event when plainclothes ICE officers approached them on the jet bridge.
DHS said the operation was targeting Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who had overstayed his visa.The agency said other passengers began obstructing federal officers during the arrest. It also alleged that Hernandez Mejia threw hot coffee at immigration agents, prompting her detention. DHS said she would face federal charges of assaulting a federal officer.
Castillo strongly disputed the allegation and said she did not assault anyone. "She did nothing. She was being shoved. They came directly at us." "When you're coming at me and my wife and you're shoving us, obviously coffee's going to be spilled," he added.
The family's attorney, Olia Catala, has also challenged the government's account. She said Hernandez Mejia was holding a cup of coffee when the confrontation began and dropped it amid the commotion.
Why were the father and daughter detained?
DHS identified both Hernandez Mejia and Larrondo Mendoza as Mexican nationals who had overstayed their visas and were living in the United States without legal immigration status. Their attorney contended that the two entered the US legally on tourist visas in 2015 and had pending immigration applications.
Catala said Larrondo Mendoza had a pending asylum application, while Hernandez Mejia had married a US citizen and applied for a green card through her marriage. She also said neither of her clients had a criminal record.The attorney argued that the father and daughter were attempting to follow the legal immigration process and should not have been detained. 
"Congress created legal pathways and Sofia and her father were using them," Catala said in a separate interview with CBS News.
"We can't tell immigrants to use the legal pathways, to follow the law and then punish them for doing just that," she added. Hernandez Mejia and her father remained in ICE custody in Tacoma, Washington, according to their lawyer. Castillo has appealed for their release, insisting that they did not deserve to be detained in the manner they were.

title: WestJet ordered to pay Canadian couple $2,000 after 16-hour delay blamed on wind
text:
A Canadian couple who arrived in Vancouver nearly 16 hours late have won $2,000 in compensation from WestJet after a British Columbia tribunal rejected the airline's argument that strong winds caused the delay. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal (CRT) ruled that WestJet had failed to prove that an unexpected weather event was responsible for the disruption experienced by Kevin and Marie Isobel Fraser. According to CP24, the couple were travelling from Minneapolis to Vancouver on 6 June 2024 when their first flight, which was due to take them to Regina, arrived one hour and 37 minutes late. This caused them to miss their connecting flight, leaving them stuck overnight in a hotel in Regina. WestJet booked the couple onto new flights to Vancouver through Calgary the following day. They eventually reached home almost 16 hours later than planned. However, when the Frasers asked the airline for compensation, WestJet refused to pay.
Why WestJet claimed a weather exemption
Under Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations (APPR), major airlines such as WestJet must pay passengers $1,000 each when a flight disruption makes them arrive at least nine hours late. 
Airlines can avoid paying this compensation if they prove that the delay was caused by something beyond their control, such as severe weather. They can also claim an exemption for unexpected maintenance work that is strictly needed to keep a plane safe. As reported by CP24, WestJet told the tribunal that the delay qualified for both the safety and weather exemptions. The airline said strong winds in Minneapolis had pushed a luggage belt loader into the aircraft, damaging the net used to secure baggage in the cargo area. WestJet argued that aviation rules do not allow planes to take off unless baggage is properly secured and cannot move during the flight. It said maintenance workers therefore had to repair the damage before the aircraft could depart.
Tribunal rejects airline's weather defence
To support its argument, WestJet gave the tribunal an internal document called a "defect report", which recorded the damage to the aircraft. However, CRT member Deanna Rivers found that the airline's own report did not support its claim that the weather had caused the problem.
"It shows that on June 6, 2024, the pilot reported that a belt loader had damaged the aft baggage door threshold net while moving away from the aircraft," Rivers wrote in her decision, as quoted by CP24. "The damage affected five lower attachment points on the sill. The report identifies the resolution as replacing the aft baggage door restraint net. This was done in Calgary on June 16, 2024." Rivers noted that the report did not mention wind or bad weather as a reason the aircraft could not leave on time.
"The defect report identifies the belt loader as the source of the damage but does not mention weather or wind conditions," Rivers' decision reads. "There is also no other documentary evidence connecting the damage to the weather."
Equipment handling deemed within airline control
When deciding whether WestJet was responsible for the damage caused by the belt loader, Rivers considered earlier decisions by the Canadian Transportation Agency. These rulings say that delays caused by airline staff failing to take proper care remain within the airline's control. Rivers used the same principle when considering the Frasers' case. She found that WestJet could not rely on the safety maintenance exemption to avoid responsibility for damage caused by ground equipment.
"Here, even if the damage to the baggage net required maintenance before the aircraft could safely operate, WestJet has not established that the damage resulted from an unforeseeable weather event," Rivers stated in the ruling.
"Rather, the evidence only establishes that a belt loader damaged the net. As WestJet has not proved the damage was outside of its control, I find the resulting delay was within WestJet's control and not required for safety purposes."
Full breakdown of the $2,226.92 payout
Because the couple arrived more than nine hours late and the tribunal found that the delay was within WestJet's control, Rivers ordered the airline to pay Kevin and Marie Isobel Fraser $1,000 each under the APPR. This brought their main compensation award to $2,000. According to CP24, the tribunal also ordered WestJet to repay the couple for other expenses they had paid during the disruption, as well as the costs of bringing their case. These included $35.28 for taxi journeys between the airport and their hotel in Regina. Kevin Fraser was also awarded $51 after being given a lower-class seat on the replacement flights through Calgary. WestJet was also told to repay the couple's $125 fee for filing their case with the Civil Resolution Tribunal, along with $15.64 for sending legal documents to the airline by registered mail. With the $2,000 compensation award and all additional expenses included, WestJet must pay the couple a total of $2,226.92.

title: Colorado man freed after 27 years for infant's murder seeks $2m, but family calls claim a joke
text:
A Colorado man who spent 27 years in prison before his murder conviction over the death of a four-month-old girl was overturned has filed a claim seeking about $1.9 million in state compensation. The baby's family has strongly opposed the request, calling it "a joke". Stephen Martinez was released in April 2026 after a Denver judge overturned his 2000 first-degree murder conviction. According to The Denver Post, Martinez has now filed a petition under Colorado's wrongful conviction compensation law, seeking around $1.9 million for the years he spent behind bars. Denver publication Westword reported that relatives of the baby, Heather Mares, strongly object to the payment and have described Martinez's compensation claim as "a joke".
Legal battle over actual innocence
Under a Colorado law introduced in 2013, people who are wrongly convicted of a felony and later cleared can seek $70,000 for every year they spent in prison. They may also qualify for benefits such as healthcare and tuition waivers. Based on Martinez's 27 years in prison, the payment could come close to $2 million. However, having a conviction overturned does not mean someone automatically receives compensation. As Denver television station 9NEWS explained, Colorado's law requires people making a claim to prove in court that they are "actually innocent".
"A court or a jury has to determine that there really was a miscarriage of justice and that they had no role at all – entire innocence – as it relates to the crime in question," 9NEWS legal analyst Scott Robinson said. Martinez's lawyers say new medical evidence supports his claim that he had no role in the baby's death. Attorney Jeanne Segil, assistant director of the Korey Wise Innocence Project at the University of Colorado Law School, told The Denver Post that the petition is based on updated medical findings.
"We are bringing this petition under the compensation statute because Stephen Martinez is actually innocent," Segil said. "What happened here was a tragedy, but it was not a crime. The medical experts in the case are all clear the baby died from natural causes. Stephen did not cause her death."
The 1998 death and 2000 conviction
The case began on 17 November 1998, when Martinez called 911 from his home in Denver. He reported that four-month-old Heather Mares, the daughter of his then-girlfriend, was choking. According to accounts reported by The Denver Post, Martinez told paramedics that he had given the baby a bottle because she was crying. He said he then put her down and went into another room. A few minutes later, he heard her choking and returned to find her in distress. Emergency workers were unable to save her.
Hospital examinations and later investigations found that Heather had a skull fracture, bleeding in her brain, swelling and burst blood vessels in her eyes. Prosecutors argued that these injuries showed she had been violently shaken. Martinez was convicted of first-degree murder in 2000. According to Law Week Colorado, Martinez was the first person sentenced under a Colorado law that made life in prison without the possibility of parole mandatory for the offence.
Why the murder conviction was overturned
Martinez's conviction remained in place for more than 25 years. That changed after lawyers from the Korey Wise Innocence Project, working with pro bono attorneys from law firm Stinson LLP, independent counsel Seth Temin and volunteer law students, filed a petition to reopen the case. In April 2026, Denver District Attorney John Walsh agreed to overturn the conviction after reviewing updated medical evidence. The new findings suggested that the baby had died from severe pneumonia rather than abuse.
At the time of Martinez's release, Walsh said the investigators and prosecutors involved in the original case had relied on the medical knowledge available to them in 2000. "This is simply an example of the criminal justice system being willing and able to reassess a case when necessary," Walsh said. Perry Glantz, a partner at Stinson LLP and a board member of the innocence project, criticised the beliefs behind the original prosecution in an interview with Law Week Colorado.
"What was wrong about Shaken Baby Syndrome was it was almost more of a belief system than a scientific reality," Glantz said. "They're like, well, he was the only one there. It has to be him. There was really no investigation."
Release from prison and next steps
When Martinez left the Lindsey Flanigan Courthouse in Denver on 21 April 2026, relatives and his wife were waiting for him. He had married his wife while in prison. Both of his parents had died during the 27 years he spent serving his sentence. "I'm so happy and so thankful to be out after being locked up for 27 years, innocent," Martinez told CBS News outside the courthouse. "But now I'm going out to absolutely nothing. But God bless you, guys, have a great day."
Martinez's compensation petition is now before the court. A judge must decide whether he meets Colorado's strict legal test for actual innocence before he can receive any money from the state. Having his murder conviction overturned was a major step, but the compensation claim requires a separate legal decision.

title: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
text:
A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.
The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the health ministry.
State media reported that the fire broke out when the fuel truck overturned. The stretch of the highway where it occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, the health ministry said.
At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene.
Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic as the road was blocked after the accident, saw the fuel truck and many cars on fire. He said he saw at least eight bodies being removed from burned cars.
“It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire,” he said, describing the fear and panic that followed. “It was a shocking scene.”
The Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.
The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.
Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.
In January, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
text:
A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.
The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.
The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.
Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.
“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”
Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.
One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”
Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.
Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.
Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.
Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.
A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
text:
The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.
Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.
In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.
Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC. He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.
A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.
The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”
She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.
Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”
A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”
Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.
Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”
She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.
Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.
Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
text:
When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.
“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”
The Kremlin-controlled forces and their Malian allies were facing a coordinated surprise assault by the al-Qaida-linked JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), whose fighters used suicide car bombs and drones to break through the city’s defences.
Leaked Russian state records suggest the losses were heavy that day. Death certificates of Russian fighters killed in Mali, held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, were obtained by the hacker groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow and analysed by the Guardian.
The records show that 43 Russians died in Mali on 25 April, including six in Kidal and one in nearby Aguelhok. Others were recorded as dying in the capital, Bamako, and in Gao, where rebels shot down a Russian military helicopter that day.
By the following morning, the Russians had abandoned Kidal, which Russian mercenaries had helped capture in November 2023 and which Moscow had since held up as a showcase of its growing influence in Africa.
In all, the records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026, most of which the Guardian was able to link to known battles with rebel groups.
The figures offer a previously unseen glimpse into the human cost of Moscow’s efforts to prop up Mali’s military junta, in what has become Russia’s largest military deployment in Africa.
Two western officials who have travelled to Mali and were shown the data said the death toll was higher than previously estimated.
“That’s over 10% of Russia’s forces killed in action,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.
Moscow does not publish its losses in Africa, and its foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The Wagner private military group, led by the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin, first arrived in Mali in late 2021, a year after a military coup had toppled President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. French forces were ordered to leave the country as relations with the junta deteriorated, bringing an end to France’s decade-long counter-terrorism operation and leaving Russia as the regime’s main foreign protector.
Wagner handed over its operations in Mali to the Africa Corps in June 2025, two years after Prigozhin led a failed mutiny on Moscow that discredited the group in the eyes of the Kremlin. By that summer, British intelligence estimated that about 2,000 Africa Corps personnel were deployed in the country.
The Africa Corps, closely overseen by Russian military intelligence, currently provides backing to several African governments in return for payment or lucrative contracts granting access to natural resources.
Despite the Russian presence, Mali’s security situation has continued to deteriorate. In late July 2024, Russian and Malian forces fought Tuareg separatists for several days near Tinzaouaten, on the Algerian border.
Wagner at the time issued a rare statement admitting losses, including the death of a commander, but gave no figure. Estimates from Russian sources ranged from about 20 to more than 80 dead.
The Rosstat records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July 2024, all but one of them in the Kidal region. The figures make the battle of Tinzaouaten the deadliest single day for Russian forces in Africa since Wagner mercenaries first deployed to the continent in 2017.
The toll in Mali may have been driven up by Ukraine, which has extended its war against Russia to the Sahel. Kyiv has been assisting Tuareg rebels there, according to two people with knowledge of the operations. CNN has reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed to Mali to help local rebel forces fighting Russian troops.
The records are probably an undercount. Registration often lags, and no Russian deaths in Mali are recorded for March 2026 although at least three Africa Corps fighters were reported killed in an ambush near Nampala that month.
The leaked data also sheds light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa. Central African Republic, where Wagner fighters guard the president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, accounts for 30 deaths. While not all could be linked to known incidents, three men died on the night drones struck Wagner camps in Kaga-Bandoro in December 2023.
In Libya, where Russian forces back the eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and use his airbases as a supply route to their deployments in the Sahel, some of the recorded deaths were probably linked to a helicopter crash at the Maaten al-Sarra base in February 2026. On Sunday, Ukrainian drones sunk a Russian warship off the coast of Libya; it is unclear whether there were any casualties.
In Niger, where Russia’s Africa Corps moved in after the military junta expelled French and US troops, a Russian fighter died two days after Islamic State militants attacked Niamey airport in January, a previously unreported casualty.
Moscow has in recent months stepped up its effort to show it is back in control in Mali. On 6 October, Malian troops and the Africa Corps recaptured Kidal after what the army called an air and ground campaign.
A report this month by the US-based Conflict Insights Group (CIG) found that the Africa Corps had sharply increased its use of drones in Mali, including Lancet suicide drones, amid an intensifying air campaign.
The group wrote that the drone campaign had also targeted civilians, boostering support for the rebels. “Civilian deaths in the intensified air campaign, which the Africa Corps leads, are likely to aid insurgent recruitment,” it said.
 
A western diplomat who works in the region said the attacks in late April had punctured the image of Russian military invincibility that Moscow and the junta had cultivated among Malians.
“Russia still wields considerable influence in Mali, but patience with its military performance is wearing thin.”

title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
text:
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.
Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.
In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.
The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The Institute for the Study of War said the Merkury had stopped over for several days, under a cooperation agreement, to refuel and resupply as it escorted Russian cargo ships that could carry military supplies en route to Russia.
The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.
At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.
Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts to use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.
More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The confirmation that Ukraine was behind the attacks was condemned by the UN-recognised government in Tripoli. It said Libya rejected any foreign military operations on its territory or in its waters.
There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”
Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.
In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.
Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, said Ukraine’s strikes in the Mediterranean “were exceptionally brazen and provocative”.
He added: “The question now is how Russia will retaliate,. Perhaps even more pressing is how the [Hafter] family will respond, given how traumatic the scale of the destruction has been for eastern Libyan authorities.”
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, police say
text:
Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one man police described as a hostage-taker was killed.
Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.
When masked and armed assailants stormed the supermarket at about 8am on Tuesday local time, customers and employees were taken hostage – the president initially said there were 30 hostages, but after the final count, police put the number at about 70.
Many of them could be seen through windows with their hands and feet tied. Ten had already been released over the course of the day.
When, after 17 hours in captivity, the final people were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday, four of the hostage-takers were arrested.
One man was killed, whom De la Espriella and police described as one of the criminals who had allegedly resisted.
“One of the criminals was killed. They were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages; they rejected that opportunity and we acted forcefully,” said De la Espriella in a video posted outside the supermarket – about 6 miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls, which are visited by thousands of tourists every year.
Local media identified the dead man as Haider Muñetón Zapata, 51, whose wife had spent the day searching for him as one of the hostages. She gave an interview to Blu Radio on Tuesday, saying they lived near the supermarket and that he had gone there to buy buñuelos, a type of fried dough ball, before picking her up to take her to work, but had stopped responding to her WhatsApp messages at 8.12am.
Zapata reportedly had no criminal record. Cartagena’s mayor, Dumek Turbay, told local media that when special forces stormed the supermarket, Zapata had allegedly resisted and attacked one of the officers, prompting police to shoot him dead.
In a video released shortly after the operation, De la Espriella described the police action as “extraordinary”, speaking with a gun tucked into his waistband, as he has done on several other public occasions as part of his populist tough-on-crime rhetoric.
The president arrived in Cartagena late on Tuesday afternoon from Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he had been dealing with the aftermath of another attack on Monday night, when a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).
De la Espriella, however, denied that the supermarket hostage-taking had been carried out by a “terrorist group”, as he describes the groups involved in Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict, saying instead that those responsible were common criminals.
The president said they had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle but, after being spotted by private security – who then alerted police – they took refuge in the supermarket.
As the lengthy negotiations continued into the night, police used water cannon to disperse dozens of onlookers who had gathered outside the supermarket.
Cartagena’s mayor said that when police stormed the supermarket, some of the hostage-takers tried to blend in with the hostages by removing their hoods and changing out of their black clothes into civilian clothing.
According to Turbay, police then had to screen the hostages before eventually identifying the four who were arrested.
Supermarket employee Héctor Puello, who was taken hostage, told Caracol Radio that he had started his shift in the store’s bakery about two and a half hours before the gunmen arrived.
“First of all, I felt like I had come back to life because those armed men were mistreating us,” he said.
Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, said that when he realised what was happening, he hid inside a cold-storage room with four other employees. “After four hours, we couldn’t stand the cold any longer and came out,” he said, at which point they were captured and taken hostage.
Commenting on the rescue operation, De la Espriella said his government was acting out of “the need to defend our people and go after all the criminals with an iron fist”.
The daylong hostage siege took place on a symbolic day for security in Colombia: the 10th anniversary of the country’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas.
In office for just over three months, the president – previously a lawyer and businessman – is a fierce critic of the peace deal and has focused his government on returning to a strategy of full-on confrontation with criminal groups, breaking completely with the “total peace” plan of his predecessor, the leftist Gustavo Petro.
Although some indicators show slight improvements in areas such as homicides and kidnappings, recent days have been marked by a strong response from criminal groups: in addition to the car bombing, another guerrilla group carried out the first-ever drone attack on a departmental capital on Monday.
On Tuesday night, five departments were left without electricity, and De la Espriella said criminals used explosives to bring down power pylons.
“These criminal acts constitute the response of terrorist groups to the forceful offensive being carried out by the national government to restore order and security across the country,” he said.

title: Lululemon founder stuns Canadian women’s leadership conference with sexist comments
text:
The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand, in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference.
Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it aims to create space for “candid conversations about the barriers women face both in business and society”.
Wilson’s talk on 23 November, titled “Little Black Stretchy Pants” after his memoir, was billed as an “intimate, fireside chat” offering insight into the “mind and instincts of the man himself”. It was moderated by Nuvyn Peters, CEO of Axis Connects.
There is no publicly available video of the event, but the Guardian spoke with people who attended it and reviewed social media posts from those present. Outrage over the event was first reported by the Globe and Mail.
According to people who were there, Wilson told the audience that companies would be reluctant to hire a 22-year-old woman because she might become pregnant at 23 and take maternity leave. He went on to suggest that women were waiting too long to have children, prompting men to import brides from Thailand.
“There were audible gasps in the room and everyone was clearly uncomfortable. It was a mix of disengaging, walking out and also just complete shock of what was being said on stage,” one person said.
“I am floored that Axis gave this man a platform. We all were saying before the event it was surprising he was there – and it’s clear that [Wilson] runs in the organizer’s circles after she opened with the fact that they go on walks [at a Vancouver mountain] together.”
The event, which was supposed to run for an hour, was cut short at 45 minutes.
The remarks are not the first time Wilson has attracted criticism for his comments about women and their bodies. He stepped down as chair of Lululemon’s board in 2013 after the company’s signature black yoga pants were criticized for being see-through and Wilson blamed the problem on the body types of some customers.
On Monday, he reportedly told the group that those prior comments about body types had been “misconstrued” and said he was referring to women who wear sizes that are too small.
Wilson, who is believed to be worth more than C$6bn, has not had a leadership role at Lululemon for several years but remains a major shareholder.
He also reportedly told the audience that poverty had largely been eradicated, and that he was looking forward to going to space with Elon Musk.
Audience members also said Wilson suggested that men were better suited to helm clothing companies that catered to women, because they knew what looked good on women’s bodies. He said the same was true of women who lead companies focused on men’s fashion.
“We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the Leadership Forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects,” Peters said in a statement. “We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community. His comments also underscore an uncomfortable reality: attitudes and assumptions that hold women back in the workplace and in leadership have not disappeared. Challenging those attitudes is central to the work and ethos of Axis Connects.”
Wilson’s spokesperson pointed to the work the Lululemon founder has done to mentor and “empower” women in leadership roles over the years and said his efforts “speak for themselves”. A number of women who were early employees of the company and worked closely with Wilson became millionaires when the company went public, he has previously noted in his memoir, and have gone on to found their own businesses.
More than 700 women attended the conference, many representing organizations they worked for. One person said the experience left her “irate”, adding that it was also indicative of what women continued to tolerate.
“It’s just sad that this is what women still have to deal with, in a forum literally for women.”

title: Colombia’s president arrives at scene of supermarket hostage siege in tourist city
text:
Colombia’s president has arrived at the scene of an hours-long standoff between security services and gunmen holding at least 20 people hostage inside a supermarket in Cartagena, a popular tourist city.
Abelardo de la Espriella’s motorcade arrived in Cartagena on Tuesday night, Agence France-Presse reported, where he will ostensibly take control of an operation involving scores of officers, the navy and special forces.
About 30 people were initially seized by the armed men early on Tuesday morning, but by nightfall, 10 hostages – five of them elderly women – had been released, police said.
There have been no reports of injuries so far.
Before arriving in Cartagena, the rightwing president said that, despite the context of growing violence perpetrated by criminal groups involved in the country’s decades-long armed conflict, the hostage-taking appeared to have stemmed from a botched robbery carried out by “common criminals”.
The past few days have been particularly challenging in the South American country, with a car bomb and a drone attack killing one person and leaving nearly 30 injured.
The supermarket where the hostages are being held is just six miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls overlooking the Caribbean. Hundreds of thousands of visitors are drawn to Cartagena every year.
The gunmen reportedly arrived at about 8.30am local time at an Éxito supermarket in La Castellana neighbourhood and, according to Colombia’s president, the group planned to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle that was due to collect the previous day’s takings from the store.
After spotting the movement on security cameras, employees reportedly alerted the national police, who surrounded the supermarket.
“My son is there,” Jacob Pérez, the father of one of the workers reportedly held hostage, told Agence France-Presse. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him,” he said.
Customers were also believed to be among the hostages. The five people initially released were “older women”, according to De la Espriella.
Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the supermarket, while local media outlets showed snipers positioned on nearby buildings in what appeared to be a standoff between the armed men and police.
De la Espriella, known for his populist rhetoric and an “iron fist” approach to crime – he sometimes wears a gun on his waist and has posed beside the bodies of people killed by police – has been in office for just over three months, and said the hours-long standoff at the supermarket “will turn out well for the hostages, but I’m not so sure it will turn out quite so well for the hostage-takers”.
He addressed the case at a press conference in Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he was dealing with the aftermath of an attack on Monday night in which a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).
“Narco-terrorism is desperate because we are confronting it decisively. It intends to intimidate us and force us to retreat in search of another false peace process,” the president said, referring to the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc – the 10th anniversary of whose signing was on Tuesday.
Internationally recognised for substantially reducing violence, the deal alone could not bring the decades-long armed conflict to a definitive end. Subsequent administrations were slow to implement the agreement, which was rejected by Farc dissidents and other rebel factions.
In the early hours of Monday, in another part of the country, gunmen believed to belong to the ELN, an armed group that never signed a peace deal, used drones to drop bombs on the local police command in the city of Cúcuta. Instead they hit homes and injured three civilians, including an 18-month-old baby.
Although drone attacks by criminal groups have become increasingly common, it was the first time they had targeted a departmental capital.

title: Kilmar Ábrego García, man at center of Trump deportation battle, leaves US
text:
Kilmar Ábrego García has left the United States of his own volition, his lawyers confirmed on Tuesday, with the Department of Homeland Security confirming that he was travelling to Spain.
A source close to Ábrego said Madrid was his first stop but that it would not be his final destination.
The Salvadorian immigrant was at the center of a months-long legal battle since he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 by the Trump administration, in defiance of a court’s protection. He was held in Cecot, a notorious mega-prison.
He was ultimately returned to the US after a decision by the supreme court three months later. Since then, Ábrego has been fighting a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials.
The Washington Post reported earlier on Tuesday that he negotiated a deal with federal authorities to depart the US voluntarily in order to avoid being forcibly removed.
In a statement, the US senator Chris Van Hollen, who has advocated for Maryland resident Ábrego and who met with him in El Salvador last year, described him as a “free man” and referenced Ábrego’s agreement with the Trump administration.
“While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said. “I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution.”
The 31-year-old has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.
He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadorian prison in what an official later called an “administrative error”. Facing public pressure and a court order, the Trump administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the justice department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Ábrego for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia.
“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” one of Ábrego’s attorneys, Sean Hecker, said in a statement provided to the Washington Post. “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
Additional reporting by Ashifa Kassam in Madrid and the Associated Press

title: Canada says it ‘does not report to the US’ after Pentagon criticizes military spending
text:
Canada is a “sovereign nation” that does not “report” to the United States, the country’s defense minister said after the Pentagon released a scathing memo that criticized the supposedly “atrophied” defence capabilities of its northern neighbour.
The document, released on Tuesday, said Canada had “yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs” necessary to meet previous defence spending pledges and become a “credible partner in the defense of our shared continent”.
The Pentagon memo said it took Canada nearly two decades to finally reach spending promises made in 2006 “despite Canada’s role as a major G7 economy as well as one of the largest and wealthiest members of the NATO alliance”.
Historically, Nato members have fallen short of meeting the security organization’s funding goals. When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, only three Nato members – the US, the UK and Greece – were meeting the alliance’s guideline of spending 2% of GDP on defence. By 2025, all 31 members with armed forces, including Canada, had reached the goal.
The document also suggested Canada faces significant operational hurdles in its air, land and sea operations, blaming political leaders for pursuing “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization”.
The Pentagon document said the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military, suggesting American taxpayers had been “footing the bill for its defense” for decades.
The defense minister, David McGuinty, told reporters he could not “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s decision to criticise Canada’s defence spending now.
“The amount of cooperation we are pushing under Norad [North American Aerospace Defense Command] has not changed. What we’re doing together at Nato has not changed. Our military-to-military cooperation has not changed. Our work on integrated air missile defence has not changed,” he said.
McGuinty also bristled at the suggestion from a reporter that the memo implied Canada required approval from the US when it came to its spending plans.
“Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States,” he said.
The memo came as a Canadian official travelled to Europe to pitch a new defence bank championed by the prime minister, Mark Carney.
Isabelle Hudon, Canada’s lead negotiator for establishing the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, is looking to cajole more countries into joining a global initiative that would lend to governments and contractors at low cost to support defense projects.
Ten countries have pledged their support but no others from the G7 have done so yet, with both the UK and Germany so far declining to join. Hudon says the €4bn in commitments secured so far is enough to start the bank up but she is aiming for up to €100bn.
Carney has made significantly increased spending commitments in defence. The country spent $63.4bn on national defence in 2025, meeting its Nato pledge to spend 2% of gross domestic product for the first time.
Last year, Nato members agreed to raise the goal to the equivalent of 5% of GDP by 2035.
Canada’s federal budget this month laid out a plan to spend about 4% of Canada’s GDP on defence and security annually by the end of the decade, and 5% by 2035, including the purchase of submarines and early warning aircraft.
Canada’s air power is a key point of friction with Washington. Carney’s government has yet to make a final decision on its order of F-35 fighter jets from the US firm Lockheed Martin and is weighing the possibility of purchasing Swedish-made Gripen aircraft instead. The multibillion-dollar purchase has been the subject of a political review for more than a year. The Pentagon memo warned that operating a “mixed fleet” of aircraft would “compound existing personnel shortfalls”.

title: ‘Trapped in grief’: wife of Japanese journalist detained by Russia pleads for his release
text:
The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release.
Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east.
Russian authorities alleged that Imai had been “conducting espionage activities” on the island, collecting information about Russian defence capabilities he intended to pass on to Japanese intelligence. Both the newspaper and Japan’s prime minster, Sanae Takaichi, have denied the claims.
His detention has inflamed tensions between Tokyo and Moscow and prompted Takaichi to request Imai’s release during a meeting with the Russian leader Vladimir Putin at last week’s Apec summit in China.
The arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over islands in the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido – which Russia has administered since the dying days of the second world war.
In a statement released to media organisations through the Hokkaido Shimbun, Imai’s wife, Nozomi Imai, said her husband’s plight meant his family were “trapped in grief”.
“Since his detention, his parents and I have spent every day worrying about him” she said in the statement, published in Japanese, English and Russian. Recalling the moment she saw TV footage of her husband being taken away by Russian authorities, she said: “I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart.”
She added: “No one could remain calm after seeing a beloved family member with his arms bound behind his back. In the video, I could even see the souvenirs in his suitcase – the gifts he was bringing home for us. I could not sleep even for a moment that night. When morning came, it still did not feel real. I could not even cry.”
Imai, 34, has barely seen his infant daughter, who was born during his posting to Russia. “He had been so looking forward to coming home,” Nozomi Imai wrote. “During his posting, our daughter was born. She is now 21 months old, and he loves her more than words can say. He had even said excitedly that he wanted to be the one to pick her up from daycare on the very day he got home.”
Japanese diplomats have been permitted to visit Imai only twice since he was detained, although he has had several meetings with lawyers appointed by his employer.
Japan’s ambassador to Moscow, Akira Muto, said he had met the journalist at Lefortovo detention centre in Moscow this week and that he appeared to be in good health. Japanese embassy officials were also granted access to Imai at the end of October.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai had been engaged in “ordinary news gathering” on Sakhalin, adding the newspaper did “not conduct reporting or gather information based on government directions”.
Shortly after his arrest, Takaichi denied Imai had been spying. “There is no such fact,” she told reporters, adding that “the protection of Japanese nationals is extremely important right now, and we intend to focus our efforts on that.”
Concerns are growing that Moscow will seek to make an example of Imai in protest at Japan’s support for sanctions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russia’s Federal Security Service, which is investigating Imai, has not commented publicly since it announced the reporter’s arrest. His detention is scheduled to expire on 12 December but could be extended, the Kyodo news agency said.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai, whose grandfather was born on Sakhalin, was an admirer of Russian culture who had used his position to promote grassroots exchanges.He even hosted Russian visitors at his home in the Hokkaido city of Nemuro.
Nozomi Imai, who said she and her husband had met as students through their shared love of Russian films and novels, said his detention was taking a toll on his ageing parents.
“They worry whether they will ever see their beloved only son again in their lifetime,” she wrote. “Yuki Imai is not only a journalist. He is a beloved son, husband, and father. Please – please return this precious papa to his little daughter.”

title: Trump tariff threat ‘unacceptable’, says Brazil, as China denounces levies as baseless
text:
Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.
Brazil’s government said on Wednesday: “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.
It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.
Brazil was particularly singled out for in the announcement after trade talks stalled. The Trump administration claimed on Wednesday that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries.
The new tariffs are being imposed under a law which allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”
The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.
China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. The US said China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%. The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was a source of excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.
“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”
Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.
