China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”
Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.
It added it was “preparing and submitting rebuttal comments on the preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions and allegations made by interested parties.”
In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in any sector, adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.
Taiwan was also singled out for new tariffs, but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing 15% tariff rate.
Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech product which account for over 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.
Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, and Thailand.
Tokyo’s top government spokesman, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.
Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.
However Democratic Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”
With Associated Press and Reuters

title: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations
text:
China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.
Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.
Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.
On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart that Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.
Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.
Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian: “Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking. Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket.
“There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”
Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites, and a Pakistani-built rover is due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.
Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.
Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he trained for seven months in Beijing, including taking intensive Chinese-language classes.
At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging but that the effort had paid off.
Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to Earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to reach another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronaut.
Beijing’s accelerated achievements in the skies have spooked its rivals. China is the third country to put humans in orbit and it has landed robotic rovers on Mars and the moon, where it hopes to send crewed missions within the next decade.
In racing to the moon before 2030, Beijing is competing with the US’s Artemis programme. The US has excluded China from the ISS since 2011, banning Nasa from collaborating with Beijing. In 2025, Nasa went further by blocking Chinese citizens from its facilities altogether.
US lawmakers have moved to try to extend the life of the ISS, citing China’s “permanent human presence in low Earth orbit” through Tiangong. Progress on turning that proposal into law has been slow. Nasa has said that after the ISS it will be “one of many customers in a robust commercial marketplace in low Earth orbit”.
The ISS was heralded as a symbol of post-cold war cooperation, but renewed cooperation with Russia seems “unlikely”, said Andrew Jones, a journalist specialising in China’s space programme.
While Tiangong is smaller than the ISS, China is understood to be preparing to double its size, “likely with the end of the ISS in mind”, Jones added. “These developments could allow China to expand its international engagement, and potentially space tourism. With the ISS nearing the end of its life and the future of western commercial space stations uncertain, China could for a time have the only permanently crewed outpost in low Earth orbit.”
China has long signalled its interest in developing Tiangong as an international hub. China Manned Space Agency documents published in coordination with the UN outline “resources for international cooperation” onboard the station. European and Chinese astronauts previously trained together with a view to a visit to Tiangong, but that cooperation ended for political and budgetary reasons, Jones said.
Curcio said he would expect countries such as Brazil and Egypt to seek out opportunities to send astronauts on Chinese missions. He added: “I think when the ISS is retired, if there is no western replacement (government or commercial), then yes, we may eventually see European or other ISS-involved countries – like Russia – send astronauts to Tiangong.”

title: UK embassy in Japan warns of rise in drink spiking and credit card fraud at Tokyo bars
text:
The British embassy in Tokyo has launched a social media campaign warning visitors to exercise caution after a rise in cases of drink-spiking and credit card fraud against tourists in the Japanese capital.
In a recent clip made in conjunction with the embassy, the British rapper and manga artist Shao Dow, a frequent visitor to Japan, notes that although the country “is incredibly safe, that doesn’t mean you can let your guard down”.
He warns that young male tourists are particularly susceptible to being lured into bars on the promise of being able to chat to attractive, English-speaking women. They are then served drug-laced drinks and enormous sums are charged to their credit cards.
Drink-spiking cases involving British and other international tourists have been on the rise in the past two years in popular nightlife districts such as Roppongi, Shibuya and Kabukicho.
Some victims have lost up to £30,000 (US$39,000) in a single night, Dow says, and wake up with no memory of what happened. “Look, do me a favour,” he adds, “Stay alert, trust your gut, keep an eye on your stuff and don’t follow strangers into bars.”
Police in Tokyo have come under pressure to tackle the rise in incidents targeting tourists. Earlier this month, 160 riot police conducted predawn raids on two establishments in Kabukicho after reports they had ripped off customers. Five people were arrested.
Between January and October, police recorded 340 cases – up 195 from last year – in the Shinjuku area after customers, some of whom were lured into bars by street touts, were charged extortionate sums. In one case, ¥9.6m ($60,000) was allegedly charged to a customer’s credit card.
According to the newspaper Asahi Shimbun, victims have paid ¥390m in total and foreign nationals had been the targets in 70% of cases. The newspaper quoted a senior investigator as saying the reported crimes were the “tip of the iceberg” since many visitors returned home before they realised they had been swindled, while others had left Japan without reporting the incidents to police.
Reports say the rise in cases was being fuelled by Japan’s tourism boom. A record 42.7 million people visited Japan last year, including 530,000 from the UK.
The Guardian has approached the Japan National Tourism Organisation for comment.

title: China misusing Interpol to target dissidents, says leading UK lawyer
text:
China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading British lawyer has claimed, as Hong Kong prepares to host the police organisation’s general assembly for the first time.
Ben Keith, a specialist in “red notices” - the Interpol system under which national authorities are requested to locate and detain suspects - said he was working on five cases involving China making questionable requests through Interpol.
He revealed that he had also contacted officials at the law enforcement organisation in July on behalf of a group of five high-profile UK-based Chinese dissidents to find out if Beijing had sought the issuance of red notices relating to them.
Interpol responded in October that they were looking into his request for information but there had been no substantive information shared, he added, raising concerns that there might be data relating to the individuals on the Interpol system.
He said: “If there’s no data, than they will tell me there’s no data. If there is data, then they have to get permission from Hong Kong to tell me. It has been sometime now. Given the profile of these individuals, I think they may have had some data on them. That’s the fear.”
Many Hong Kong democracy campaigners who fled to the UK in recent years have British national (overseas) status but this does not protect them from red notices outside the UK and potential extradition to China.
A red notice is a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action. It is based on an arrest warrant or court order issued by the judicial authorities in the requesting country. Member countries apply their own laws in deciding whether to arrest a person.
Keith said: “The Russian playbook was to accuse political opponents or business opponents of some sort of really technical criminal offence of fraud, employment law breach, regulatory offence, that sort of thing, to disguise the real purpose of the request. The Chinese have taken that on.”
Hong Kong will host the 94th Interpol general assembly between 30 November and 3 December, attracting police chiefs from its 196 member countries to set global policing policy, approve budgets and activities, and pass binding resolutions.
Keith said that hosting the assembly offered an opportunity for China to “reputation wash”, arguing that Beijing ran a sophisticated public relations machine to hide the high proportion of red notice and extradition requests that were politically motivated.
The red notice system is used by China to target those sought under the state campaigns launched under President Xi Jinping to track down fugitives overseas and recover illicit funds, known as Operations Fox Hunt and Sky Net, it is claimed.
A new report, The Red Notice Trap, by Ben Keith and Rhys Davies of the legal firm IHR Advisors, draws on court judgments, Interpol records and Chinese-language official documents, to show how red notices fit into Beijing’s campaign to silence critics and bring them home for persecution.
It notes under a 2025 revision of the implementing regulations for the People’s Repubilc of China’s supervision law that red notice requests sit with extradition, judicial assistance, law enforcement cooperation, prosecution abroad, asset seizure and ‘ideological education’, as tools for the recovery of people.
Among the cases cited in the IHR Advisors report is that of Yidiresi Aishan – a Uyghur activist who is also known as Idris Hassan – who was arrested in July 2021, when arriving at Casablanca airport on a flight from Turkey, where he had been living.
He was detained on the basis of a red notice issued by Interpol at China’s request “for belonging to a terrorist organisation”. Within two weeks, Interpol suspended the notice as it breached its rules and it was later cancelled.
The Moroccan extradition proceedings carried on regardless and in December 2021 the country’s court of cassation approved Hasan’s surrender to China.
The UN committee against torture found that Hasan’s extradition would breach article 3 of the convention against torture and Morocco did not carry out the extradition But Hasan remained in detention until 12 February 2025 after spending nearly four years in prison on the basis of an Interpol red notice.
“His case shows the central weakness this report returns to: Interpol can correct its own data, but it cannot undo what national authorities have already set in motion”, the authors write.
Hasan, who now lives in Canada, said he no longer travelled and that his life had been thrown “upside down”.
“Four years of life have gone, just spent in prison, I could not be with my children,” he told the Guardian. “Everything has changed. I cannot describe this. But I trust Canada.”
Hasan added: “I don’t understand how this kind of the big organisation like Interpol how they took my name down without evidence, without nothing. Just put my name out.”
The Chinese embassy has been approached for comment.
An Interpol spokesperson said: “Interpol knows Red Notices are powerful tools for law enforcement cooperation and is fully aware of their potential impact on the individuals concerned, which is why Interpol has a number of systems in place to avoid misuse of our systems, and these have been significantly strengthened over the last few years.
“Interpol’s constitution affirms the Organisation’s neutrality. Under Article 3, Red Notice requests must not be of a predominantly political, military, religious or racial character.”

title: Coalition would privatise Melbourne’s sewage treatment while selling state land and renewables to fund Victorian election promises and cut debt
text:
A Victorian Coalition government would privatise two sewage plants and sell off state-owned land, renewable energy assets and the “air rights” between Richmond train station and the Melbourne Cricket Ground if elected.
The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, released the Liberal and Nationals’ pre-election policy costings on Thursday, just two days before the state election and after more than 1.5 million Victorians have already cast their vote.
Labor, which has been releasing its costings throughout the campaign, also provided its overall budget projections on Thursday, showing a $1bn reduction in the state’s debt, from $196bn in the 2029-30 financial year to $195bn.
Central to the Coalition’s costings is a reduction in capital spending by $14.47bn, including via a $13.6bn “asset recycling” program – a term typically used when a government sells or long-term leases existing public assets.
It includes a 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western treatment plants that process the vast majority of Melbourne’s sewage, run by Melbourne Water, estimated to be worth $9.2bn. The Coalition took a similar proposal to the 2018 and 2022 state elections.
Wilson said there would be “no change” to water bills and the Essential Services Commission would still regulate prices across the sector. She denied the lease was akin to privatisation.
“It’s not a privatisation at all. It’s a long-term lease on the sewage assets,” she said. “At the end of the day, the government will continue to hold the assets.”
“This is about making the responsible and disciplined savings to ensure that we can reduce the debt.”
Wilson also denied it was a broken commitment. In August, when the Australian revealed the Labor government had costed the privatisation of Melbourne Water’s assets, Wilson told ABC News the opposition had “never considered” doing the same.
“We’re not touching it,” she said on 5 August.
Other aspects of the “asset recycling” program is the sale of $1.3bn worth of government-owned land to housing developers and $92m for the air rights between Richmond station and the MCG, on the condition the precinct is “revitalised”.
The Coalition estimates it will also save about $1bn by selling the renewable projects owned by the State Electricity Commission back to the private sector.
The agency was revived as part of a 2022 election commitment by the Andrews Labor government and was later enshrined in the constitution. Wilson said the SEC had a number of services it could continue to provide without being dismantled altogether.
The Coalition has also proposed savings of $5.73bn from drawing down on contingencies – money set aside for “future unexpected programs” – and $1.23bn in deprioritising several planned level crossing removals.
This includes cancelling planned level crossing projects in Brunswick, Parkville, Yarraville and Spotswood, with the latter two requiring a cost of $90m to cancel contracts that have already been signed. Other projects will be delayed to beyond 2030 to further reduce capital spending.
The independent Parliamentary Budget Office has found the Coalition’s plan would lower net debt to $176bn by 2029-30.
Wilson said it would save the state $4.2bn in interest payments.
The costings also reveal plans to scrap international travel allowances for all MPs, saving $3.38m over the forward estimates, as well as $639m in funding to guarantee free kinder, though the Coalition will limit the rollout to 15 hours per week, instead of the proposed 30 hours. The PBO also maintains it will cost nothing to pause and review the Suburban Rail Loop.
Beyond the new measures, the Coalition has already announced a public service hiring freeze that Wilson said would save $23bn over a decade, including $5.7bn over the next four years, which is $1bn more than first estimated by the PBO earlier this year. It has also said it will save $407.6m by scrapping Australia’s first treaty with First Nations people and $578m from the privatisation of the Melbourne Market.
Wilson said it was standard practice to release costings at this point in the campaign.
“Victorians decide when they vote and decide why they vote,” she said.
However, the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, said it was a “bombshell” announcement at the 11th hour of the campaign.
“Our public land, our publicly owned renewable energy and our sewerage infrastructure belong to Victorians. They’re not Jess Wilson and the Liberal party’s to sell off,” Sandell said.
The treasurer, Labor’s Colin Brooks, similarly described the move as a “massive, radical sell-off, all hidden from Victorians until just before the eve of an election”.

title: Australian politics live: Senior Liberal slams Blyth in email to members, saying ‘you gave her your trust, she threw it away’
text:
Senior Liberal slams Blyth in email to party members
The Liberal shadow minister Anne Ruston has issued a scathing statement on former colleague Leah Blyth, claiming her fellow South Australian “put her own interests ahead of” voters.
Ruston, the senior Liberal from SA, said in an email to members that she was “incredibly disappointed” in Blyth’s defection to One Nation. She noted Blyth was “never elected to the Senate seat she holds”, and was instead appointed by the Liberals – the party she just quit – to fill a casual vacancy, and hadn’t faced the ballot box.
“You gave her your trust. Today she threw it away,” Ruston wrote to members.
“South Australians sent a Liberal to Canberra to fight for them. Today, Leah chose to put her own interests ahead of theirs.”
Blyth ‘has shown disloyalty to her leader, party and state’, Wilson says
The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, says his former colleague Leah Blyth’s defection to One Nation is disloyal.
Blyth’s move blindsided Coalition MPs who branded her a “turncoat”, raising further scrutiny of chaos inside the opposition.
Wilson says he discovered the South Australian senator’s move by reading about it “in the newspaper like everyone else”:
I actually just think it’s sad, to be honest.
I think one of the things that conservatives value is loyalty. And we know that Barnaby Joyce, as an example, showed disloyalty to his leader, his party and his community. And now we’ve got Leah Blyth, who has shown disloyalty to her leader, party and state.
About half of Labor’s forecast savings lost in private health deal with Greens, Butler says
The health minister, Mark Butler, has appeared on the ABC where he is asked about the federal government striking a deal with the Greens to carve out all pensioners from its private health insurance rebate changes.
Butler acknowledges the government has lost about half of the $3bn forecast savings to get the legislation passed in the final sitting week of the year.
He says it is “unlikely” to be reconciled in next month’s mid-year budget update:
We need to reconcile that in a future budget update, of course.
In the following budget update, which will be next May, we’ll have to have reconciled that.
Senior Liberal slams Blyth in email to party members
The Liberal shadow minister Anne Ruston has issued a scathing statement on former colleague Leah Blyth, claiming her fellow South Australian “put her own interests ahead of” voters.
Ruston, the senior Liberal from SA, said in an email to members that she was “incredibly disappointed” in Blyth’s defection to One Nation. She noted Blyth was “never elected to the Senate seat she holds”, and was instead appointed by the Liberals – the party she just quit – to fill a casual vacancy, and hadn’t faced the ballot box.
“You gave her your trust. Today she threw it away,” Ruston wrote to members.
“South Australians sent a Liberal to Canberra to fight for them. Today, Leah chose to put her own interests ahead of theirs.”
“It’s the economy, stupid,” was the Coalition’s MO today, trying to corner Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers on inflation, jobs and mortgage rates.
The pair tried to turn the attention back to the Coalition, taking every chance they could to taunt Angus Taylor on Leah Blyth’s defection to One Nation.
There were several bootings out of the chamber today: the Labor MP Rowan Holzberger, before QT even started, Nationals deputy leader, Darren Chester, and Liberal MP Simon Kennedy together, and Labor MP Matt Burnell.
Albanese fired up over a question from the independent MP Kate Chaney over a contentious defence bill that experts have warned could have serious human rights implications.
And independent Rebekha Sharkie asked the aged care minister about unspent funds – he said it was because the sector was slow to respond to additional funding.
Aged care minister asked about unspent budget funds
Back to the crossbench, Rebekha Sharkie asks the aged care minister, Sam Rae, why the government underspent on aged care by $1.4bn in the last financial year, when “more than 190,000 older Australians remain waiting for an assessment or Support at Home, and last year over 6,400 older Australians died while waiting for their approved aged care.
Rae has a long preamble and says Labor has “effectively doubled the size of the aged care budget” since it came to government and that by the end of this financial year, “this homecare system will have tripled in size since 2020”.
He then gets to the meat of the question.
He says the money unspent is a small proportion of the total budget (which this financial year will be $44bn) and was largely due to the sector responding to investing in the sector at a “slow rate”.
The money to which the member’s question pertains, that was not spent through that period, was obviously, as a proportion, a relatively modest part of that, but had to do with the slower rate at which the sector has been able to respond to investments both in the residential space, through challenges in construction particularly, of new residential aged care facilities, as well as the Support at Home system and the rapid increase of places, the workforce challenges making it difficult to respond.
Chalmers says unemployment rise a 'very bad development'
Back to the opposition, the Liberal MP Henry Pike says last month, 43,000 Australians lost their jobs and asks the treasurer, how many Australians are “at risk of losing their job and losing their home?”
Jim Chalmers says the uptick in unemployment last month was “a very bad development”, but defends the government, saying:
We ask those opposite to acknowledge that what we’ve seen under this government is the lowest average unemployment of any government in the last 50 years.
On house prices, he still says they are up about 15% over the past five years.
Even in the context of some serious challenges – inflation, productivity, global volatility – a tick-up in the unemployment rate, what we’ve been reminded of this week, whether it’s dwelling investment or business investment more broadly today, is that we do have a lot coming at us, but we’ve got a lot going for us as well. And if those opposite really cared about confidence in our economy, they’d stop talking the place down.
‘Conspiracy theories and misinformation’: Albanese frustrated by defence bill concerns
Anthony Albanese has fired up over a question by the independent MP Kate Chaney about scrutiny over a controversial defence bill, angrily branding criticisms as “nonsense” and misinformation.
For a recap on the bill, see here:
Chaney says that bill, which “allows ministers to set aside commonwealth, state and territory laws, sometimes without publication, and to declare security zones where failing to follow criminal directions is an offence”, passed with limited parliamentary scrutiny and little time for public submissions. She asks what the minimum amount of scrutiny for such a consequential bill should be.
Albanese quickly starts shouting at Chaney, irritated by the question:
I have seen some nonsense on social media – not from the member for Curtin, but from others – that simply feeds conspiracy theories that don’t just come from the far right, but can come from the far left as well. And what this legislation is about is simply making sure that our defence institutions and infrastructure are kept safe.
And quite frankly, to suggest that a minister would abuse powers in order to designate something that was not associated with defence of this country as somehow needing protection is quite frankly irresponsible, and those spreading that misinformation online should know better.
Chaney tries to make a point of order, saying the question was about minimum scrutiny.
The Labor MP Matt Burnell shouts out, “don’t want to keep Australians safe”, and promptly gets kicked out of the chamber.
Treasury and RBA not forecasting recession, Chalmers says
Staying on the economy, the Nationals MP David Batt says Gerry Harvey, the chair of major retailer Harvey Norman, has warned recession is inevitable and asks the treasurer if he will “guarantee Australia will not go into recession”.
The Labor benches laugh as Batt mentions Harvey, forcing him to ask the question twice.
Harvey has previously been critical of Labor and was criticised for repaying just $6m of the $22m in jobkeeper payments Harvey Norman received during Covid, after it posted record profits in the 2020-21 financial year.
Jim Chalmers says more seriously that he respects Harvey, but tries to stick it to the Coalition, accusing the opposition of wanting the economy to fail, to score a political win.
When it comes to the prediction that [Harvey] has made – and there are a range of predictions, a range of opinions – all I can say … is that neither the Treasury nor the Reserve Bank forecasts have the Australian economy going backwards.
I know that’s a matter of great disappointment to those opposite, because those opposite desperately want the Australian economy to fail, because they see that as the only way that they might succeed.
‘Stop talking the Australian economy down’: Chalmers under pressure over inflation numbers
The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, is next and asks if the prime minister, who yesterday said Australia’s inflation rate is at least better than the Philippines, can “identify a single major advanced economy with a higher core inflation rate than Australia?”
Jim Chalmers takes the question (cue groans from the Coalition benches) and says broadly, “inflation is going up around the world”.
Around the world, I think every major advanced economy, from memory, has seen inflation go up in October.
But Chalmers won’t name any countries – other than the Philippines.
Wilson tries to bring Chalmers back on track, making a point of order on relevance, which Milton Dick isn’t having.
Chalmers goes for the jugular.
I hear the leader of the opposition interjecting. He’s very mouthy for someone who lost a shadow minister, Mr Speaker. Stop talking the Australian economy down.
Chalmers defends budget: ‘I won’t be taking lectures on budget responsibility from those opposite’
The Nationals MP Jamie Chaffey doesn’t bother asking the government this time how much more mortgage holders are paying than when the Albanese government was first elected.
Chaffey says, after 17 interest rate rises, the average new mortgage holder is more than $30,000 a year worse off, and asks the treasurer to admit “he has broken the economy” and apologise to households.
Jim Chalmers says he acknowledges the extra pressure that interest rate rises put on households.
He then pivots, taking a shot at the Coalition, accusing opposition MPs of wanting to “talk about budget repair – they like to talk about responsible economic management. They just don’t like to vote for it.”
You know what they did when inflation was north of 6% and roaring? They had a net spend in their last budget of $40bn. And you know how many saves they had in that last budget, Mr Speaker? Absolutely none. So I won’t be taking lectures on budget responsibility from those opposite.
PM urges parliament to support gas reservation scheme
Over to the crossbench, the independent MP Dai Le asks the prime minister if he will support her bill to ensure 30% of goods in commonwealth projects are made in Australia.
The government rarely, if ever, supports crossbench bills.
Anthony Albanese says by that measure, Le should be a fan of the government’s Future Made in Australia program.
“No!” shout a bunch of Coalition MPs.
Albanese says Le and the Coalition should support the gas reservation scheme:
One of the reasons why we have had a domestic gas reservation for the east coast that hopefully will pass the Senate today is because of what that will do – make Australian manufacturing more competitive by making sure that there is a limit on the price of gas, which is absolutely critical for Australian manufacturing.
The government’s dixers have so far been used to talk up the gas reservation scheme and pressure the Coalition to support it.
So far, the Coalition have said they “will not oppose it”.
At the end of a dixer, Pat Conroy finishes his answer with this burn to the Liberals: “Time to get off the fence, otherwise you’re just going to get some splinters.”
Milton Dick then reckons it’s time to thin out the chamber a little. He kicks out deputy Nationals leader, Darren Chester, and Liberal frontbencher Simon Kennedy.
Taylor ‘can’t even run his own frontbench’, Albanese says
Angus Taylor is back to the dispatch box with another tight question: “How much has the cost of the average annual mortgage payment gone up over the last four years?”
Spoiler alert: he won’t get a number.
Anthony Albanese says very broadly that house prices have risen more than 400% since the capital gains tax discount was introduced by the Howard government.
Taylor, obviously unhappy with the answer (or lack thereof) so far, gets up with a point of order and says:
It’s a very specific question – how much has the cost of the average annual mortgage payment gone up over the past year? I’ll give you a hint – it’s over $30,000 a year.
Milton Dick calls that an “abuse” of points of order.
Albanese continues:
He wants to run the country, but he can’t even run his own frontbench, Mr Speaker … We understand why he’s angry.
That’s too far for the manager of opposition business, Dan Tehan, who makes a point of order, and then another point of order when his first isn’t adhered to.
Albanese ends his question continuing his attacks.
Liberal members 'tossing up whether to leave or remain', PM says
The Coalition’s got its focus set on the economy again today, with Angus Taylor asking Anthony Albanese if he can “name a single economic indicator that has gone in the right direction this year”, with inflation and wages going backwards.
The prime minister says employment numbers and the gender pay gap are going in the right direction.
The employment rate – now, there is 14.7 million Australians employed. There were 13.5 million employed when we came to office. So that’s up … The gender pay gap is at a record low, 11.3%. It was 14.2% when we came to office.
He then also tries to take a crack at Leah Blyth’s defection. You can tell his office has spent some time trying to come up with different ways of sticking in the knife:
People are looking at ways in which they could have growth. My friend Andy Burnham in the UK is looking at revisiting Brexit there.
It looks like Liberal members are also tossing up whether to leave or remain.
Before questions even begin, Tony Burke takes the opportunity to have a crack at the Coalition over LeahBlyth’s defection.
Referencing a new frontbench “list” submitted by the Coalition to the house after the shadow home affairs minister Jonno Duniam’s resignation, Burke points out that it’s already out of date.
When there’s a change in the government or the opposition executive, that the new list is tabled. The list that’s been tabled for the opposition includes someone who’s no longer even a member of the Coalition. And so the ordinary practice would be for an updated list to be tabled at the start of question time.
There’s plenty of shouting across the chamber and the Labor MP Rowan Holzberger has just been kicked out.

title: Flinders Island bushfire: Out-of-control fire with flames 10-metres high destroys at least six homes in Tasmania
text:
Residents in the north of Flinders Island in Tasmania have been told to take shelter, as an out-of-control bushfire destroys homes and sends smoke hundreds of kilometres south.
By Thursday midday, the uncontrolled fire involving 10-metre high flames had burned through 14,500 hectares – about 10% of the island – with at least six properties damaged or destroyed and authorities warning more were at risk.
Steve Richardson, the northern deputy regional chief for the TFS, said the fire front was making a “significant run” towards the south-west of the island on Thursday, after “horrendous conditions” on Wednesday made it too dangerous for firefighting crews to get close to the flames.
Emergency services warned residents in the Killicrankie and Mt Killicrankie recreation area it was too late to leave. “You are in danger and need to act immediately to survive,” the warning said, with the fire threatening evacuation routes.
Residents were told to enact their bushfire plan, shelter in a room with clear exits, bring pets inside, and close all doors and windows. Killiecrankie beach was identified as a place of last resort.
Communities in nearby Leeka, Mt Tanner, Mt Boyes, Carnacs Flat and surrounds have been warned it was not safe to return, while a smoke alert was issued for the island and the north-east and east coast of Tasmania.
Parts of the island in the path of the fire contain highly flammable material, which has strengthened the blaze.
“These conditions have made it unsafe for crews to undertake direct firefighting operations in some areas,” Richardson said in a statement.
“The situation is changing quickly, and emergency alerts are being updated regularly.”
Three other areas in the northern part of Flinders Island remain under a watch and act warning, with residents urged to prepare to take shelter or to leave.
Phone service may be disrupted due to impacts to communications systems, but officials said triple zero services were being prioritised.
Weather conditions were expected to deteriorate again on Friday, with strong winds expected.
The Tasmanian premier, Jeremy Rockliff, said there would be government emergency assistance grants for people on the island who had to relocate due to the fires.
Applications for the grants – which included $250 per adult and $125 per child, with a maximum of $1,000 for any one family – would open from 2pm Thursday, Rockliff said in a social media post.
“For those on the frontline fighting the fire, thank you,” Rockliff said. “We could not be more grateful for your efforts.”
Residents on the island, which is about 130,000 hectares in size and home to 900 people, posted photos of massive plumes of smoke on social media.
Mick Grimshaw, a farmer, helped friends move cattle from their property and said they had lost some fences.
“We were under the ashes. Right there. But we’ve got them safe,” he told ABC radio.
“The fire threat for this farm looks like it has abated a bit but certainly not further down the island.
“We can see the smoke front heading right down the guts of the island.”
Nearly 40 firefighters were working to control the bushfire, plus 12 parks and wildlife staff, five helicopters and three aircraft. Nine additional vehicles arrived on Thursday.
Flinders Island is known for high-quality exports, including beef, lamb, wool and seafood.

title: Teen’s homicidal thoughts dismissed as ‘crap’ days before she killed 10-year-old, inquest hears
text:
Two days before a teenager killed a young girl while in the grips of psychosis, her father dismissed her homicidal thoughts, delusions and visions as “crap”, an inquest has been told.
On 6 July 2020, the 14-year-old wrote in her diary: “I’m getting sick and tired of being told I’m a liar when I say I see cat eyes in a dark room and feel like I’m going to kill someone.”
Just 48 hours later, the teenager killed 10-year-old Bridgette “Biddy” Porter at a property in rural NSW.
Biddy, remembered as a clever, creative and kind child, died of multiple injuries while staying at the farm in the school holidays on 8 July 2020.
The details of her death are subject to a non-publication order.
During closing submissions at an inquest on Thursday, the barrister representing Biddy’s parents argued it was unreasonable for the teenager’s parents not to seek urgent help.
“It is open to this court to make findings there were a constellation of symptoms they were aware of,” Tahn O’Rourke told the NSW coroner’s court in Lidcombe on Thursday.
“They were aware they were linked … and that there was a potentially serious mental illness emerging.”
The teenager killed six chickens on the family farm in mid-2019 and subsequently told relatives about hearing voices, experiencing visions and having a sense of not feeling real, the inquest was told.
In the weeks before attacking Biddy, the teenager told her mother she thought about killing people “all the time”, including her parents.
The mother said she did not seek mental health support for the girl because it did not occur to her.
“I never believed in mental health. I didn’t understand mental health, so it didn’t come up to me as something I needed to do,” she told the inquest in June.
The father’s police statement said he told the teenager her visions and violent thoughts were “crap and she was just looking for attention”, O’Rourke said.
The mother sought advice from a naturopath in mid-2020, who told her to go to a GP.
The GP referred the family to a psychiatrist soon before the killing, but didn’t organise urgent care because the mother did not reveal the teenager’s violence or homicidal thoughts, the inquest was told.
That was an “opportunity lost” in preventing harm, O’Rourke said.
Biddy’s killer, who cannot be identified, was charged with murder, but a NSW supreme court judge ruled she was not criminally responsible due to mental illness in 2021.
The teenager, who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and was in acute psychosis at the time of the killing, remains in a forensic facility.
Counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer SC said the actions of the parents should be seen in the context of evidence that early symptoms of schizophrenia can be “vague” and hard to separate from typical teenage behaviour.
Forensic psychiatrist Olav Nielssen gave evidence the girl’s early development of schizophrenia was “extremely rare” and he had never seen a presentation like hers before.
Dwyer said there was a gap in the parents’ understanding.
“[They] were not aware [she] was suffering a serious mental health condition … even if looking back now, it seems so obvious,” Dwyer said.
State coroner Teresa O’Sullivan will hand down findings and recommendations at a later date.
- In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800; adults can seek help at Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380

title: Australia projected to completely miss 2035 emissions target without new climate policies
text:
Australia is nearly on track to reach its 2030 emissions reduction target but will fall massively short of a 2035 target unless the federal government substantially ramps up its climate policies, according to new official projections.
Under existing policies, the country is on track by 2035 to cut climate pollution by only 48% compared with 2005 levels – far below its target reduction of between 62% and 70% by that date, climate department projections suggest.
Australia’s progress towards the 2035 target has not improved since the last projection released a year ago.
In an annual climate statement to parliament on Thursday, the climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, said that while the country was “making good progress, we are facing undeniable headwinds”.
Bowen, speaking after a bruising experience over failed climate talks at Cop31, attacked the Queensland Liberal National government’s decision to “abandon its renewable energy targets and extend the operation of coal-fired power plants”, saying it would “significantly impact” national emissions.
“Continuing to sweat intermittent and unreliable coal just isn’t the answer to the question of our future energy security. And walking back previously approved renewable projects creates uncertainty, which then goes on to jeopardise future renewable investments,” he said. “Our system needs certainty. It does not need sovereign risk.”
The projections suggested Australia’s climate pollution was on track to be 42% below 2005 levels by 2030 – “within reach” of its 43% 2030 emissions reduction target.
However, that forecast assumes the government will reach its goal of 82% of electricity coming from renewable energy nationally by 2030. Several experts say that is unlikely to happen due to delays in the rollout of large-scale wind and farms and new transmission lines.
The department’s assessment said if unforeseen delays and supply chain bottlenecks pushed the 82% target back to 2032, Australia would only cut emissions by only 38% by 2030.
A separate report released on Thursday found that climate pollution fell by 1.3% – 6.2m tonnes – in the year to June. Bowen said this represented “a reduction at one-and-a-half times the rate of the last 10 years”. Australia’s total annual emissions were 25.3% below 2005 levels.
Emissions from generating electricity were down 3.6%, reflecting “record renewables generation and the ongoing displacement of coal and gas”. Gas generation fell by 23.2% and coal generation decreased by 3.6% over the year.
A third report, an annual progress assessment by another government agency, the Climate Change Authority, warned the country’s pace of emissions reduction must “accelerate substantially”. It said achieving the 2030 and 2035 targets would require sustained average annual emissions reductions of about 25m to 30m tonnes.
The authority found transport was approaching a “tipping point”, with electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles accounting for 29% of new light vehicle sales in 2026, up from 13% in 2025. The authority said more responsibility for emissions cuts would shift towards other areas, including “industry, resources, agriculture and other harder-to-abate activities”.
It warned additional action was needed to deal with methane – a potent greenhouse that amplifies global heating over a short time period. It recommended more be done to deploy established technologies, such as detecting and repairing leaks at mining sites and minimising avoidable venting and flaring of fossil fuel gas.
In a reply to Bowen’s climate statement, the shadow energy and emissions reduction minister, Dan Tehan, focused on electricity prices and the Cop31 breakdown – and the cost of free coffee at the Australian pavilion at the summit – rather than addressing the climate crisis.
He said national emissions had increased since Labor was elected in 2022, but did not mention that climate pollution was suppressed in 2022 due to economic shutdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Greens’ deputy leader and climate spokesperson, Steph Hodgins-May, said the government’s rhetoric on climate change “is just so far apart from the action”.
She said the government was basing its climate strategy on further electrification, “while still waving through new coal and gas”.
“They’re telling us they want to take climate action, but [are] simultaneously approving 38 new coal and gas mines,” Hodgins-May said.
The Australian Conservation Foundation’s head of advocacy, Gavan McFadzean, said the government report card showed strong progress in some areas but there was clear room for improvement.
“The renewables build is progressing, but it faces headwinds from uncooperative states and other forces whipping up opposition to wind and solar in rural communities for political purposes,” he said.
McFadzean said Australia’s exported emissions from the burning of coal and gas overseas, totalling 1.1 bn tonnes in 2025-26, “is not in this statement and remains a blind spot”.
“Exported emissions are the biggest handbrake on Australian climate action,” he said. “For Australia to be a positive climate player, we need to phase out exports of coal and gas.”

title: UK to invest £9.5m in Ukraine windfarm to bolster war-hit energy system
text:
Britain will add to its multimillion pound investments in rebuilding Ukraine’s energy system by funding a windfarm project capable of powering 300,000 Ukrainian households.
Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, said Britain would invest £9.5m to build a 200 megawatt windfarm in an undisclosed location to bolster Ukraine’s energy reserves as its war with Russia approaches the five-year mark.
Kyiv believes Moscow’s strikes have destroyed or damaged more than 80% of Ukraine’s prewar power generation capacity, which was mostly fuelled by gas imported from Russia.
The UK government has offered more than £770m to rebuild Ukraine’s power system, which has included emergency support and long-term investments in renewables and nuclear generation to cut the country’s reliance on gas.
Ukraine is estimated to have installed more than 3GW of renewable energy capacity since the 2022 full-scale invasion, or 20% of the country’s installed generation capacity. About a third of that is from wind power.
Miliband said the money would help deliver “major new renewable generation, strengthen Ukraine’s energy independence and support its recovery, while deepening the economic partnership between our two countries”.
The new windfarm is expected to be built and operated by Elementum Energy, a company registered in the UK with offices in London, Kyiv and Odesa.
“While Russia seeks to plunge Ukrainians into darkness, the UK is helping Ukraine build the secure and resilient energy system it needs for the future,” Miliband said.
He set out the plans to help rebuild Ukraine’s electricity infrastructure within days of Moscow’s renewed attacks on the country’s energy system. On Wednesday, Russian strikes on a thermal power plant near Odesa in the south-west of Ukraine led to power, heating and water supply outages in parts of the city.
Ukraine’s largest private energy investor, DTEK, said that attack was the third massive strike against the company’s power plants in November alone as winter temperatures plunge.
DTEK became the first company to build a windfarm in a war zone when it completed the first phase of the Tyligulska project, generating enough clean electricity to power about 200,000 homes just 60 miles from the frontline in the southern region of Mykolaiv in early 2023.
The second phase of the Tyligulska plant was initially scheduled to be completed by the end of 2026.

title: Spain’s election: the end of a leftwing icon? - podcast
text:
He has become an icon of the European left. A great political survivor, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez has been in power for eight years while – across the continent – the right has been on the march.
The Socialist party leader has championed immigration, stood up to Donald Trump and been a notable voice for Palestinians in Gaza.
But on Sunday, Sánchez might be replaced by a conservative government in league with the far right.
Madrid correspondent Sam Jones and European community affairs correspondent Ashifa Kassam report on a pivotal Spanish election, and the gamble that led Sánchez to call it.
Where will this leave the left in Spain, asks Nosheen Iqbal, and across Europe too?

title: Kilmar Ábrego García, target of Trump’s immigration crackdown, lands in Spain after ‘leaving happy’
text:
Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadorian national whose mistaken deportation turned him into a symbol of Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts, has landed in Spain.
Ábrego García arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after leaving the United States of his own volition.
“I feel free of everything evil that has followed me up until this point,” he told reporters on a video call just hours after he touched down. “I’m happy … because this time I’m leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely.”
He added: “The government does not decide where my story continues. My family and I will decide our future.”
Prior to his departure, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents met him at the airport and removed his ankle monitor, according to We Are Casa, a Maryland-based advocacy group.
As he made his way through the Madrid airport, Ábrego García did not speak to reporters, instead raising his fist in the air as he climbed into a waiting van.
Ábrego García became a lightning rod in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador in what an official later called an “administrative error”.
The 31-year-old had been living in the US since 2019, after a judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador due to the dangers posed by a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under ICE supervision, but he was not given residency status.
Married to an American woman, the Maryland resident was part of a group of more than 200 people sent by the US to Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison, in violation of the US immigration judge’s 2019 order.
Amid public outcry, he was returned to the US after a decision by the supreme court. Since then, Ábrego García has been fighting government efforts to deport him for a second time to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.
On Wednesday, his lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said the Trump administration had wanted to deport Ábrego García “handcuffed, on an ICE flight bound for Liberia” on Tuesday.
“And what happened? He walked out a free man, without any restrictions, without shackles on his feet. He left for the country of his choosing, and he did so on a commercial flight, alongside everyone else,” Sandoval-Moshenberg added.
He described it as a “complete victory”, adding: “Instead of flying ICE Air, he flew United Airlines. Instead of being in shackles, he was in economy plus.”
He said Ábrego García had negotiated a deal with federal authorities in which they had agreed to allow him to leave the country, removing obstacles such as the ankle monitor and taking him off the no-fly list, as long as he left by 24 November. The Department of Homeland Security said on Tuesday Ábrego García had “self-deported” to Spain.
Sandoval-Moshenberg described Ábrego García’s departure from the US as temporary, saying that he would decide where to settle for the next two years as he waited out the remainder of the Trump administration.
“Mr Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child,” he said. “We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritise reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland.”
On Wednesday, Ábrego García’s lawyer, Chris Newman, said his client had landed in Spain as a tourist and that he had no plans to meet with any politicians while in Spain. “I can confirm that he’s coming here with the intention of staying for just a few days and that he already has tickets, one could say, for his next appointment,” he told Spanish media.
His departure this week was celebrated by many who had sought to push back against the Trump administration’s pursuit of Ábrego García.
“They wanted to leave him there to rot for the rest of his life. Instead, we saw our judicial system work alongside a strong legal team to produce this outcome, where Kilmar Ábrego García is able to chart his own future,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat who traveled to Cecot to visit Abrego Garcia in April last year.
Van Hollen, who is vying to become Senate majority leader when Democrats regain control of Congress next year, has made Ábrego García’s case and opposition to the administration’s sweeping deportation crackdown central to his vision for the party.
“Ábrego García’s journey is an example of our constitution working despite the attacks of the Trump administration,” Van Hollen added. He said he had spoken with the Spanish ambassador to the United States, Ángeles Moreno Bau, and briefed her on “all the wrongs that have been committed by the Trump administration against Kilmar Ábrego García”, adding that he was pleased Ábrego García was now in Spain and “able to continue telling his story”.

title: EU nationals will pay higher tuition fees than UK students, Burnham indicates
text:
European students will have to pay higher fees than their domestic equivalents at UK universities under a still-to-be-finalised part of the new deal with the EU, Andy Burnham has indicated.
The issue of fees paid by EU nationals studying at British universities is the main element of the arrangement hailed by Burnham in Brussels on Friday that has not been agreed, with both sides giving an extra six months to reach a solution.
Since Brexit, EU students – aside from Irish nationals and those with settled status in the UK – are treated as overseas entrants, so pay tuition fees which can exceed £30,000 a year, rather than a home student rate capped at £9,790.
The EU has been pushing for a lower rate, as part of the reset deal agreed at Friday’s summit in Brussels, which also included plans for looser checks on food and drink, emissions trading and a mutual exchange scheme for young people.
There have also been reports that Brussels has pushed for EU students to pay the domestic rate, while an annual charge of about £12,000 was suggested as a possible compromise.
Asked by Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions to rule out an equal rate between UK and EU students, Burnham indicated that this was requested by the EU but it would not be granted.
“In relation to the deal, the right honourable lady is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position,” he told her. “That has not been put on the table, and it will not be put on the table.”
Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “Both sides have agreed to negotiate a reciprocal agreement, and any deal would have to be in our national interest.”
Higher overseas fees are an important source of income for most UK universities, and dropping them significantly for EU students could cost the sector hundreds of millions of pounds a year.
Burnham said the deal on tuition fees with the EU was “not done” when asked by the leader of the opposition if the government would compensate universities.
He reiterated the UK’s position that the implementation of the deals agreed on Friday would not be dependent on an agreement about tuition fees, something EU officials took a different view of on Friday.
Burnham said Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, referred to the tuition fees talks as being “a separate piece of paper” to the main deal at the summit, meaning they were not linked.
He also said the Conservative party had to be clear on whether it opposed the plans: “Will it stand against a deal that will remove mountains of paperwork from British businesses and British exporters? A deal that the vast majority of Britain’s major supermarkets support because, they say, it can bring down pressure on the weekly shop? The Conservatives were once the party that opposed the imposition of red tape; they are now the red tape Tories.”

title: ‘Russia wants more than Ukraine,’ Germany’s Merz warns – as it happened
text:
'Russia wants more than Ukraine,' Germany's Merz warns, as he says Moscow is 'escalating on a massive scale'
In his wide-ranging budget speech, Merz talks about Germany “neglecting fundamental issues for far too long” on defence, infrastructure, demographic change, and the economy – and the need to address these issues urgently.
But the starkest part of his speech comes as he talks about the external situation – and particularly the threat from Russia - to explain why some decisions, particularly on defence, are needed.
“Russia knows exactly what it wants and Russia wants more than Ukraine,” he warns.
“Anyone who fails to grasp this either does not understand the world as it is, or is pursuing an entirely different agenda – one that stands in opposition to the freedom, openness, and liberal values of our own country.”
Merz warns that “Russia is escalating tensions in the Baltic region, in Poland, in the Black Sea, and even in the outer space.”
“It is escalating on a massive scale – including here within our own borders, even at the cost of human lives. That is the situation, ladies and gentlemen.
And that is why we, as Europeans, must—and will – set clear boundaries for Russia.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that “Russia knows exactly what it wants and Russia wants more than Ukraine,” as he said Moscow was “escalating tensions” in the region “on a massive scale” (10:04).
Merz told German lawmakers that “by supporting Ukraine, we are supporting and protecting ourselves,” as he presented the 2027 draft budget (10:07).
His stark warnings come just hours before Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte is due to meet the US president, Donald Trump, at Mar-a-Lago (9:53).
In other news,
Ukraine’s military has said it hit five Russian military aircraft at key Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region (12:41).
Poland wants Nato allies to consider shooting down Russian drones and missiles on the Ukrainian side even before they cross the alliance’s borders, after three cruise missiles crashed in Poland last week amid a broader attack on Ukraine (13:56).
The Kremlin has brushed off reports that up to 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in its almost five-year-long offensive on Ukraine (11:59).
The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including the EU, China, and Japan (15:04, 15:36, 15:38, 15:53, 15:54)
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Why are Spanish politicians saying so little about climate crisis before the election?
Sam Jones
in Madrid
Beneath the blackened branches of a pine tree that rises high above a landscape of scorched hillsides and the odd charred and ruined house, two older men address the obvious. Four months after one of the summer’s many wildfires threatened to devour the hamlet of El Morro, an hour west of Madrid, local people are still counting the cost and awaiting compensation.
“Look at that house,” said Esteban Pérez, pointing to one of the properties that did not make it through July’s flames. “Everything inside is scorched, completely destroyed. You can still see the windows, but they’re gutted. The entire structure of the house next to mine had to be torn down, too. And they’ve given the owner nothing so far.”
His friend nods and offers a more laconic observation: “We’re still screwed here.”
The ruling socialist party – which describes the climate emergency as “one of the greatest challenges of our time” – has promised to “speed up a just ecological transition, boost renewable energy, move towards greater energy autonomy, and turn sustainability into a source of employment, innovation and prosperity”.
The conservative People’s party (PP) has vowed to “act from science and without dogmatism” when it comes to fighting climate change and pursuing decarbonisation.
Meanwhile the far-right Vox party, which could well form a coalition with the PP, has pledged to tackle “climate fanaticism” and to put an end to international agreements that “hinder our productive development and the prosperity of Spanish workers, families, businesses and industries”.
Even though Spain’s three biggest parties enthusiastically defend their very different climate policies on paper, some observers are unsurprised at their reluctance to place them centre-stage at rallies and in interviews.
Will Spain’s snap election on Sunday bring a far-right party into government?
We are keeping an eye on Spain, with the country going to the polls on Sunday in perhaps the trickiest test of Pedro Sanchez’s ability to come back from losing positions in his career.
As mass protests over a nationwide housing crisis have forced him into an early general election, the Guardian travelled to Spain’s Andalusian coast to find out what’s driving the housing crisis, what solutions are on offer and why rightwing populists are gaining ground.
Donald Trump is keeping true to his threat of “obnoxious” tariffs after the supreme court ruled that he had overstepped his legal authority in imposing his “liberation day” tariffs last spring.
In this explainer, we looked at the various backdoors available to him to reimpose tariffs, which he once described as his favourite term.
The 301 tariffs, which he is threatening to impose today, were considered the most “obnoxious” allows for unlimited tariffs to be imposed for four years against countries with unfair trade practices.
If applied to the EU today and not challenged or overturned, they would hold until 25 November 2030, two years after Trump’s current term of office ends.
But the EU has already passed legislation including a sunset clause that would blow up the tariffs on 31 December 2029.
MEPs had originally sought a 2028 expiration date but pushed it back in negotiations with member states keen to keep Trump sweet.
For what it’s worth, here’s the European Commission’s response in full, via a commission spokesperson:
“The EU takes note of the publication by the US of preliminary findings pursuant to its Section 301 investigation concerning structural excess capacity in manufacturing sectors.
We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity.
The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action.
We will continue engaging with the US Administration on implementation of the EU-US Joint Statement, notably through exploring new products for tariff exemptions/reductions and possible other areas of enhanced cooperation.
Under the Joint Statement, the 15% all-inclusive ceiling applies to EU goods. We expect any measure from this investigation to respect it in full, including when combined with existing duties.”
EU 'strongly rejects' premise underpinning new US tariffs
Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent
The EU has hit back at Donald Trump’s plans for more tariffs which come almost a year after his previous “liberation day” levies were struck down by the US supreme court.
Washington’s proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan, South Korea and the EU to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global trade tensions.
According to a statement by the US trade representative, “the EU’s unreasonable cars, policies and practices” include “industrial plans to expand manufacturing”; policies to “promote production an exports”, “sustained market access barriers” and “preferential lending” to target domestic sectors.
These increase the US economic security risks especially in cars, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, it says.
The current tariff plan is to impose a 15% levy on EU imports, pegging it at the same level agreed with the EU and Trump’s course last July.
The EU said it would study the findings, but added:
“At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” it said a possible reference to imports flooding in from China.
It added:
“The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action.”
US plans new tariffs against China, Japan, EU and other partners
Meanwhile, the Trump administration has proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, according to reports.
The US Trade Representative’s office announced the duties after completing an eight-month Section 301 unfair trade practices probe into 16 trading partners, including close allies Japan, the EuropeanUnion and SouthKorea, Reuters reports.
The move is designed to clamp down on “structural excess industrial capacity”.
The new proposals largely stick to rates set with trade deals, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC in an interview, adding that some may be “topped up” a few percentage points.
We are covering the news on our business live blog here:
Russia expects European negotiators to come to Moscow to explain their position before taking a wider role in talks on the Ukraine war, Russia’s ambassador to Germany has told AFP.
In an interview, Sergei Nechayev said Russia understood that “the Europeans do not intend to travel to Moscow” and that if this remains the case “we remain ready to... carry on with negotiations – at the very least within the trilateral format involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States”.
Poland wants Nato to shoot down Russian missiles flying towards its borders
Jakub Krupa
Poland wants Nato allies to consider shooting down Russian drones and missiles on the Ukrainian side even before they cross the alliance’s borders, after three cruise missiles crashed in Poland last week amid a broader attack on Ukraine.
The discussion has resurfaced just days after three Russian cruise missiles breached Poland’s airspace and fell deep inside its territory last Friday.
The foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, said Nato should “anticipate threats, and not only respond when someone gets hurt.”
“Ukraine keeps asking us to shoot down threatening objects over its territory. Shooting [missiles] down does not mean they simply vanish; the shot-down piece of junk still falls on the ground and can hurt someone or cause damage … So a missile or drone approaching our airspace already poses a direct threat to us,” he told Poland’s public broadcaster Polskie Radio this morning.
“I believe that shooting them down over Ukraine, at Ukraine’s request, would fall within the definition of self-defence,” he said.
Sikorski will represent Poland at next week’s meeting of Nato foreign ministers in Brussels. He declined to comment if the proposal came up during a meeting of Nato’s North Atlantic Council on Monday.
The defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz,told RMF FM that “this discussion did not start now, it has been ongoing for a while,” but allied countries showed little “determination” to follow through on the proposals so far.
“I have not yet seen any readiness on the part of our allies – because this must be an allied response – to take such a decision. … I do see, perhaps, a greater willingness to discuss the matter, but I do not see any determination in this regard,” he said.
Kosiniak-Kamysz suggested on Wednesday that he was unhappy with the level of support given to Poland by Nato allies, particularly the US, after the incident, with no public condemnation of the incident by Donald Trump or his senior officials.
“It’s not the first time,” he said.
“All information is being passed on to the Pentagon on an ongoing basis, and a meeting was held at Nato headquarters with the ambassadors of all member states, including the United States… but, once again, as was also the case in July, there has not been the kind of reaction we would have expected.”
The minister urged Nato’s Mark Rutte to raise the security of the alliance’s eastern flank with the US president, Donald Trump, during their meeting at Mar-a-Lago later today.
“I would like Mark Rutte to speak on behalf of the countries on Nato’s eastern flank and explain the consequences we are facing as a result of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. … I think it is necessary to reiterate this every time [he meets Trump],” he said.
Poland is hoping that, as part of a broader review of the US military presence in Europe, Washington will soon confirm plans to deploy up to 5,000 soldiers to a new permanent base in western Poland.
Three sites in western Poland are being actively considered for the base, following a series of meetings with senior US officials in recent months. Polish officials suggest a final decision should be made around 5 December.
The base, which would cost Poland around £3bn to build, would strengthen Poland’s defence amid growing tensions with Russia.
“Until it’s signed [by Trump], we can’t say for certain, but … as I’d put it today, it’s highly likely,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
There are currently about 6,000 US troops stationed in Poland, mostly on rotation and down from 10,000 last year, with about 200 permanently deployed at the missile defence base in Redzikowo, northern Poland.
Russia's overnight attacks damaged Ukraine's power sector, PM says
A Russian overnight attack on Ukraine’s power sector damaged energy and gas infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions, prime minister Sergiy Koretskyi said, as reported by Reuters.
“The most difficult situation is in Zaporizhzhia, where all attention is now,” Koretskyi said on Telegram.
Ukraine says it hit five Russian fighter jets at key military airfield
Ukraine’s military has said it hit five Russian military aircraft at key Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region.
“According to preliminary information, three Russian MiG-31s and two Su-34s have been struck and will be unable to fly for some time. The extent of the damage and the exact number of affected aircraft are currently being verified. There is a possibility of even better news,” it said in a statement on Telegram.
The Ukrainian army also said it struck Russia’s “fuel supplies and storage facilities” in the Russian-occupied areas.
“Operations targeting key enemy military assets will continue until Russia completely ceases its armed aggression against Ukraine,” it said.

title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
text:
A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.
The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.
The nine workers had their contracts terminated in January 2024 “in the interests of the agency” and were told in termination letters that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”. The dismissals were confirmed after a UN investigation found they might have been involved in the 7 October attacks.
The decision, which was taken by former Unrwa commissioner general Philippe Lazzarini after consultation with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, was apparently made in the hope that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work to continue in Gaza.
Critics warned at the time that the decision, on the basis of allegations rather than evidence, compromised the UN’s integrity and had the opposite effect, giving credence to unproven allegations.
The dismissals failed to prevent the Biden administration ordering a pause in funding, a measure that was echoed temporarily by other backers, leading to a financial shortfall of $450m (£340m).
“I have always said on the record that the Israeli allegations against Unrwa were the mother of all lies,” said Chris Gunness, a former Unrwa spokesperson. “Sacking the workers without any evidence confirmed their guilt unfairly, in the minds of journalists, led 16 top donors to abandon Unrwa and produced the worst financial crisis in the agency’s history, from which it may never recover.”
The Unrwa dispute tribunal that ruled in favour of one of its sacked workers, Abu Awad, described the Israeli allegations as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability”.
The tribunal also found that an internal UN investigation had not interviewed the 19 staff members initially accused by Israel of involvement in the 7 October attacks because of “safety and security” concerns.
“The allegations against the applicant and the other staff members, it seems, are therefore based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession,” the tribunal said.
It cast doubt on intercepted mobile phone conversations and messages offered by Israel as evidence, noting that one case had involved mistaken identity based on a cloned sim card, a common phenomenon in Gaza.
It also said that voice recognition claims made by Israel were dubious and some transcripts of conversations were found by UN investigators not to support claims that they proved links to Hamas or the 7 October attacks.
The allegation against Awad was that he was a “platoon commander” in Hamas’s military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, a claim he rejected. He was not alleged to have physically taken part in the 7 October attack and witness statements to the tribunal said he was on an Unrwa staff bus as normal.
The specific allegation against Awad was that he “had been instructed in a telephone call intercepted by Israeli intelligence to monitor the events of 7 October 2023, while simultaneously receiving Hamas intelligence updates related to the attacks”.
The tribunal said the Israeli security services had failed to clarify who was alleged to have made the call to Awad and in what way the mobile phone that received the call was associated with him.
Unrwa did not respond to a request for comment. Asked by the tribunal to provide evidence underpinning the dismissal of the workers, the agency cited the Israeli government as well as a report in the Times of Israel and another on the website UN Watch, a pro-Israel pressure group that has campaigned against Unrwa.
In its ruling, the tribunal said Unrwa’s claim that the cited sources had informed the decision to dismiss the workers was “open to some doubt” because all the supporting documents it had submitted were produced after the disputed decision was made on 26 January 2024.
Lazzarini, a Swiss humanitarian expert who left the commissioner general post in March, said he understood the tribunal’s finding might be appealed so he could not discuss the case in detail. In February 2024, he admitted his decision to sack the workers represented “reverse due process” in that the investigation followed the dismissal.
“My judgment, based on this going public, true or untrue, was I need to take the swiftest and boldest decision to show that as an agency we take this allegation seriously,” he said, adding that “the ability of the entire agency to continue to operate and deliver critical humanitarian assistance was at stake”.
The tribunal said it could not decide on the allegations against Awad but ruled that Unrwa had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to sack him. It awarded him a year’s pay and $5,000 for “moral damages”.
In the wake of its allegations against the sacked workers, Israel claimed that Unrwa was heavily infiltrated by Hamas and its parliament voted in 2024 to ban the agency from operating in Israel or in the occupied Palestinian territories.
The international court of justice stated in October 2025, however, that “Israel has not substantiated its allegations that a significant part of Unrwa’s employees are members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions”.

title: Palestinian journalist killed by Israel in Gaza wins Rory Peck prize
text:
