Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists, the organisers announced on Wednesday.
She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said.
Dagga, who has a teenage son named Ghaith, was killed in August 2025 in an Israeli airstrike on a southern Gaza hospital, which claimed the lives of four other journalists.
The independent photographer and reporter had been working with the AP news agency since the beginning of the current conflict, triggered by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
Dagga was renowned for her relentless reporting despite the personal losses she suffered throughout the war. She filmed the death of a protester who was shot during the 2018 Great March of Return in Gaza, when Israeli forces shot protesters marching towards the Gaza border fence, killing more than 220 people and wounding more than 9,200. She later discovered that the protester was her brother.
The war correspondent continued her work as a journalist during the war in Gaza over the last 22 months, working as a freelancer with the AP and Independent Arabia.
The AP’s executive editor, Julie Pace, said: “Journalists play an essential role in documenting events and informing the public, often at enormous personal risk.
“We honour Mariam and all journalists killed during this conflict and other conflicts – and remain committed to seeking answers about their deaths.”
French photographer Robin Tutenges was the recipient of the first Rory Peck award for photojournalism in recognition of his work on the conflict in Ethiopia’s northern Amhara region.
Sudanese freelance photographer and video journalist Ahmed Mohamed Abdalla, who works with Agence France-Presse, was shortlisted for the same award for his coverage of the fall of El Fasher to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan’s civil war.
Abdalla was not allowed to attend the prize-giving ceremony in London as the UK government refused to grant him a visa.
In a recorded video message shared during the ceremony, he told of how the capital of the North Darfur region’s besieged inhabitants had to eat livestock feed to survive amid the daily deluge of missiles.
The prize has been awarded since 1995 in memory of Northern Irish video journalist Rory Peck, who was killed in Moscow in 1993, to celebrate the work of freelance video journalists.

title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
text:
James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”.
Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
The complaint also includes riot and conspiracy to riot charges stemming from 2023 protests against New England branches of Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit.
Chambers was speaking from his Madrid apartment in his first in-depth interview after a Spanish appeals court ordered his provisional release on bail on Friday. That release was due to issues with the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported by the Guardian.
“Support for my case doesn’t imply support of me, or my ideas,” Chambers said. “It’s about my right to have those ideas – and not be falsely accused of things.”
Chambers, whose case has gained attention across the world, had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.
The order granting Chambers’s provisional release asserted that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”. Spanish judges had previously denied bail three times.
The wealthy heir to at least $250mn from his family’s business – Atlanta–based Cox Enterprises – was in the middle of his first visit without being separated by glass with his mother, Lauren Hamilton, when he was summoned to receive the “good news” on Friday, Chambers told the Guardian.
Minutes later, he returned to tell his mother he was being released. “She freaked out crying. We went nuts for about five minutes. Then we got to contacting my lawyer and getting my kids on a plane to Spain.”
On Monday, Chambers’s five-year-old son with actor and activist Stella Schnabel could be heard in the background. The tableau was in stark contrast to his months in prison.
“I tried to build a cocoon to deal with the immense unknown, the immense fear,” he said of his time in Aranjuez prison. “I would pray a lot. The only idea I could hold onto was, my home is the truth. The truth of who loves you. The truth of my own innocence. And the truth of what is happening in Palestine and all the things connected to what is happening in Palestine – other wars, gas prices. No one can take that away from you.”
Chambers has been supported by his mother throughout his case, and has reconnected with his father, James Cox Chambers – who owns an estimated 17% stake in Cox Enterprises but does not play an active role in the company – for the first time in five years.
“Speaking with my parents has provided emotional stability – and intelligent, adult minds to help make decisions,” Chambers said.
Although he has had political disagreements with his father, a donor to the Democratic party, Chambers said his father “sees this situation as totally unthinkable and out of step with anything resembling a just society”.
He also invoked his grandfather, the ACLU civil rights lawyer James Cox Hamilton, who died in 2014. “He would’ve turned in his grave over this,” Chambers said.
While locked up, Chambers, a US citizen, received hundreds of letters of support from friends, family and strangers, postmarked from Atlanta to Barcelona – including, he said, “from a guy who had been imprisoned under [Spanish dictator Francisco] Franco, who painted the ‘key of return’ [a symbol of homes lost in the 1948 Nakba] on the Palestinian flag”.
Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
His release followed a separate decision on Thursday by a three-judge panel at Spain’s high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.
The US admitted to making several of the changes, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent”. These and dozens of other changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian last week.
It was also recently revealed that there is no indictment behind the complaint, meaning the federal government has not had a grand jury evaluate evidence against Chambers, and instead is seeking his extradition based on the affidavit of a single FBI agent, the core of the sealed criminal complaint.
During his time in prison, Chambers also began the process of applying for political asylum in Spain. He cannot be extradited until the asylum case runs its course, and also cannot be extradited if he is granted asylum. His legal team has notified the government office evaluating his asylum petition of the altered translations.
Chambers was arrested 10 July as he and Schnabel pulled into the driveway of a school they were visiting to see about enrolling their five-year-old, part of plans to move to Spain. They had been staying in Ireland, where Schnabel was working on a film.
Although the arrest came as a surprise – “I was confused! Did I speed?” he thought – Chambers revealed to the Guardian that a car had been following him around Dublin only days before, and that someone had broken into their car parked outside their house at night, without taking anything of value.
“I noticed signs of surveillance,” he said. Months later, last Wednesday, Irish police raided the same house, acting on a request from US authorities.
With his immediate future uncertain, Chambers said he was “looking forward to sharing a couple of nice dinners with my family this week”.
As for the past, he said the millions he has donated to an estimated 100 projects in about 20 countries is “the most important thing I’ve done”.
“Somebody with the political orientation I have and with resources, no matter how good of an activist I am, it’s not gonna be as effective as medical aid or feeding children in Gaza, supporting independent media that wouldn’t otherwise exist, or paying people’s bail who have been arrested for protesting.
“I’m giving a lot of money to things that other people aren’t giving money to.”
Chambers also said he was “grateful for the way Spanish courts have dealt with this – just focusing on the facts. It shouldn’t matter that I’ve made some emotional statements.”

title: ‘They don’t believe in freedom’: Yemenis plan their escape as Houthis advance on Aden
text:
Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far south as he could to the port city of Aden, where there was a measure of safety.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government had made the city its temporary capital; the hundreds of kilometres between it and the Houthis were well fortified.
Today, Hussein is once again considering the painful decision of leaving home. In September, the Iran-aligned Houthis swept aside Yemeni government forces, and now have set their sights on Aden. Houthi fighters are amassing to the north and east of the city, and have begun encircling the government-controlled territory.
“I fled my home in Sana’a and came here. I don’t think the Houthis plan to take over Aden right now, but if they get closer, I will have no choice but to flee again to Marib or Hadhramaut,” said Hussein, who was speaking under a pseudonym.
Hussein works as a schoolteacher and was formerly a member of the Islah party, an Islamist political party aligned with Saudi Arabia that is in opposition to the Houthi movement. He fears that if the Houthis take control of Aden he could face persecution for his former affiliation.
“The Houthis don’t believe in freedom, they just want to hear one voice, the one they like,” he said.
Hussein is one of many residents and organisations nervously watching the Houthi advance. The militia is still about 50 miles (80km) north of Aden, but local people fear government forces may not be able to resist another Houthi assault, having seen the dramatic collapse of government forces and allied militias in September.
Aden has been the seat of the Saudi-backed government of Yemen since 2015. If the Houthis took the city, it would be a huge blow for the government, and a massive failure for the Saudi-led coalition which has for years fought against the Houthis.
The 12-year-long civil war would tilt dramatically in the Houthis’ favour and be a boon for Iran, which has long invested military and political support in the insurgent movement.
The Yemeni government has pulled back many of its fighters to help defend Aden and the surrounding areas, announcing last week that fighters were redeployed from areas along the south-western coast towards the port city.
Saudi Arabia has tried to halt the Houthi advance with a renewed bombing campaign, carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in Yemen since September, killing and wounding 822 civilians, including 181 children, according to statistics from the independent Yemen Data Project.
Houthi authorities have alleged that Saudi Arabia has carried out 5,500 air and missile attacks since July.
The Houthis have not announced any intention to take Aden, but have instead been amassing troops north of Kirish, and in al-Bayda, areas which, if taken, would cut off the northern and eastern roads to Aden.
“The buildups in al-Bayda could threaten Aden’s eastern road links through Abyan and Saudi supply lines into the city,” said Mohammed al-Basha, the founder of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report.
“The Houthis appear to be testing how well Aden’s defences will hold. If they collapse, the Houthis could try to seize the city. If government forces hold, the Houthis could try to lay siege to it,” al-Basha added.
Houthi forces have begun striking Aden and its surrounding areas, rupturing the relative safety the city has offered for years. Residents have watched anxiously as explosions grow nearer, and displaced people from surrounding areas have started to arrive in greater numbers.
“Since last week, we’ve started following the news every hour. When I get busy, I tell my daughter to follow it and update me,” said Rami, a resident of Aden who spoke under a pseudonym.
The 53-year-old bitterly recalled his experience during the four-month battle for Aden in 2015, when he was stuck in the crossfire between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces. He, like other people in Aden, is trying to make his own calculation of when, or if, the Houthis will arrive.
International organisations are also making contingency plans in case of a Houthi takeover of the city.
“We were informed by management that they are issuing termination notices to all staff this week. If the Houthis don’t reach Aden, they will continue operations and renew our contracts; otherwise this is the end of the road,” an aid worker with an international NGO said.
Already, several NGOs were forced to shut down in the city of Taiz after sweeping Houthi gains.
Not all NGOs would leave in the case of a Houthi takeover, but some are unable to work in Houthi-controlled areas either due to fears for the safety of aid workers, or because the US Treasury designated the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation in 2025.
Yemen has for years faced a severe humanitarian crisis, with about 18.7 million people facing acute food insecurity.
Fighting has only exacerbated conditions, severing transport routes, pushing up the prices of goods and worsening the country’s displacement crisis – including more than 350,000 people displaced since August.
“I earn daily wages, and when there is no work, my six family members don’t get enough food,” said Ahmed, a restaurant worker in his 50s. “I don’t care about politics or wars, and I’m not involved in any of it. I’m just like millions of Yemenis struggling to provide basic necessities for their families.”
For many of Aden’s residents, the prospect of a Houthi takeover has shattered the sense of safety that they sought by coming to the government stronghold in the first place.
“I’m not stocking up on food because I won’t stay in Aden and wait for the battles to reach the city. It isn’t only me; my family is also ready to flee at any time … staying at home won’t be safe and we might get trapped,” Rami said.

title: Israel attempts to jail Palestinian student at Hebrew University without trial
text:
Palestinian student Mahdi Tounsi appeared in a closed-door court hearing in Jerusalem, as academics and activists warned that Israel’s attempt to jail him without trial marked a serious escalation in attacks on Palestinian rights.
Yael Berda, a lawyer and sociology professor at Hebrew University, who has taught Tounsi for four years, came to court to call for his release.
“I have no doubt this is a case of political persecution based on identity and political activity,” she said outside the courtroom. “Mehdi’s arrest is part of a campaign that we’ve seen very much escalating since the elections.”
Her student was “almost unrecognisable” when he appeared on a video link in the courtroom, deprived of his glasses, with his hair and beard shaved and with visible bruising, she added.
Tounsi, a sociology and criminology student at Hebrew University in Jerusalem, was seized from his dorm on 8 November. He is held at Megiddo prison where documented abuse includes starvation rations, violent attacks on prisoners and rampant scabies and other diseases.
Thousands of Palestinians from the occupied West Bank are held under administrative detention orders but they have rarely been used against Palestinians who have Israeli citizenship or residence status in occupied East Jerusalem.
Prison authorities had not complied with a judge’s order to return Tounsi’s glasses, his brief public appearance on Tuesday showed.
Israeli prosecutors are seeking an administrative detention order, which allows for up to six months’ detention without trial or public presentation of evidence.
Security forces presented a summary of evidence in a hearing closed even to Tounsi and his lawyers, making a defence effectively impossible.
Tounsi’s arrest comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.
Noa Dagoni, executive director of Jerusalem-focused rights group Ir Amin, described Tounsi’s arrest as a dangerous escalation in political persecution of activists, particularly those “at the junction of human rights, dialogue and non-violent action”.
Many of the Ir Amin staff count Tounsi as a personal friend after years working together in his home community of Silwan, where Israeli authorities are forcing mass displacements of Palestinians, including to make way for a theme park.
Dagoni fears he may have been targeted for this work. “We’re very concerned that this [arrest] has to do with his being a non-violent peace activist, also dealing with the displacement in his community,” she said.
“The partnership of Israelis and Palestinians is very intimidating for this government because it can be effective, it can build real political power.”
Officers from the Shin Bet security force failed to appear in court to present evidence at a first hearing last week, so the judge reconvened on Tuesday.
Reflecting concern about the case, his family and lawyer were joined in the courthouse by prominent activists, Knesset member Ofer Cassif, diplomats from Ireland, the Netherlands and the EU, his tutor and the dean of students from Hebrew University.
Hundreds of Jewish and Palestinian demonstrators gathered in the street outside calling for his immediate release.
Many knew Tounsi personally from classes or activism, including Lana, a Palestinian citizen of Israel.
“Someone who I know being kidnapped was really frightening,” she said. “It makes me think of my place here also, how it might affect me and if there are more people who I know who are going to be arrested soon.”
Many protesters were angry with university authorities, including Arielle, 27, a former student at the same campus. “Israeli universities need to take accountability for this, like they can’t allow students to be kidnapped from their dorm rooms,” she said.
Hebrew University’s dean of students, Zohar Kampf, said the university asked to testify but its request was rejected. The university has not commented on Tounsi’s violent arrest, deprivation of glasses and other mistreatment.
Cassif, the Knesset member, called for a global pressure campaign. “Where is the international community, especially academia. What are they waiting for?” he said. “Speak up, do something, raise your voice.”
The police did not respond to questions about visible marks of abuse or details of the case against Tounsi. A spokesperson said: “The suspect was lawfully arrested as part of an investigation conducted by the Jerusalem District Central Investigations Unit concerning ties to an act of terrorism.”

title: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
text:
A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi high court to give him permission to fly to the UK after immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him boarding a flight early on Tuesday morning.
The court is scheduled to hear Saurav Das’s case on Thursday morning. His lawyer asked the court for a quick hearing because Das has by now already missed some of his engagements at British universities and can only attend the other events on his itinerary if he is allowed to fly out as soon as possible.
Das, 27, is one of the main faces of the Cockroach movement, which shot into the political firmament out of nowhere in May to challenge the Narendra Modi government with street protests.
The movement succeeded in forcing the education minister to resign in July over exam leaks and has since functioned as a pressure group.
Das had been invited by the Oxford Union Society to participate in a “fireside chat” on the movement.
Indian student groups at Edinburgh, Cambridge, Queen Mary University of London and the London School of Economics have also invited him to speak.
“Students want to know how we succeeded without any violence, how we began and where we are going. There is a great curiosity about the movement,” Das told the Guardian.
Reports in the Indian media have alleged that Das was informed well before the flight that his passport contained discrepancies.
“None of these reports is true,” said Das. “I received an email five hours before my flight saying that I should not use my passport for travel. It gave no reason. And I did not see the email until I arrived at Delhi airport. What’s more, I’ve travelled abroad before on this passport since it was issued in 2019 so what’s the problem with it now?”
He suspects that the government is using a frivolous case filed in Chennai against him as a pretext. The case has been filed, Das surmises, by someone hostile to the Cockroach movement and disputes his citizenship.
Das believes he was deliberately stopped by a government that is “scared” of someone such as him speaking abroad about the ideals of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru (independent India’s first prime minister) and that it wanted to make an example of him.
“It’s a chilling signal to young Indians that we can do what we like, that if we can do this to a leader of a movement, we can do this to you too,” said Das.
In recent years, the government has stopped foreign speakers and academics, including several from the UK, from entering India.
Last year, Francesca Orsini, a professor at Soas University of London, was stopped at Delhi airport and deported despite holding a valid visa. The government said she had been blacklisted for allegedly conducting research and speaking at events while visiting on a tourist visa in 2024.
Also last year, Nitasha Kaul, a professor at Westminster University, was detained at Bangalore airport and deported for “anti-India activities”.
Some people who find themselves blacklisted have chosen to fight back. In 2023, the UK-based journalist Amrit Wilson had her overseas citizen of India card which allows free movement into India cancelled, also for alleged “anti-India activities”.
She took legal action and earlier this week, the Delhi high court ruled that the government had failed to give any concrete details of what it meant by “anti-India activities”.
The court has given the government a week to issue a fresh notice, this time giving specific reasons.

title: World Chess Championship 2026 Game 1: Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov play to 38-move draw – as it happened
text:
Everything you need to know about the World Chess Championship
India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is defending the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov in the youngest title match in the competition’s 140-year history. The best-of-14-games contest is scheduled to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer outside Geneva, with an overall prize fund of $2.5m (£1.9m).
Game 1 starts at 3pm in Geneva, 2pm in London, 9am in New York and 7.30pm in India
Sindarov will have the white pieces for Game 1 and make the first move
Gukesh and Sindarov are both 20 years old, making this the youngest matchup in world championship’s 140-year history
An interesting question at the press conference about the players’ contrasting body language. Sindarov was seen repeatedly shaking his leg during the early stages of the game, while Gukesh sat with his eyes closed in apparent meditation. But it seems neither player is reading much into the other’s behavior.
“I don’t know, maybe it was a little bit of nerves also,” Gukesh says. “But I think both of our habits are similar in a sense. I think in general he taps his foot or shakes his leg and I close my eyes in any tournament, not just the match. So I think it’s just how we behave at the board.”
Sindarov concurs: “I do it in every tournament, not just here. And I saw all the players from India are always meditating. Whenever we meet, he’s also meditating, so I think nothing special here.”
Both players give their approval to the unusually intimate playing conditions at the Fondation Martin Bodmer, where Fide has dispensed with the traditional soundproof glass enclosure that separated the players from spectators at previous world championship matches.
“Some people go out, some people come in, sometimes there’s some creaks on the floor,” Gukesh says. “But nothing too distracting. I was quite OK with it. And also I think it’s quite nice that spectators get to experience the world championship with actually seeing the players up close. I’m completely fine with it.”
Asked how it compares with playing inside purpose-built “fishbowl” in Singapore two years ago, the defending champion says with a laugh: “In the glass box, I’m used to seeing even less people in the room, so maybe it’s a welcome change.”
Gukesh adds: “As a sportsperson, you need to just adapt to different conditions and find a way to perform at your best.”
Sindarov, who has spoken of the peculiar loneliness of playing a tournament with only one other competitor, is similarly enthusiastic.
“As a professional, first of all, you need to be ready to play in any conditions,” he says. “It’s nice to have more people in the playing hall, otherwise it would be too boring.”
Sindarov singles out Gukesh’s adventurous king move (27 ... Kf6) as one of the most impressive moments of the game, admitting he had underestimated the safety of the black king in what appeared to be an exposed position.
“Kf6 was super strong,” the challenger says. “I didn’t give a good evaluation for this one. And the king is really pretty safe on f6.”
Gukesh, for his part, suggests he was entertaining thoughts of playing for a win at that stage. Asked by moderator Maurice Ashley whether he had calculated in advance that his king would be safe on f6, the champion replies: “I thought I’m more than safe.”
“More than safe even?” Ashley asks. “You started thinking maybe more?”
“Yeah, maybe more,” Gukesh says.
Sindarov also addresses the unusual denouement to the game, when his incorrect claim of a draw by threefold repetition resulted in Gukesh being awarded an additional two minutes.
“I was thinking we already did it two times,” he says. “But then, yeah, you need to offer it on the right move.”
“Then I just played two more moves and I offered the draw correctly. I was thinking we already did it three or four times.”
Gukesh sounds less concerned about the time trouble he faces than those of us watching. “Obviously, in the opening I started thinking quite a bit and had some little problems to solve,” he says. “But I knew that overall I didn’t really make any unsound moves. I thought I should be fine. I think overall it was a pretty good game. Maybe around when I went [31 … Bc3], I was getting a little optimistic.”
The Indian credits the time he spent earlier in the game with helping him find his moves quickly once the clock became a factor.
“I thought I was always under control, at least not in a place where I really needed to be worried. When I got into the time trouble, I’d already thought about the next few moves, what I was going to play. So I was happy that I managed to spend some time and find a good solution. And then the moves after that were pretty easy.”
Sindarov, meanwhile, makes no secret of his desire to exploit the disparity on the clock.
“Of course, I’m trying to push every moment because of the clock,” he says. “But in general, I understand my position is very close to equal. I’m trying to keep finding some interesting ideas, but then he defended very well.”
“It’s the easiest thing to actually go and play the game because there’s so much thinking, so much work to do before that,” Gukesh says at the post-game press conference, admitting the anticipation surrounding the match was more difficult to handle than the game itself. “Once you get to the game, it’s like your home. It’s a game you’ve been playing for a lot of years. It feels safe. Before that, with all the nerves and all the hype, I think it’s a little tougher to handle all that.”
Sindarov, making his world championship debut, expressed similar sentiments.
“Before the start of the tournament, I was very nervous, thinking a lot about the game and everything,” he said. “But today I’m just trying to enjoy the game.”
Asked whether he approached the opener as a feeling-out game, the Uzbek said: “In general, if you get a chance, you will always try to win. It doesn’t matter which game. But in the first game, I think mostly you try to learn about your opponent and play safe.”
Gukesh: 'I never felt like I was too much in trouble'
Both players seem satisfied with the quality of the opening game in a brief walk-and-talk interview with Fide presenter Charlize van Zyl en route to the post-game press conference.
“It felt like a really high-level game,” Gukesh says. “It just looked equal the whole time. As usual, some little problems to solve, but I think both of us played just a very good game.”
The defending champion admitted his mounting time trouble had become a concern. “There were some opening problems to solve, so I took my time. But I never felt like I was too much in trouble. Obviously, the time was getting a little scary.”
Sindarov acknowledged he had been looking to exploit his considerable advantage on the clock but ultimately decided the risks of playing on outweighed the potential rewards.
The players have shaken hands after 38 moves (37 ... Kh7 38 Rh5 Kg8), bringing a tense opening game of the world chess championship to a close by threefold repetition. Gukesh has survived considerable time pressure to emerge with a half-point from his first outing with the black pieces, while Sindarov will have to wait at least another day for his first win on the world championship stage.
A curious bit of drama! Sindarov has incorrectly claimed a draw by threefold repetition and, in accordance with Fide’s by-laws, Gukesh has been awarded an additional two minutes on his clock. A welcome reprieve for the time-strapped defending champion, even if the game still appears headed for a draw.
Sindarov has picked off the h6 pawn to restore material equality (31 Rh5 Bc3 32 Bxh6+ Kg8). And now we have a repetition of moves (33 Rg5+ Kh7 34 Rh5 Kg8 35 Rg5+ Kh7 36 Rh5 Kg8 37 Rg5+), with Gukesh’s king shuttling between g8 and h7. The opening game appears destined for a draw by threefold repetition, which is permitted even before the 40th move under the match regulations.
A couple more moves (28 Rf2 Rgd8) and Gukesh is offering an exchange of rooks on the d-file. Surely any simplification would come as a relief to the champion. But Sindarov declines to accommodate, instead bringing his other knight into the action (29 Nd3) and attacking Gukesh’s bishop on b4.
The ensuing sequence (29 ... Bxf5 30 Rxf5+ Kg7 31 Rh5) sees the players exchange a bishop for a knight, with Sindarov turning his attention to black’s vulnerable h6 pawn. That leaves Gukesh with barely seven minutes to make his next 10 moves, but he appears to have escaped from danger.
Gukesh marches his king further up the board (27 ... Kf6) rather than retreating. The champion is down to 8min 39sec for his next 13 moves, while Sindarov still has more than 25 minutes.
And we have our first material imbalance of the game (23 ... Nxe5 24 f4). Gukesh has won a pawn but Sindarov has immediately attacked the knight that captured it. The champion responds by threatening Sindarov’s own knight on the kingside (24 ... g6 25 Ng3).
The challenger has retreated and now Gukesh must navigate a delicate position with barely 10 minutes to make his next 16 moves.
A flurry of activity on the board (22 Ne1 axb3 23 axb3). Gukesh has initiated an exchange of pawns on the queenside, opening up the a-file for his rook. The game is becoming more dynamic at a moment when the champion can least afford to spend time calculating variations.
Sindarov has been in the think tank for 15 minutes and counting, but his overwhelming time advantage affords him that luxury.
Meanwhile, over on the Chess.com broadcast, Judit Polgar is telling war stories. Sindarov’s decision to play 21 g4 rather than Stockfish’s preferred 21 Ne1 has reminded the Hungarian grandmaster of a painful defeat to Veselin Topalov in a similar Berlin endgame during the 2005 Fide world championship tournament in San Luis, Argentina.
“At some point I played g4,” Polgar recalls. “Not because I wanted to play for a win desperately, but because I thought that was the best move I could make in that position.
“And after the game people came to me: ‘Why did you play for a win in that position? It was not better anymore.’ I said: ‘I was not playing for a win in that position. I just thought that was the best move.’”
Two more moves (21 g4 Ke7) and Gukesh is putting his king to work in the center of the board. For all the Berlin’s reputation as a drawish opening, this is shaping up to be a three-result game.
Gukesh has pushed another pawn forward (19 ... c5), reinforcing his bishop on b4 and restricting the movement of white’s pieces. Sindarov quickly moves his knight to the edge of the board, prompting Gukesh to bring his rook across to defend his g7 pawn (20 Nh5 Rg8).
The champion has reached the halfway point to the first time control with barely 16 minutes to spare, while Sindarov still has more than 55 minutes at his disposal. The defending champion is effectively going to have to play rapid chess against an in-form opponent who has the luxury of thinking things through.
That said, despite Gukesh’s visible suffering, the Hungarian grandmaster Peter Leko is beginning to warm to black’s position on the official Fide broadcast.
“Nh5 was played clearly out of ambition,” Leko says. “I don’t know how much this choice was influenced by the clock situation, whether Sindarov wants to keep the game going because of the time situation. And I was praising the move Ng3 because of the clock factor. Looking at the position now, with the knight on h5 stuck and black having a clear b7-b5 push in the air, I already kind of wonder if I would not be much happier with black now.”
Sindarov takes more than 18 minutes before repositioning one of his knights (19 Ng3), keeping his options open and maintaining the tension on the board. The Uzbek challenger still has 57min 11sec on his clock compared with less than 24 minutes for Gukesh.
Gukesh has finally nudged his h-pawn forward (18 … h6), denying a square from Sindarov’s bishop and knights. Even if the position remains objectively equal, the clock is giving Sindarov a significant practical advantage.
Latvian grandmaster Arturs Neiksans has entered the chat, suggesting that Gukesh’s struggles today could have implications well beyond the opening game. If the Berlin defense was intended to be a mainstay of the champion’s opening repertoire for this match, Sindarov may already have given him reason to rethink his preparations.
“It’s probably too early to draw any firm conclusions, but Gukesh’s opening choice is already looking concerning,” Neiksans writes on X. “If you’re facing this much discomfort in Game 1 with what could be one of the cornerstones of your repertoire against 1.e4 for the match, it’s hard to see how you can confidently rely on it in the games to come. Hopefully, Gukesh has a solid backup plan.”
Gukesh has been on the clock for nearly five minutes as he considers his response to Sindarov’s 18 Re2. That’s left him with 24 minutes to make his next 23 moves.
And finally Gukesh has made his move (17 ... Bb4), bringing his bishop forward to attack one of Sindarov’s rooks. But the champion has burned through 36min 14sec of precious time in the process. He now has less than 29 minutes to make his next 23 moves, an average of roughly 75 seconds per turn.
Sindarov thinks for just three minutes before moving his threatened rook out of harm’s way (18 Re2). The position remains finely balanced, but the disparity on the clock is becoming one of the major storylines of this opening game. Gukesh has put himself in a situation where even relatively straightforward decisions will need to be made quickly.
Gukesh has been pondering his response to 17 b3 for more than half an hour. That’s a considerable investment of time given he still has 24 moves to make before receiving another 30 minutes on his clock.
The clock is becoming a factor for Gukesh, who is below 50 minutes remaining with another 23 moves to make before he receives any additional time. Grandmasters Judit Polgar and David Howell, commenting on the Chess.com broadcast, have identified a tempting rook move (17 ... Ra5), but one that would land the champion in trouble if Sindarov answered with 18 Bg5. An important decision awaits Gukesh, and he can ill afford to spend too much time making it.
Two more moves in Geneva (16 ... Be6 17 b3). Gukesh has moved his bishop out of the path of Sindarov’s rooks, while the challenger has reinforced his position on the queenside.
A few more moves to bring us up to date (15 Rd2 a4 16 Rad1). Sindarov has brought both of his rooks into the center of the board, while Gukesh has been steadily advancing a pawn down the left-hand side. Neither player has lost any material since the eighth move, with both looking to build up incremental advantages rather than force the issue. All of the popular engines and supercomputers continue to assess the position as dead even (0.00).
An excellent question from Justin Horton, writing in from Aragón, Spain, about the decor in the playing hall:
What are the books in the players’ lounge? They look like chess books but you wouldn’t have thought players would be allowed to consult chess books during a game. Nor would they be wise to do so given the cameras are there, but I can’t believe they’d put the players on an honour system not to open them. So are they real, or are they facsimiles, Potemkin books as it were?
Given the decidedly bibliothecal setting, it’s a particularly fitting question. The Fondation Martin Bodmer is one of the world’s great repositories of rare books and manuscripts, its 160,000 treasures including a Gutenberg Bible, Shakespeare’s First Folio and a copy of Isaac Newton’s Principia Mathematica once owned by his great rival Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.
The subject of the books came up at Sunday’s opening press conference. Gukesh said he had inspected the chairs, lighting and even the floor of the playing hall to ensure he would be comfortable during games that could last four or five hours, but admitted he had barely glanced at the books. “I don’t think I’ll be reading in between the games,” he joked.
A nugget of arcana from the Macedonian grandmaster Alex Colovic that may bode well for Gukesh. Of the four players who have deployed the Berlin defense in a world championship match, three of them (Vladimir Kramnik, Magnus Carlsen and Ding Liren) went on to win their matches. The lone exception? Vishy Anand against Carlsen.
Sindarov has expanded on the queenside and Gukesh has responded by pushing his a-pawn (14 c4 a5). The battle lines are becoming clearer: Sindarov has the more active pieces in the center, while Gukesh is looking for counterplay on the queenside to offset white’s long-term structural advantage.
“I think there were a lot of small surprises at first,” the Dutch grandmaster Anish Giri says on the Take Take Take stream. “I think on move one, maybe 1 d4 was a little more expected than 1 e4. Then from black, I think within the Spanish, maybe the Marshall was a little more expected than the Berlin.
“But then within the Berlin, I think finally the actual surprise is coming from Javokhir. I think this particular Ne4 move, we are in very rare territory. It is not something that I or many of my colleagues have studied deeply. I can imagine it’s a little bit of an obscure position.
“And yeah, a very exciting endgame ahead because there’s still a full board of pieces.”
A little diversion for those of you who, like Sindarov, have been looking forward to getting stuck into Grand Theft Auto VI. It turns out there’s a chess Easter egg buried in Rockstar Games’ sprawling recreation of Florida.
The eagle-eyed team at Chess.com have spotted a chessboard in the game which appears to reproduce a position from an actual game between the English grandmaster Daniel Gormally and Brazil’s Alexandr Fier at the 93rd Hastings Masters in 2017-18. Gormally, rated 80 points below his opponent, went on to win with the white pieces.
Something for Sindarov, who has been mulling his response to 13 ... Bd7 for more than 20 minutes, to investigate when he finally gets his hands on the game after the world championship.
The American grandmaster Maurice Ashley has joined the official Fide broadcast and admits he was hoping for something a little more combustible than a Berlin endgame to get the match under way.
“Obviously, the Berlin is one of those you see and you go, ‘Oh, OK, how’s he going to break down this wall?’ It’s obviously a big challenge when you have the white pieces, but clearly it looked like Sindarov was well prepared for this eventuality. So I’m excited to see the match get off, but it would have been nice to see something wild, crazy, queens on the board.
“I feel like [Hungarian grandmaster] Peter Leko here is excited by these kinds of positions. We were talking about endgames and his ability when he was young to play these extremely well. But I think the fans probably wanted some more sauce.”
And finally Gukesh makes his move! After a think of more than 15 minutes, the world champion has opted for 13 ... Bd7, bringing his last minor piece into play. The bishop also shields the black king from a potential check along the d-file, giving Gukesh greater flexibility in repositioning his king and coordinating his rooks. He’s more than 35 minutes behind the challenger on time, though.
Gukesh is in another deep think as Javokhir leaves the board for the nearby lounge chair inside the cramped playing hall.
“Now I understand what Javokhir was playing for,” English grandmaster David Howell says on the Chess.com broadcast. “I would have expected this opening from two older players, not maybe two 20-year-olds. But now I understand he’s trying to bait Gukesh. He’s trying to tempt him into some line where he has a deep, deep idea. Yeah, it’s very provocative.”
Gukesh has developed his dark-squared bishop and Sindarov has centralized his queenside knight (12 ... Be7 13 Ne4). The pace of play has slowed considerably as the players begin to grapple with the strategic subtleties of the Berlin. Both Stockfish and the Sesse supercomputer assess the position as dead even (0.00).
An email from the always welcome Gary Naylor, who sees parallels between the world chess championship and another of Europe’s great endurance events:
Given the location, the schedule, the fact that each leader has a team supporting him and, more than anything, the stamina required, this feels like the Tour de France. I suppose players have the ability to make stages – games – hard or easy by their strategies too.
Any sign of lycra?
No lycra to report, Gary, but there’s certainly something to the analogy. The ability to conserve energy over a three-week campaign, knowing when to attack and when to settle for a quiet day, is an underrated component of world championship matchplay.
Gukesh has been mulling his response to 12 Be3 for more than 10 minutes, after spending about eight minutes on his previous move.
“He still knows the position, but he is taking time to make sure he makes the right moves,” Russian grandmaster Peter Svidler says on the official Fide broadcast. “But Gukesh is already down almost 18 minutes on the clock. Considering he’s playing one of the most topical openings of the past 25 years, that’s some time expenditure.”
Gukesh has brought his knight to g6, putting pressure on the advanced white pawn on e5, and Sindarov has continued his development by bringing his bishop into play (11 ... Ng6 12 Be3).
Gukesh has returned his king to its original square and rerouted his knight (9 Rd1+ Ke8 10 Nc3 Ne7 11 h3). Sindarov’s last move prevents black’s light-squared bishop from coming to g4 and pinning the knight on f3, while giving his own king some breathing room.
“I think it’s important to highlight for our viewers that black is not playing for a draw,” the Hungarian grandmaster Judit Polgár says on Chess.com’s broadcast. “Black is just deciding to go into an endgame or a middlegame without queens, where it seems like only white has a slight edge. Black has doubled pawns on c6 and c7, black has the bishop pair, but basically black can go b6, develop the pieces properly.”
We’re heading straight into the famous Berlin endgame (4 O-O Nxe4 5 d4 Nd6 6 Bxc6 dxc6 7 dxe5 Nf5 8 Qxd8+ Kxd8). The queens are off the board after only eight moves, leaving white with a kingside pawn majority and black with the bishop pair but doubled c-pawns and a king that has forfeited the right to castle.
Don’t mistake the early exchange of queens for a lack of ambition. The resulting position is deceptively rich in strategic possibilities and has been the subject of decades of analysis at the highest level. Gukesh has continued with 9 Rd1+, and both players are still moving quickly.
The players have shaken hands and we’re off! We have a Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez (1 e4 e5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 Bb5 Nf6), one of the most thoroughly analyzed openings in modern chess.
The Berlin famously helped Vladimir Kramnik dethrone Garry Kasparov in their 2000 world title match in London and has been a staple of elite chess ever since, earning a reputation as one of black’s most reliable weapons against 1 e4.
We’re eight minutes to the scheduled first move, but American grandmaster Maurice Ashley has started with his introduction of the players to the playing hall. Gukesh enters first and takes his seat behind the black pieces. Sindarov, playing as white after Sunday’s drawing of lots, enters second.
If you’re looking for some pre-match reading, the Guardian spoke exclusively with Javokhir Sindarov on Sunday about his meteoric rise, his love of Lionel Messi, his plans to play GTA VI once the match is over and why chess’s happy warrior believes there’s more to life than the game. A taste:
“I’m the guy who can’t play games just for fun,” Sindarov tells the Guardian less than 48 hours before Tuesday’s world championship opener in Geneva, smiling at the absurdity of it. “If I play something, I always try to learn, trying to become better.”
That means poring over Counter-Strike tactics and watching YouTube tutorials before joining in with his mates. There is, it appears, no such thing as a casual game in Sindarov’s world, much less a friendly. “I always like to beat my friends,” he says. “I watch some video lessons and then come and beat them after some tournaments. I think the best thing is to beat your friends in some game.”
It is a revealing admission from a young man who has acquired a reputation for being uncommonly relaxed at the chess board. While many of the world’s elite players seem to carry the weight of every position on their shoulders – the viral clip of Sergey Karjakin agonizing for 25 minutes over a move during the 2016 world title match remains a cult classic in chess circles – Sindarov frequently gives off the impression of someone who is simply enjoying himself. The easygoing mien of the sport’s happy warrior is a quality that has caught his opponent’s attention. “One thing I learned from Sindarov is that he seems to be so happy while playing chess,” Gukesh Dommaraju, the reigning world champion, said in an interview published last week.
We’ve gone through the 140-year history of the world championship and chosen 22 of the most memorable games. You can go move by move through each of them here. It’s the perfect timesuck in the final run-up to today’s first move.
But not until Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort sat down in a small room at 80 Fifth Avenue in New York City on the afternoon of 11 January 1886 did a formal competition to determine the best player on the planet come to pass. Their first-to-10-wins encounter was held in three US cities over the next 78 days for a prize fund of $4,000. Since then, the world chess championship has provided the stage for countless unforgettable contests showcasing the precision, imagination and brilliance of the royal game at the highest level.
The legitimacy of the world championship, of course, remains a subject of lively debate. The absence of Magnus Carlsen continues to cast a long shadow over the sport’s showcase event. The 35-year-old Norwegian has held the world No 1 ranking for more than 15 consecutive years and was widely regarded as the game’s strongest player even before he defeated Vishy Anand for the world title in 2013. He only strengthened his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021, when he crushed Ian Nepomniachtchi in Dubai in his fourth successful defense of the crown.
But Carlsen declined to defend his title for a fifth time in 2023, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long grind of preparation that championship matches demand. Only twice before had the chain of succession that stretches back to Wilhelm Steinitz in 1886 been broken: when Alexander Alekhine died as champion in 1946 and when Bobby Fischer forfeited the title in 1975.
Ding Liren went on to defeat Nepomniachtchi for the vacant title before losing it to Gukesh Dommaraju in Singapore the following year. Now Gukesh faces Sindarov in a match between two 20-year-olds ranked No 26 and No 4 in the world respectively, while the planet’s top-ranked player remains on the sidelines – at a time when his No 1 ranking is looking more vulnerable than any time in anyone’s memory. The generational stakes are undeniable, but the question that has dogged the championship since Carlsen walked away remains unresolved: can the winner truly claim to be the best chess player in the world?
For two elite players born in the same general part of the world barely six months apart, their competitive history is remarkably sparse: just three encounters in classical chess. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. Sindarov also holds a 2-1 edge in their three rapid and blitz contests this year.
Gukesh’s form has largely gone off the rails since reaching the summit 23 months ago in Singapore. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad.
Many of the world’s top grandmasters have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently. “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.”
Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September. “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.”
Here’s a review of the format for the world championship match. Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played).
The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours, testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter.
If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023.
The complete official regulations can be found here.
Hello and welcome to Geneva for day one of the World Chess Championship. Over the next three weeks, India’s defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will compete in a scheduled best-of-14-games match for the sport’s most prestigious title and a share of a $2.5m prize fund. The setting is the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, an affluent suburb overlooking Lake Geneva, where the two 20-year-olds will make history as the youngest pairing ever to contest a world championship match in the competition’s 140-year history.
Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world chess champion in history when he defeated China’s Ding Liren in Singapore in December 2024, aged just 18, shattering the record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in 1985. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai-born grandmaster has struggled badly for form since winning the crown, sliding from a career-high No 3 to No 26 in the world rankings and raising questions over his chances of retaining the title in his first defense.
Sindarov, meanwhile, has emerged as one of the most formidable talents of a new generation of Uzbek grandmasters. Born in Tashkent, he became a grandmaster at 12 years and 10 months, the second-youngest in history at the time, and secured his place in Geneva by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament earlier this year. A fearless, resourceful player in a rich vein of form, he enters his first world championship match ranked fourth in the world, up from No 25 last year and a remarkable 22 places above the reigning champion, and with a favorable head-to-head record against Gukesh in classical chess.
We’re roughly 80 minutes away from the ceremonial opening moves. Fide president Timur Turlov will do the honors for white, with five-time world champion and Fide deputy president Viswanathan Anand moving for black. Plenty more to come between now and then.
Everything you need to know about the World Chess Championship
India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is defending the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov in the youngest title match in the competition’s 140-year history. The best-of-14-games contest is scheduled to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer outside Geneva, with an overall prize fund of $2.5m (£1.9m).
Game 1 starts at 3pm in Geneva, 2pm in London, 9am in New York and 7.30pm in India
Sindarov will have the white pieces for Game 1 and make the first move
Gukesh and Sindarov are both 20 years old, making this the youngest matchup in world championship’s 140-year history

title: Leader of India’s Cockroach movement says he was stopped from boarding flight to UK
text:
A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has said he was prevented from leaving Delhi to fly to the UK to give talks on the viral group’s protests.
Saurav Das, 27, has been at the forefront of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which has amassed millions of social media followers since its launch in May. Das, who was due to fly out early on Tuesday, said immigration officials told him at the airport that his passport had been flagged.
The incident comes a month after he was detained for defying a security crackdown in Delhi during protests demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner.
“This coward government did not allow me to board my flight to London where I was invited by prestigious universities like Oxford, Cambridge, LSE (London School of Economics), Edinburgh to deliver talks on the Cockroach movement,” Das said in a social media post late on Monday. “Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual government was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions.”
Das was due to speak at the Oxford Union society on 1 December.
CJP-organised protests in July over alleged examination irregularities forced the education minister to resign, marking a rare climbdown by the government of Narendra Modi.
Critics say human rights and press freedoms have declined since Modi came to power in 2014. Earlier this month, India barred more than 100 foreign speakers from attending a democracy summit organised by the opposition Congress party. Those denied visas included a Norwegian journalist who had previously questioned Modi about press freedom.
In 2022, authorities prevented Sanna Irshad Mattoo, an award-winning photographer from India-administered Kashmir, from flying to the US to collect her Pulitzer prize.

title: After 80 years in Oxford, Naga ancestors are finally going home
text:
The lacerating legacy of colonialism survives in many spaces, particularly in museum collections and private holdings across the western world. And it’s not just limited to inanimate artefacts or cultural objects.
For almost 80 years, human remains were displayed on crowded glass shelves at Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford University, one of the world’s most celebrated institutions.
Many of them were, in fact, skeletal remains taken from Nagaland brought to the museum by two British colonial administrators, John Henry Hutton and James Philip Mills between 1910 and 1940. Now, after six years of consultations, negotiations and a concerted effort to build consensus across Naga communities, 39 skeletal remains are finally coming home. In early November, the museum handed custodianship to a Naga delegation of leaders and scholars. The repatriated remains include those of two children, a woman and a village chief.
“This is the first such repatriation of human remains to India,” Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist and professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told me. She had contacted the Pitt Rivers Museum in 2020 after reading in the Guardian that the museum was removing human remains from public display following an ethical review, setting the repatriation process in motion. In a statement, the museum’s director, Laura Van Broekhoven, acknowledged that it has been a “long journey”, adding that “hope is possible as we work towards reconciliation and healing”.
The review was part of a broader reassessment of the museum’s display practices and how it presented human remains from communities across the world. Among its most contentious displays were the shrunken heads known as tsantsa, from the Shuar people in South America. Pitt Rivers – one of the world’s leading anthropology and ethnography museums – has acknowledged that its display reinforced racist stereotypes about the culture. The Naga remains were displayed alongside artefacts and human remains from a number of communities, including from Nigeria and Papua New Guinea.
Naga academics have challenged the perception that the remains were exclusively associated with the practice of headhunting. While Naga warriors traditionally collected the heads of enemies killed in raids, the anthropologists say that British collectors acquired Naga human remains under duress during colonial expeditions.
For the Naga community, that was just the beginning of a long journey. India, unlike countries such as Australia, Canada and the US, has no national laws for the repatriation of Indigenous ancestral remains, says Kikon. “We had to ensure the process was community-led, in the absence of a policy and make sure the focus remained on healing and reconciliation. It was all unprecedented.”
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a collective working toward peace and reconciliation among Naga Indigenous communities, facilitated the repatriation, and a voluntary research group, Recover, Restore and Decolonise (RRaD), was formed to build wider community awareness. Its volunteers travelled to urban centres and villages, talking with students, elders and intergenerational audiences about the human remains kept at the museum and what the community wanted to do with them.
The museum still has around 178 objects that contain, or may contain, human hair. It also has 6,500 Naga objects, including clothing items, weapons, vessels and musical instruments, many from Mills and Hutton, while some items, like weapons, were bought from auction houses. “The Pitt Rivers Museum has one of the largest collections of Naga objects, artefacts and human remains in the world. What we have focused on for now is the skeletal remains, but this is only a first step in thinking more broadly about these collections,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at Edinburgh University.
The question of restitution of Indian artefacts and cultural heritage items has long occupied a prominent place in public discourse. At its heart is the Koh-i-noor diamond, which passed through Mughal, Persian and Afghan hands before Britain wrested it from the 10-year-old king, Maharaja Duleep Singh. Today, it is part of the British crown jewels, a symbol of the plunder of the empire and, for many in India, a theft that continues to rankle. Last year, an Indian parliamentary committee recommended establishing a dedicated heritage recovery taskforce to pursue the return of cultural objects held abroad, particularly those taken during the colonial period.
 
In the case of the human remains, the question is about the right to honour the ancestors and give them a dignified resting place. “How we imagine a shared future depends on how we understand our history. We have to look back and make sense of the past in order to think about the kind of future we want to create,” Longkumer told me.
“The Naga repatriation addresses a very deep colonial violence,” Kikon says. “It is about the dehumanisation where the remains of human beings were stored in museums and exhibited as exotic objects.”
The return prompted Kikon to reflect on the contradiction between the longstanding reverence for Oxford University by Indians, many of whom have aspired to study there, and the institution’s history of exhibiting the remains of their ancestors. “Repatriation is not just about bringing back bones. It was about starting a process of deep introspection,” she says. “Ultimately, it leaves us with a greater responsibility to reflect on how we live our lives.”
The remains will be buried at Naga Solidarity Park in Kohima, the capital of Nagaland.
What else we’re reading about
Crime | A federal judge in New York sentenced Indian national Nikhil Gupta to almost 20 years in prison for an assassination plot against the Khalistan separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, an American citizen. The prosecutors argued that Gupta had been directed by an Indian government employee, a charge that India denies.
Politics | In a new report, Human Rights Watch argued that India’s democratic institutions have been systematically hollowed out under the Modi government, which has used state agencies to target critics, undermined parliamentary oversight and promoted Hindu majoritarianism. Based on dozens of interviews, and drawing from news reports, HRW describes these actions as part of a broader authoritarian move to concentrate executive power.
Arts | The second edition of the India Biennale, organised by the Ministry of Culture, begins in Delhi on 4 December. Highlights include photographer Dayanita Singh’s work on show at Humayun’s Tomb and artist Paresh Maity and fashion designer Ritu Beri’s installation at Qutub Minar.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Writer Gayatri Rangachari Shah, a founding member of the Women Leadership Circle, recommends an inspiring model of rural development. “If there is an institution that captures an alternative vision of India, it’s the Barefoot College in Rajasthan. Set up by Sanjit ‘Bunker’ Roy in 1972, it has spent more than five decades putting rural communities at the centre of their own development. Its Solar Mamas programme has enabled women of all ages who had never been to school to learn to make and install solar lights. Its other initiatives include digital learning centres for young women, night schools for those working during the day, menstrual-friendly toilets in government schools, rainwater harvesting, waste management and recycling.
Roy died on 10 November but he passed on his work to a younger team.”
Count it
99,000
India’s top wildlife body approved the clearance of ecologically sensitive land and wildlife corridors covering an area of at least 99,000 hectares (244,530 acres) – an area about a third larger than Singapore – between 2014 and 2026, an analysis by Article 14 concluded. Defence projects, mining and irrigation were the top sectors for which the board granted clearances at the expense of forests and wildlife habitats, according to the investigation by Prakriti Srivastava and Prerna Singh Bindra.
Vibe check
Grand Theft Auto VI, billed as the biggest cultural event of the year, has smashed sales records. It has also helped propel a little-known 1982 Indian disco track to global fandom. Aaj Shanibar by the Bengali singer Rupa Biswas features on Worldwide FM, one of the radio stations in the game.
The song was part of an album called Disco Jazz that Biswas recorded during a visit to her brother in Canada. The album never made a splash and faded into obscurity, but years later her son discovered the track had found a following in DJ sets and was reissued by the US label Numero Group. Now, with GTA VI, the song has reached a generation who were not even born when the original was released 44 years ago.
