title: Myanmar has been found guilty of genocide. Should Israel be worried? – podcast
text:
For seven years, Yasmin Ullah had been part of the delegation arguing that Myanmar had committed genocide – one of the gravest human rights crimes – against Rohingya Muslims.
The genocide has directly affected Yasmin and her family. Last week she was in court to hear the international court of justice’s landmark verdict against Myanmar. “I was really kind of pinching myself. It felt like we were all able to breathe again,” she tells Annie Kelly.
The verdict could have far-reaching consequences – especially for Israel, which is also facing a genocide case at the ICJ. The Guardian journalist Kaamil Ahmed explains how the case unfolded and what could happen next.

title: Ministers to create new stalking offence and scrap need for proof of fear or distress
text:
Ministers will create a new stalking offence so that victims will no longer have to prove fear or distress to seek protection under the law, the Home Office has announced.
Under current laws, the underlying offence of harassment in England and Wales, as well as additional factors such as the victim’s alarm, must be established for it to be considered stalking. The new law, alongside other changes, will focus on the perpetrator’s behaviour instead, officials said.
The move has been welcomed by family members of murdered stalking victims and organisations campaigning on behalf of women who have been the target of sustained harassment.
The parents of 24-year-old Alice Ruggles, who was murdered by her obsessed ex-partner in 2016, welcomed the findings and said they were “heartened” by the government’s commitment to clarify and strengthen the law.
Clive Ruggles and Sue Hills said changes would “bring in due protection for stoic victims like Alice”.
The victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the plan was welcome but added that the announcement was “an opportunity missed” because the government had not introduced measures to tackle convicted stalkers.
A review commissioned last year by the government and led by the barrister Richard Wright, who acted for the prosecution in Ruggles’ case, said the offence of stalking “needs to be both uncoupled from harassment and redrawn in its ambition and scope”.
Under two stalking offences introduced in England and Wales in 2012, the underlying offence of harassment must be established and additional factors such as fear or distress proved for it to be considered stalking.
In his review, Wright said that despite good intentions “we have arrived at a position where there are dozens of offences, all with very similar foundations, all tackling similar behaviour, using slightly different terminology, and having an array of different maximum penalties”.
He said: “If we add to that landscape the minefield of protective orders, with so many varieties and initialisms, created and amended in so many different pieces of legislation, the legislative position as a whole across the realm of interpersonal abuse offences is cluttered and confused.”
Alongside pledging to change the law to make stalking a standalone offence, the government has said it will strengthen sentencing so stalkers could face up to 10 years in prison.
In an immediate change, the Home Office said courts could now directly impose stalking protection orders (SPOs) to protect victims by restricting the alleged perpetrators’ behaviour, even if they have not yet been convicted.
A so-called “super-complaint’ from anti-stalking organisations in 2022 set out concerns including how there had been flawed investigations, instances where stalking was not being properly identified, and police officers “minimising or trivialising” such behaviour.
Waxman, who has been the victim of a stalker for 20 years, said the government had “missed a crucial opportunity by failing to address stalking that continues after conviction”. Her office wanted the government to give police powers to arrest convicted stalkers who repeat their criminal behaviour on one occasion.
“A conviction should not be a reset button for a stalker. Victims should not be left trapped in a cycle of abuse because the law fails to recognise continuing patterns of behaviour,” she said.
Emma Lingley-Clark, the interim chief executive of the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, said: “We fully support the government’s commitment to introduce a standalone stalking law, which we hope will reduce confusion and increase the shockingly low conviction rate for stalking, which is currently only 1.2% of stalking incidents recorded by police.”

title: Social media making it harder for UK parents to raise families, survey finds
text:
Parents of children aged five and under say pressure from social media influencers to be “the perfect parent” is making it harder to raise a family, according to a survey.
Three-quarters (76%) of those who took part in the UK-wide poll agreed social media had increased anxiety around parenting, while three out of five (59%) complained of “impossible expectations” and “feeling judged”.
What information to trust also emerged as an issue, with almost half (49%) concerned about conflicting online advice. While one in five (21%) said they were using AI tools such as ChatGPT for parenting information, only 12% trusted it.
There was also a lack of trust in official advice. Almost half (48%) thought it was harder to trust professionals’ advice than it was for previous generations, with many relying on their own instincts and online research instead.
Many of those who participated took the view that parenting today was more difficult than in the past – 66% said children’s needs were more complex, yet 71% believed parents today had a better understanding of their children’s needs.
Families who had a child with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) faced greater challenges – 69% reported difficulty accessing professional support, compared with 31% of non-Send families and 64% had struggled to understand information about services compared with 28%.
The survey also reveals parents living in social isolation without a safety network. One in eight (12%) had nobody outside their immediate household they could call on at an hour’s notice in an emergency. The risk of isolation is higher for social housing tenants and parents whose first language is not English.
About 3,500 parents of children aged five and under took part in the 2026 National Early Childhood Parenting Survey by the early years charity Kindred Squared, which also includes a range of parents’ voices drawn from focus groups.
On lack of trust in professional advice, one parent in the south-east said: “I feel like nowadays, your GP doesn’t really know you as much any more. Everything feels rushed, basically. You kind of have to diagnose yourself before you go to them.”
On social media pressures, a London parent said: “I was feeling this pressure to be perfect. You have to be perfect in everything. I think social media influencers really get into your head and make you think it’s possible to be that way, but in reality, it’s not.”
A parent in the south-west disagreed: “For me personally, social media did not increase my anxiety around parenting. They make it easier … It takes the pressure away from me and just lets me enjoy the moment.”
The survey, published on Thursday, suggests parenting has changed significantly in the space of a generation. “I love my parents,” said a West Midlands parent, “but they have no idea what it is like bringing up a child in 2026 … they don’t quite understand that it’s not as simple.”
“For me, I would say it’s different in the sense that we’re more emotionally aware of what’s happening with our children, with ourselves,” a parent in the south-west said. “Whereas I feel like the older generation … you just get on with it basically.”
Felicity Gillespie, Kindred’s chief executive, said the survey showed that most parents felt capable of looking after young children but the “levels of isolation, the feeling of being under pressure and the lack of trust in official advice are all striking”.
She went on: “I think this report clearly sets out that, for many parents, they feel that the task of raising children is tougher today than in previous generations.
“I hope these findings will inform policymakers at all levels who have a role in supporting parents and families because it’s quite clear that families with the youngest children need trustworthy, easy-to-access advice, the space to be the parents they want to be and, above all, we need to remove that overriding fear of being judged or being all alone.”
A Department for Education spokesperson said: “We want every child to have the best start in life, and that means supporting parents too with practical advice alongside measures to give families breathing space with the cost of living. That’s why we are giving working parents 30 hours of childcare, saving some families up to £8,000 a year.
“We’re also investing £900m for Best Start Family Hubs across England, giving parents a trusted place in their community for parenting support and help with their child’s health and development.
“Building on the proud legacy of Sure Start, we’re bringing early education, advice and support closer to families and giving children stronger foundations to thrive.”

title: Children in overcrowded homes get poorer GCSE results, study finds
text:
Children who share a bedroom and lack a quiet place to study at home get worse GCSE results than their peers, according to a major report on how poor housing affects education.
The research, carried out by leading academics at University College London for the Sutton Trust, a social mobility charity, urged UK ministers to ensure all young people in rented accommodation have space for a desk.
Nick Harrison, the chief executive of the trust, said: “The country’s housing crisis is blighting the prospects of a generation. The link between a child’s housing situation and their education shouldn’t be underestimated.
“Even the brightest child will struggle to succeed at school if they don’t have a safe and stable learning environment at home.”
The study found that children living in the worst housing conditions were less likely than their peers to get five good GCSEs, and less likely to get any A-levels.
The report called for a new policy ensuring children have a bedroom with space for a desk under the decent homes standard, a UK government benchmark for quality and safety in rented homes.
It also suggested schools and local authorities could be required to provide young people with access to quiet study space outside of the home, through extended opening hours, homework clubs and local libraries.
The record number of children living in temporary accommodation in England, which now stands at more than 170,000, is expected to exacerbate the attainment gap. The report found that those who had been homeless by age 14 were 18 percentage points less likely to achieve five good GCSEs.
The report’s co-author Gill Wyness, a professor of economics at UCL, said: “The raw differences between this homelessness experience, and GCSE and A level outcomes, were phenomenal.
“There are a bunch of kids out there who have to sit the same exams and are held to the same standard in their education, but don’t have the same conditions to learn in. It feels very unfair, and there are things we can do to improve this.”
Unlike previous research in this area, which normally considers a child’s access to learning materials and activities, academics looked at the “physical home learning environment” for children.
This was defined as whether they had their own bedroom, a quiet place to work and a home that was not considered overcrowded or noisy.
They found that young people from poorer families were more likely to lack space and a quiet place to study, and more than half (52%) of young people in the poorest fifth of families shared a bedroom at age 11, compared with 7% in the richest fifth.
The lack of a quiet place to study led to lower exam results: those who didn’t have a suitable study area scored lower at age 18 than their peers, despite being level at the end of primary school.
The report also found poor housing in childhood was linked to worse long-term employment, worse mental and physical health and lower life satisfaction into their mid-30s.
Each additional housing problem experienced by 11- to 15-year-old children left them three percentage points less likely to have a degree and three percentage points less likely to be in work in adulthood.
The Sutton Trust has called for a cross-departmental review of how housing policy impacts education, saying the Department for Education and the Ministry of Housing should work more closely.
Harrison said: “If we’re serious about improving educational outcomes and social mobility, we need to pay much greater attention to the housing circumstances in which young people are growing up.”
Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said: “Every child deserves the opportunity to build a better life and a safe, secure home is vital to this.”
She said the government was committed to ending the use of bed and breakfasts to house families and was putting a new duty on councils to ensure children in temporary accommodation get the support they need at school.

title: Patrick Radden Keefe’s London Falling named Waterstones book of the year
text:
London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestselling investigation into the mysterious death of a London teenager, has been named Waterstones book of the year.
The book follows the parents of Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell from the balcony of a luxury London apartment after pretending to be the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch, as they discover the murky, dangerous underworld of the city that their son had been drawn into.
In a Guardian review, Ian Thomson called it “a scrupulously researched work of narrative nonfiction”. “Grimly absorbing from start to finish,” he wrote, the book “opens a window on to a world of financial dirty work and Walter Mitty-like fantasies of aspirational wealth.”
Waterstones’ head of books, Bea Carvalho, said its word-of-mouth success “has been one of the defining features of the literary year”. Reading nonfiction is “vital, enriching, gripping and the buzz surrounding London Falling has helped so many readers discover this,” she added.
Radden Keefe, a staff writer at the New Yorker whose previous book Empire of Pain won the Baillie Gifford prize, said that at heart London Falling “is a story about family – about parents and children, about the perils of contemporary adolescence, and about how little we sometimes know the very people we love most”. The book was shortlisted for this year’s Baillie Gifford prize.
Meanwhile, Taiwan Travelogue by Yáng Shuāng-zǐ, translated by Lin King, which won the International Booker prize earlier this year, was named fiction book of the year. Yáng said it was “especially precious to see this story about Taiwan embraced and adored by the booksellers at Waterstones”.
Is This a Plum? by Oscar-nominated director Dan Ojari and his eight-year-old son, Finn, was named children’s book of the year. The cut-out picture book began when the pair realised “a plum looks a lot like a hippo’s bum”, said Dan. “Me and my dad made this book together – it’s very easy to read and will probably make you laugh at least once,” added Finn.
The winners will receive the “full and committed backing of Waterstones shops and booksellers across the UK”, according to the company.
Also on the shortlist were Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke, Stations by Louise Kennedy, The Book of Birds by Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris, Redwood by Ben Macintyre, Land by Maggie O’Farrell, May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry, Ottolenghi Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghi and Verena Lochmuller, The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout and John of John by Douglas Stuart, among others.
Both the shortlisted titles and the book of the year are nominated and chosen by a panel of Waterstones booksellers.
Last year’s winner was The Artist by Lucy Steeds, while The Café at the Edge of the Woods by Mikey Please was named children’s book of the year.

title: Andy Taylor, guitarist in Duran Duran, dies aged 65
text:
Andy Taylor, the guitarist with 80s pop megastars Duran Duran, has died aged 65.
He had been diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, which he disclosed publicly in 2022 when Duran Duran were about to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” read a statement shared with Variety. “He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.”
Taylor’s wife of more than 40 years, Tracey Wilson said his last few years were faced with “so much courage and determination” and that he “never los[t] his love of life”.
A statement from Duran Duran added: “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”
Musicians paid tribute once the news broke. Rod Stewart remembered Taylor as his “dear pal”.
“We made some good music together and at the same time had some outrageous fun,” Stewart wrote on Instagram.
Singer Belinda Carlisle called Taylor a “genius”. “He played the guitar solo on Mad About You, appears in the video and he made special appearances onstage for some of my first solo shows. What a talent,” she captioned a video of the pair performing together.
“Thank you Andy for the music and all of the joy you brought to the world which will live on forever. I hope you are feeling the love… Godspeed.”
Taylor was born in 1961 and grew up in Cullercoats, Northumberland, in a family who worked in the local fishing industry. He began playing guitar from the age of 11 and was tutored by Dave Black of the David Bowie backing band the Spiders from Mars. He left school early to start playing in bands on the working men’s club scene.
In 1980 he joined the nascent Duran Duran, who had formed in 1978 but whose lineup was far from settled – they advertised for a guitarist in Melody Maker, and Taylor travelled to Birmingham to audition. “A couple of days later they rang me and said out of 40 or so I was the only one who knew how to tune up, let alone play,” he later recalled.
The following month Simon Le Bon joined as frontman, by February 1981 they had released their debut single Planet Earth, and with the July release of Girls on Film – a song propelled by Taylor’s ultra-tight and rhythmic playing – they became major stars in the UK and US. Rio, their second album released in 1982, cemented their international playboy image and went Top 10 in both countries, and follow-up Seven and the Ragged Tiger topped the UK chart. Speaking to Smash Hits in 1983, Taylor described his new-found career as “a hobby gone mad”. That year Taylor also opened a wine bar called Rio, in Whitley Bay in his native Tyneside.
Following their third album Duran Duran went on a brief hiatus, during which time Taylor and bassist John Taylor (no relation) formed a new funk-rock group, the Power Station, with singer Robert Palmer and former Chic drummer Tony Thompson. Two singles, the original track Some Like It Hot and a cover of T Rex’s Get It On, reached the US Top 10 in 1985.
Later that year Taylor rejoined Duran Duran to record A View to a Kill, the US chart-topping James Bond film theme, and perform with them at Live Aid in Philadelphia. But amid drug use, relations had become strained: drummer Roger Taylor left due to exhaustion, and Andy Taylor himself left to pursue the rockier direction he began with the Power Station – though his Duran Duran bandmates initially believed he would be continuing with the band.
“I’d come close to a nervous breakdown from the stresses of our crazy life and my own cocaine problem,” Taylor later said. “Combine that with all the shouting matches and the icy silences – I just knew I had to get out. So I did. The day after Live Aid, I stopped drinking and taking drugs. And I quietly started getting legal advice on extricating myself from Duran Duran.”
Collaborating with Sex Pistols’ Steve Jones, he released a solo LP, Thunder, in 1986, and the single Take It Easy was a minor US hit. As well as recording a covers album, Dangerous, he spent a number of years as a writer and producer for hire, with his song Lost in You becoming a transatlantic hit for Rod Stewart in 1988.
The Power Station briefly reunited in 1996, and then in 2000, the classic lineup of Duran Duran reformed and released a new album together, Astronaut, in 2004. He also toured with the band and worked on another (later scrapped) album Reportage, but was hit hard by the death of his father to cancer, and left the band again in 2006; he was diagnosed with depression the following year.
He spent the next decade away from music, first publishing his memoir Wild Boy: My Life in Duran Duran in 2008. He released a new solo single in 2019 and joined British rock band Reef as a tour guitarist, also producing their 2022 album Shoot Me Your Ace.
Despite the at-times fractious relationship with Duran Duran over the years, Taylor said in his statement accompanying the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction that there was no “bad blood … just pure love and respect for everything we wrote, recorded and achieved together”.
He married Wilson in 1982, and they had four children together: Andrew, Georgina, Bethany and Isabella.
Following his cancer diagnosis, he credited his successful music career with keeping him upbeat. “I’ve been very fortunate, I’ve had so much, in terms of living the dream, but because I do music, I think that’s probably really helped me to live with pessimism of an incurable disease,” he said.

title: Chris Van Hollen picks up more support for Senate majority leader role ahead of Democrats vote next week – as it happened
text:
Senator-elect Troy Jackson backs Van Hollen over Schumer for Senate majority leader
Senator-elect Troy Jackson, of Maine, has endorsed Chris Van Hollen for Senate majority leader, a blow to the current minority leader, Chuck Schumer, ahead of a vote among Senate Democrats next Tuesday.
The Maryland senator has successfully cast himself as a “change” candidate following Democrats’ sweeping success in the midterms, whereas Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for the last decade, is seen as the “establishment” figure in the race, representing the status quo.
Van Hollen and the argument for a new generation of leadership has received backing from Bernie Sanders, incoming senators Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan and others, as well as some celebrity backing from the likes of Robert De Niro, JaneFonda, and others.
“I’ve talked with Mainers about what they need from the Senate, and I believe it’s time for a change in leadership.I’ll be voting for Senator Van Hollen,” Jackson said in a statement. “When we spoke, I told him Maine needs a seat at the table when the caucus decides what gets funded and what we’re going to fight for. I was impressed by his vision for the caucus, and I came away confident he’ll take Maine’s priorities seriously.
“From one end of Maine to the other, I heard the same thing. People are working harder, falling further behind, and getting tired of being told to wait. Senator Van Hollen and I agree that it’s time to end the filibuster, pass Medicare for All, and give working people a raise by increasing the minimum wage. I want a leader who’ll bring those fights to the floor and make every senator say where they stand.
“Mainers voted for change in November, and they ought to get it. Whoever leads this caucus, I’ll fight like hell to make sure the Senate takes on the problems Mainers sent me to Washington to solve.”
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:

Donald Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year.

Trump administration tries to blame Obama for explosives in Iowa US army was concerned about in 2004
Faced with criticism for the US army’s potentially hazardous detonation on Wednesday of a stockpile of the bomb-making material lead azide in Middleton, Iowa, the Trump administration made a concerted effort on Wednesday to place the blame on former president Barack Obama.
In public comments, Donald Trump, JD Vance and Stephen Miller, all claimed, without evidence, that the hazardous explosives were improperly stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in 2009.
They made this claim despite the fact that the US army said in a 2014 publication still available online that a project to move away from the use of lead azide “started in 2004 in response to the Department of Defense’s concerns over a 40-year-old stockpile of lead azide deteriorating at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.”
In 2004, Obama was an Illinois state lawmaker running for the US Senate and George W Bush was president.
The White House did not reply to a request to explain how it came to the conclusion that a problem identified in 2004 could be called “a dangerous mess the Obama Administration left behind,” or say what action the first Trump administration took to address the problem between 2017 and 2021.
The dangers of the lead azide at the Iowa plant were noted decades earlier, in a report from the US army’s toxic and hazardous materials agency, published in January 1980, when Jimmy Carter was president and Obama was a freshman in college. The report explained that, between 1966 and 1970, 4,700 canisters containing lead azide were destroyed there.
Nonetheless, Rob Cekada, the director of the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives claimed on Wednesday, “we were handed a problem frankly that started in 2009”.
“We learned that these lead azide explosives were brought here from a stockpile outside of the Middleton area and transported here to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant and placed in the earthen-covered magazines, H2 and H3,” Cekada added, without offering any explanation of what his assertion was abased on.
“At the time those records showed that these were already old, degraded lead azide explosives and were already a concern for the military at that time,” he went on, again failing to explain what records he was referring to. “Unfortunately, under that administration, nothing was done to handle that issue.”
“This administration came together quickly in March of 2026, developed a plan to properly mitigate the threat caused by these explosives,” Cekada, a former police officer with no military background said.
A day earlier, Cekada told reporters: “from what we’ve learned, in about 2009 the nation’s stockpile was moved here to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. That stockpile contained approximately 10,000 pounds. Some of that lead azide was already 60-plus years old, and in many cases it was noted that there was some deterioration, in 2009.”
Earthjustice, a nonprofit public interest environmental law group that challenged the detonation permit given to the army by the Environmental Protection Agency, told the Guardian that the same claim was made in a sworn declaration filed in court on Monday by a senior military officer. In that declaration, Major General Eric P. Shirley told the court: “The lead azide has been stored at IAAAP since 2009”.
Senator Chris Van Hollen calls out Trump administration 'lies' about Kilmar Ábrego Garcia
Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat who played a central role in helping his undocumented constituent Kilmar Ábrego Garcia fight his unlawful deportation to El Salvador last year, denounced the Department of Homeland Security for making unsubstantiated allegations about Ábrego on social media on Wednesday.
Ábrego voluntarily left the United States on a flight for Spain on Tuesday night, bringing an end to the 20-month legal battle that followed his wrongful deportation to El Salvador, in violation of a court order.
In an interview with CSPAN earlier on Wednesday, Van Hollen said that he spoke with Ábrego and his wife, Jennifer, who is a US citizen, shortly before the boarded a flight from Madrid.
“What the Trump administration has been trying to do for the last year and a half is engage in a vendetta against Kilmar Ábrego Garcia because he stood up for his constitutional rights,” Van Hollen added. “So they brought a malicious and vindictive prosecution against him and they tried to force him to go to a country or countries that have records of human rights abuses. They essentially tried force him into one of those countries and punish him because he’d stood up for his constitutional rights. They were forced to back down from that.”
On Wednesday, the senator, who is running to lead the new Democratic majority in the Senate, responded to a post from the DHS calling Ábrego a gang member, writing:
Lies, lies & more lies from the same folks who called Renee Good & Alex Pretti “terrorists” after they were gunned down by DHS agents. Your “goal” was for Kilmar to rot forever in a gulag & deny him the due process he, & every person in this country, is owed under our Constitution. As I said from day 1, this was never about Kilmar, it was about his rights. It is BECAUSE we fought to protect his rights that all of ours are a little safer today.
The incoming US House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, said on Wednesday that the new Democratic majority in Congress must “move aggressively to end the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran; not simply in the first 100 days, but during the first 100 hours.”
Jeffries made the comment in an interview with Ben Meiselas, a founder of MeidasTouch, an influential progressive podcast network.
Meiselas also asked Jeffries to commit, on-camera, to a list of 14 legislative priorities so that they could do another interview at the end of next year “and see what was it that the House Democrats accomplished”.
Here is the list of policies Jeffries committed to pursue in 2027:
pass the Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act, which the AFL-CIO says “restores the right of workers to freely and fairly form a union”;
advance a constitutional amendment to overturn the Citizens United ruling that undermined campaign finance spending limits;
advance legislation toward universal health care;
ban partisan and mid-decade gerrymandering;
ban congressional stock trading;
raise the federal minimum wage;
end the Iran war;
repeal Trump’s tariffs';
reverse Medicaid and SNAP cuts;
restore Affordable Care Act tax credits;
reform the immigration system and pass the Dream and Promise Act;
pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Act and combat voter suppression;
Trump's efforts to rollback birthright citizenship face latest setback
A federal judge has barred the Trump administration from restricting the birthright citizenship of babies born in the US to foreign government workers.
“Children born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are American citizens from birth. That rule, enshrined in the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause and codified in the Immigration and Nationality Act, derives from the English common law and is deeply rooted in our legal tradition,” US district judge Christopher Cooper wrote in a Wednesday opinion.
The ruling comes months after the Supreme Court blocked an executive order, where Trump sought to deny automatic citizenship for US newborns, whose parents were not citizens.
The president signed new executive orders in August with a narrowed scope, targeting the infants of foreign diplomats and members of “foreign terrorist organizations.”
That directive was also aimed at people engaged in birth tourism, a practice where people travel solely to the US for the purpose of giving birth and securing citizenship for their child.
Although birth tourism represents a small portion of annual births, it has been touted often in Trump’s case against automatic citizenship.
Former vice-president Al Gore, who started his career as a journalist, is returning to the industry as a newspaper owner in his Tennessee town.
The Lake family, which has operated the Carthage Courier for five decades, said yesterday that it will sell the paper to Gore in the coming weeks. The weekly paper serves Smith County in central Tennessee, which has roughly 20,000 residents and sits about 55 miles east of Nashville.
As the beleaguered news industry struggles with newspaper closures and growing news deserts, Gore characterized the purchase as a move that preserves an independent local voice in Carthage and Smith County.
“Having spent my early years as a military reporter in Vietnam and later at the [Nashville] Tennessean, I am a firm believer that a free, independent local press is irreplaceable for the enduring health of our community,” Gore said in a statement to the Associated Press.
Before entering politics, Gore spent six months as a military reporter in the US army during the Vietnam War. He returned to Tennessee and worked for a few years as an investigative reporter at The Tennessean before running for Congress in 1976.
Gore, a Democrat, represented Tennessee in both chambers of Congress, served as Bill Clinton’s vice-president from 1993 to 2001, and ran for president twice. After losing the 2000 presidential election to George W Bush, he went on to win the Nobel Peace Prize for his climate activism. He also narrated and was the subject of the Academy Award-winning documentary film “An Inconvenient Truth”.

The vice-president told reporters he supported Huang being reinstated after receiving “assurances” from the attorney general, Todd Blanche, and other top US officials that Huang was “under no investigation”. Trump and Vanceintervened in Nvidia’s leadership drama and put pressure on the tech company’s board to reinstall Huang despite other lawmakers’ concerns over whether he posed a national security risk for having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Ariana Baio has the story.

Instead, Blanche concluded that there was no evidence the tech titan had broken any laws based on the DOJ’s ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China, said Reuters’ sources.

Donald Trump’s meeting with Mark Rutte, the secretary-general of Nato has been moved to 7pm and will be followed by a dinner, the White House has said.
Trump administration approves Elon Musk’s plan for datacenters in space
Edward Helmore
US federal regulators approved a constellation of datacenters to process data in space today, saying that they would “support America’s booming super intelligence economy”.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said in a statement that regulators had approved 1m Starmind orbital satellites, or compute modules, built by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. It is the first such authorization in US history.
The FCC said that the authorization “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”.
“America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence,” said the FCC chair, Brendan Carr.
Boosters of the plan have argued that datacenters in space are essential as the AI industry grows and their cost on Earth on the power grid and water supply are high.
“By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial datacenters,” SpaceX had argued to the FCC.
But critics say the technology for such space datacenters is still being developed, and their deployment is a long way off.
Under the license approved today, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of the maximum number – or 100,000 – no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038, the FCC said.
Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under investigation before reinstatement as Nvidia CEO
JD Vance has said that he was assured by the US Department of Justice that Jensen Huang “was under no investigation” ahead of his surprise reinstatement as Nvidia CEO yesterday.
Speaking to reporters at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio, the vice-president said:
We received assurances that he was under no investigation.
“It was ultimately the board’s decision to bring Jensen Huang back,” he added, a day after Donald Trump took credit for “convincing” Nvidia’s board of directors to reinstall Huang as chief executive.
Trump earlier today expressed he’d be open to pardoning Huang for potential crimes but didn’t think it would be necessary. Asked about that, Vance replied, “Well, I don’t think he needs a pardon at all,” as, he said, there was no evidence that Huang committed a crime.
Nvidia’s products are a very important part of the “SI race”, , Vance continued (referring to Trump’s preferred term “super-intelligence”, rather than “artificial intelligence”).
“We really do care about those chips not falling into the wrong hands,” Vance said, adding this was an opportunity for Nvidia “to focus on complying with American export controls and we think Jensen Huang is going to take it very seriously.”
Earlier, Reuters reported that the US justice department did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his return as Nvidia chief executive this week, despite active probes into the chipmaker’s customers and allegations Huang conducted an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Instead, attorney general Todd Blanche concluded that there was no evidence the tech titan had broken any laws based on the DOJ’s ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China, said Reuters’ sources.
That determination, which is subject to change as the probes continue, was reportedly crucial to Blanche’s decision to tell Trump and Vance over the weekend that he possessed no evidence that Huang posed a risk to national security.
Speaking to reporters today, Sandoval-Moshenberg confirmed that US district judge Paula Xinis ordered the federal government to “withdraw all impediments” for Abrego Garcia to leave the country — including a GPS ankle monitor. In exchange Abrego Garcia was required to leave the US by 24 November.
“I’ll just share candidly that when we tried to check him in online on Monday, we couldn’t do it,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said. “And then on Tuesday, we were able to because the government had, presumably, complied with the judge’s order to take him off of any sort of no fly list.”
'I feel free of everything evil': Kilmar Abrego speaks to reporters just hours after arriving in Spain
Shrai Popat
Kilmar Abrego Garcia told reporters on Wednesday that he feels “free of everything evil that has followed me up until this point”.
“I’m happy this time because this time I’m leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely,” Abrego Garcia said on a press call just hours after arriving in Madrid, Spain.
He added: “The government did did not decide where my story continues. My family and I decide our future.”
Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant who had been living in Maryland, was deported by the Trump administration to Cecot last, the country’s notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison, even though a court had barred his removal to El Salvador because of gang threats against his family.
“I’m glad that the Trump administration did not succeed at what they wanted to do,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat who traveled to El Salvador to visit Abrego Garcia in April last year. “They wanted to leave him there to rot for the rest of his life. Instead, we saw our judicial system work alongside a strong legal team to produce this outcome, where Kilmar Abrego Garcia is able to chart his own future.”
Van Hollen, who is vying to become Senate majority leader when Democrats regain control of Congress next year, has made Abrego Garcia’s case and opposition to the administration’s sweeping deportation crackdown central to his vision for the party.
“Abrego Garcia’s journey is an example of our Constitution working despite the attacks of the Trump administration,” Van Hollen added. He said he had spoken with the Spanish ambassador to the United States, Ángeles Moreno Bau, and briefed her on “all the wrongs that have been committed by the Trump administration against Kilmar Abrego Garcia”, adding that he was pleased Abrego Garcia was now in Spain and able to continue telling his story”.
Abrego Garcia, who is married to a US citizen and shares a young son with her, was returned to the United States following a supreme court ruling. The administration has since sought to deport him again, exploring transfers to several African countries.
“Instead of flying ICE Air, he flew United Airlines,” said Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, Abrego Garcia’s co-counsel.“Instead of being in shackles, he was in economy plus. And there’s really no other way to see this other than Mr Abrego Garcia’s decision to hold strong throughout the last two years of this process.”
Sandoval-Moshenberg said his legal team would eventually be able to disclose Abrego Garcia’s next destination after Spain, but added that a pathway exists for him to obtain permanent residency in the United States in the near future.
“This is a short-term absence from the US,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said.
While Abrego Garcia did not take questions on Wednesday, he underscored the need to “keep fighting”.
“I’m happy. My family’s with me. There’s a tremendous community with me,” he said.
The Trump administration did not open a formal investigation into Jensen Huang, the Nvidia CEO, before Donald Trump urged the board to reinstate him, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Instead, Todd Blanche, the attorney general, concluded the Justice Department (DOJ) had no evidence to indicate Huang broke any laws based on the department’s ongoing investigations into two of Nvidia’s clients, including Megaspeed International – the company suspected of smuggling chips into China.
Blanche was vague with reporters on Tuesday, refusing to directly say whether the DOJ had conducted an investigation, instead claiming law enforcement “looked into” the situation to make a final determination.
The probe of Nvidia’s clients found no evidence that Huang acted as an agent of China or provided sensitive information about semiconductors to China, sources told Reuters.
Donald Trump insisted, on Wednesday, that stocks were down “because of the November Third Election results” rather than waning confidence in AI and tech companies, new tariff proposals or rising inflation.
“Stocks are down sharply because of the November Third Election results. I wasn’t on the Ballot, but if I was, the results, just like all three times before, would have been much different, and the Stock Market, and your 401-k’s, would be BOOMING. I told you so!!!” Trump wrote, indirectly blaming the Democratic Party’s sweeping wins earlier this month.
However, other facts appear to be contributing to the stock market’s performance.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index also fluctuated in the wake of drama over Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang. Despite being reinstalled as the company’s leader, the Nasdaq was down by more than two percentage points.

title: Record-breaking California tides cause major flooding of roads and businesses
text:
Super El Niño weather brought record-breaking high tides up and down the California coast on Wednesday, sending seawater rushing into beachside communities and flooding roads and businesses.
As big waves battered the coast, the tip of a landmark pier in Pacifica, south of San Francisco, was slammed into the sea, local news outlets reported. The pier, which had once housed a favorite local cafe, had previously suffered structural damage and had been closed to the public, the San Francisco Chronicle reported, and collapsed after contact with ocean swells 12 times stronger than on an average November day.
Los Angeles and Santa Barbara tied or broke all-time high tide records on Wednesday, at 8.19 and 8.21ft, respectively, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). La Jolla, California, just north of San Diego, also set an all-time high tide record of 8.11ft (2.5 meters), according to the NWS, while preliminary data suggested that tides in Monterey, south of San Francisco, might also have set an all-time record at 8.03ft.
The city of Monterey closed multiple beaches to the public over safety concerns, with closures lasting until Friday. Beaches in Santa Cruz county were also closed.
“That sun may be out, but the beach and surf zone remain dangerous,” NWS San Francisco warned, citing waves around the San Francisco Bay area as high as 24ft.
“This is a preview of things to come,” California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, said in a San Francisco press conference about Wednesday’s flooding. “That’s why it’s so important that we not just situationally address and reflect on moments like this, but sustainably get under the hood and try to solve for some of these things.”
In Pacifica, giant waves and tide waters swept over beaches and piers, flooding coastal roads including Highway 1 near the famous local landmark Taco Bell Cantina, America’s poshest Taco Bell. (The iconic restaurant was unharmed by the tides, NBC Bay Area reported.)
“This El Niño is unprecedented with its strength,” the San Mateo county supervisor Ray Mueller told the Los Angeles Times. “For this to be happening when it is a beautiful day on the coast side today, in clear sunshine and no wind, is really significant.”
Multiple coastal homes in Sunset Beach, in Orange county, had flooded, the Los Angeles Times reported, but a local fire chief said the overall damage had been mitigated by how aggressively local homeowners had fortified their homes in advance.
Low-lying coastal roads around the Bay Area also saw flooding, including a stretch of road near the Golden Gate Bridge, which was temporarily closed, the Chronicle reported.
However, most of the state avoided the worst-case scenario – coastal flooding amplified by intense winter rainstorms.
“We’re past high tide, and San Francisco has made it through the worst of this round of king tides,” mayor Daniel Lurie said in a social media statement just after noon local time, saying officials were “only aware of minimal impacts across the city”.
Local officials had been preparing for weeks for the risk that flooding would disrupt travel during Thanksgiving week, one of the busiest times of the year. Experts warn that flooding risk will only worsen in the next two months.
Flooding risk at the San Francisco international airport, a major transit hub situated on low-lying coastal land, had been of particular concern. At least three airlines offered free trip changes to travelers whose journeys took them through San Francisco on Wednesday, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
But the airport announced at noon that “We’re in the clear,” and said it was deactivating its emergency operations center after avoiding any impact from the high tides on Tuesday and Wednesday.
On the north coast, the NWS reported that Humboldt Bay saw its second highest tide on record, and advised residents to prepare for major coastal flooding in low lying areas. The county sheriff warned the public to stay away from beaches during the storm.
A local news outlet in Oregon shared a video on Tuesday that illustrated the risk of the west coast’s high-tide surf, showing a man and his dog almost getting swept away by unexpectedly high waves during the king tides in Cannon Beach, Oregon. Both man and dog escaped without injury, police told KVAL News.
The California governor’s office of emergency services deployed crews and equipment around the state to assist with storm response. In the Bay Area, crews could be seen preparing sandbags to help protect buildings from flooding.
California’s flooding risk this week is the result of a combination of factors, some of them driven by this year’s super El Niño weather, including the lingering effects of the massive Kelvin wave that traveled up California’s coast. The overlap of unusually high Pacific coast water levels this year with the seasonal high tides called “king tides” has sparked alarm from weather experts, who have warned that the most dangerous flooding is likely to occur if a strong winter storm with heavy wind and rain hits areas of the coast at the same time as the high tide’s peak.
So far, it seems like California has avoided the worst of that risk during the November king tide period. But the amplified king tides will return twice more, around late December and then in late January, in periods where big winter storms remain likely.
Dani Anguiano contributed reporting

title: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie settle years-long legal battle over joint French winery
text:
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a years-long legal battle over their French winery, according to a joint statement from the former Hollywood couple.
“We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further,” representatives for Jolie and Pitt said in a statement. “Any comments in media stories attributed to ‘sources’ are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us.”
Both sides have moved to dismiss claims against each other. The terms of the agreement were not made public.
The couple had bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008, and married there in 2014.
Jolie initiated divorce proceedings in 2016, and the couple was declared legally single in 2019, although their divorce settlement continued to play out until 2024. Jolie was cleared to sell her share in 2021 for $164m (£125.06m) before their wider financial settlement was finalized.
Pitt filed the lawsuit against Jolie in February 2022, after the actor sold her stake in the French winery to the Stoli Group, a spirits maker controlled by oligarch Yuri Shefler. In the suit, Pitt said Jolie had broken their agreement not to sell their interests in the winery without the other’s consent after she sold her stake to the Russian businessman.
In October 2022, Jolie filed a counter lawsuit against Pitt, which for the first time described alleged abusive behavior that led to their divorce. The actor’s attorneys said negotiations for Jolie to sell her share in the winery to Pitt broke down over his demand that she sign “a nondisclosure agreement that would have contractually prohibited her from speaking outside of court about Pitt’s physical and emotional abuse of her and their children”. Pitt denied the accusations.

title: New York City’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade postponed due to weather
text:
New York City’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade has been postponed due to excessively windy weather and will now be held on Saturday.
Forecasters say an impending storm on Thursday may spoil the street party, which is marked by a march of huge balloons. AccuWeather is forecasting winds of 12 to 25 mph (19 to 40 km/h) and rain later on Thursday.
Under guidelines, large balloons must stay grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 km/h) or gusts exceed 34 mph (55 km/h). The parade balloons have been grounded only once previously, in 1971.
NBC quoted Macy’s as saying: “The safety of our participants and spectators is our priority.”
Macy’s added: “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.”
This year the parade will include a tribute to Dolly Parton led by Megan Hilty, and special appearances by Melissa Joan Hart, Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer and Holly Robinson Peete, all leading the way for Santa Claus. Nine Broadway shows will be featured as part of a 10-minute medley, replacing the traditional sprinkling of full show numbers.
The Macy’s parade began more than a century ago in 1924 as a way of creating buzz for the giant department store’s holiday windows at Macy’s Herald Square flagship store in Manhattan. Macy’s borrowed animals from the Central Park Zoo for the first parades but in 1927 ended that practice after children were getting scared.
The animals were then replaced with air-filled balloons and, a year later, balloons that could be filled with helium – a now familiar sight for people around the world from countless Hollywood movies set in New York City.
The parades have been fully cancelled previously only in 1942, 1943 and 1944 because the valuable materials needed to create the huge balloons were diverted for the the second world war effort against Germany and Japan.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Oregon man and dog narrowly escape being swept away by high tides as officials urge caution at beaches
text:
The US west coast has seen record-breaking tides this week and authorities have urged residents to avoid beaches, but not everyone is heeding those warnings.
In Cannon Beach, Oregon, viral footage showed a man and his dog nearly getting swept away by a so-called king tide on Tuesday morning. The man had been standing on a staircase holding his leashed dog, who was walking in the sand, when the water suddenly surged, knocking him to his feet.
They ultimately escaped without injury, according to the Cannon Beach police department. Earlier that morning, police had cited the same man for driving on the shoreline. He had reportedly “indicated” to an officer he wanted to get a better look at the high tides.
Other footage captured around Cannon Beach on Tuesday morning showed a jogger narrowly avoiding a major wave, while another stood amid the wave seemingly filming.
King tides are the highest tide cycles of the year. This winter, conditions caused by the super El Niño have pushed these tides to record levels, contributing to widespread flooding, powerful waves and coastal erosion.
The Cannon Beach police department advised residents to stay off beaches and keep pets away from the water.
“King tides are an impressive natural phenomenon, but no photograph, video or closer look is worth risking your life, the life of your pet or the lives of the first responders who may be called upon to rescue you,” the police department said in a statement.
A coastal flood advisory is in effect for the region through Thursday, according to the National Weather Service, as “king tides, elevated seas, and the arrival of fresh swells likely lead to tidal overflow”.

title: Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court cancels major power contract
text:
Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court cancels major power contract
The court’s five-to-four ruling ends Luma Energy’s operations after a contentious legal battle.
In a tight vote, Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has ruled in favour of ending the government’s contract with Luma Energy following a controversial legal battle with the private power company.
The five-to-four ruling made public on Wednesday envisions a one-year transition period.
Power outages have continued to dog the Caribbean island since Hurricane Maria inflicted vast damage to power infrastructure in 2017, leading to years of bitter recriminations over financial and policy autonomy in the US territory.
The San Juan government sued Luma nearly a year ago, following up on a campaign promise made by Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez to cancel the contract.
Luma has faced protests for years from Puerto Ricans, who raised concerns about the cost and quality of its services.
Gonzalez said her administration would seek a new company within the year awarded by the court. She assured that transmission and distribution operations would not revert to Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority, from which Luma had initially taken over in 2021.
She blamed Luma for “constant interruptions” and “unnecessary outages”, asserting they have enough funds to provide proper service, as she accused the company of driving the cost of electricity in the territory to record highs.
Meanwhile, a federal control board that oversees the island’s finances issued a statement saying its immediate concern is the continuity of power services.
“The Puerto Rican government’s decision to terminate the contract creates enormous uncertainty at a time when the people and businesses of Puerto Rico look for stability,” the board said, noting that there is no “clear plan or successor company in place”.
But Gonzalez rejected those concerns, bluntly saying, “There will be no chaos.”
Tensions in court
With the narrow ruling came allegations that judges had been pressured to vote in favour of cancellation.
Judge Angel Colon Pérez, who voted against the cancellation, asserted that the final ruling stemmed from “an excessive eagerness to satisfy a capricious request from the leader currently in power”, in an apparent reference to the governor.
However, Judge Roberto Feliberti Cintron, who was part of the majority vote, sharply denied the allegations.
“We do not bow to external pressures, we do not yield to intimidation, nor do we allow smear campaigns to influence the exercise of our judicial function,” Cintron wrote. “Our obligation is to the Law, Justice, the People, and our conscience.”
Luma also commented on the allegations.
“In light of the serious allegations that have been raised publicly regarding attempts to influence the Court, we reiterate our call for an immediate, rigorous, and transparent investigation,” it said.
The company said in a statement on Wednesday that it disagrees with the court’s decision but will respect the judicial process and is “carefully evaluating all available legal alternatives”.

title: Six killed, including children, in plane crash off Mississippi coast
text:
Six killed, including children, in plane crash off Mississippi coast
US authorities are investigating the reason behind the crash that killed members of the Stokes and Knox families.
First responders have found the bodies of six members of two families, including three children, killed in a small plane crash off the coast of Mississippi, United States.
Authorities are investigating the cause of the crash on Tuesday. Relatives said they were on their way home from a fishing trip.
The passengers were members of two families returning home to Fort Myers, Florida, from New Orleans Lakefront airport, Louisiana.
The plane’s pilot, Brent Stokes, 50, was president of a marine contracting company based in Fort Myers, according to Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd Jr. Stokes’s company’s website described him as an “avid fisherman and life time boater”.
The other victims were Stokes’s 16-year-old son, Hunter; Stokes’s sister, Arlyn Knox, 43; her husband, Michael Knox, 43; and their two sons, 12-year-old Charles Holden Knox and 10-year-old Truett Knox.
Lynd said autopsies are being performed on Brent Stokes and Michael Knox, who was also a licensed pilot.
Responders searched for hours and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane’s cabin floating on the water, according to coastguard spokesperson Juan Ros.
Divers found their bodies in the fuselage part of the plane after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore.
The Knox and Stokes families confirmed their deaths in an emailed statement provided to The Associated Press news agency.
“They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family,” the statement said.
Weather’s potential impact
The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported at about 3:45pm (21:45 GMT) on Tuesday that it had lost contact with the aircraft, according to the coastguard.
Shortly before losing contact with the plane, an air traffic controller at Gulfport–Biloxi International airport advised the pilot of precipitation and adverse weather in the area.
The plane had been flying at about 9,000 feet (2,743 metres), above the bottom of the cloud layers when it began descending rapidly in a right-hand turn, according to FlightAware tracking data analysed by Steven Arroyo, a retired airline captain with 50 years of flying experience.
“It’s highly, highly irregular,” Arroyo told AP. “I think it’s safe to say this aircraft had some serious problems.”
Todd Curtis, an aviation expert and former Boeing safety engineer, said that nothing appeared out of the ordinary based on the publicly available audio recordings.
But he noted that precipitation in below-freezing temperatures can cause dangerous icing, potentially leading to inaccurate instrument readings or loss of lift. It is unclear whether the plane had a de-icing system.

title: Brazil blasts ‘unacceptable’ new US tariff proposals
text:
Brazil blasts ‘unacceptable’ new US tariff proposals
President Lula’s office says Brazil will not yield to threats and aims for a negotiated resolution.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has voiced outrage over new tariffs proposed by US President Donald Trump’s administration on Brazilian aircraft and sugar.
Brazil was not ruling out “reciprocal measures”, Lula’s office said in a statement on Wednesday after the US proposed a 10 percent tariff on finished aircraft made by Brazilian planemaker Embraer.
“The unilateral decision by the USTR [Office of the United States Trade Representative] is an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the statement continued.
Washington also plans to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas to rectify what it calls “unreasonable” trade practices.
The new tariff rate would ensure that sugar from Brazil could not be shipped through third countries into the United States, the USTR’s office said.
The move is part of a broader wave of proposed tariffs targeting 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said his office was proposing changes to tariffs imposed in July after Brazil made “no meaningful progress” on the issues.
Greer said Washington remains open to talks.
Brasilia said it had been negotiating “in good faith” with Washington for more than a year and that the two sides had agreed to establish a working group on trade issues in August.
The president’s office said Brazil would continue to seek “a negotiated solution” without indicating whether the country would exercise its right to challenge the proposed tariffs before the World Trade Organization.
The tariffs, which could take effect as early as January, could raise the price US carriers pay for Embraer jets at a time when they are already grappling with a surge in jet fuel prices due to the US war on Iran.

title: Anthropic CEO Amodei denies wanting humanity to ‘surrender’ free will to AI
text:
Anthropic CEO Amodei denies wanting humanity to ‘surrender’ free will to AI
Dario Amodei’s remarks come amid predictions that AI may soon match or surpass human intelligence.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has denied believing that humanity should “surrender” control to artificial intelligence amid predictions that models potentially far exceeding human intelligence are imminent.
In a lengthy post on X on Wednesday, Amodei said he does not support surrendering “human free will” to AI and has long argued that the frontier technology should be subject to “legitimate democratic processes”.
“If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years,” Amodei said, responding to an Axios report about a purported “consensus” inside Anthropic that some decision-making authority should be passed to the technology.
“But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.”
Amodei’s remarks come amid a flurry of commentary by top industry executives suggesting that AI will soon match or surpass human intelligence.
The prospect of AI that equals or outperforms the best human minds – referred to as artificial general intelligence (AGI) and artificial super-intelligence (ASI), respectively – has fuelled intense debate in Silicon Valley and beyond about whether such technology can be harnessed for good without exposing humanity to catastrophic harm.
AI safety advocates have raised fears that models being developed by firms such as Anthropic, which made history last week in the biggest initial public offering of all time, could slip out of human control, particularly once systems start improving without human input, a process known as recursive self-improvement.
In his X post, Amodei criticised commentary he said conflated the idea of AI taking over specific tasks with surrendering control in a “grand sense of global governance”.
“This is not AI ‘running the world’, but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end,” Amodei said.
“Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc.”
“It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives,” he added. “But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.”
Citing unnamed sources, Axios reported on Wednesday that Amodei and other Anthropic executives believe it would be irrational “or even unethical” not to hand over authority to AI for tasks it can do better than humans, such as curing diseases.
‘We’re getting close now’
David Krueger, the founder of Evitable, a nonprofit that advocates for a pause on development of ASI, said Anthropic should pause its work if Amodei is genuinely concerned about humanity losing control of frontier models.
“We don’t have to consciously surrender control to AI to lose it. As AI becomes increasingly capable, there will be mounting pressure to push humans out of decision-making roles across society,” Krueger told Al Jazeera.
“Meanwhile, researchers at Dario’s own company are warning that AI capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to control them. We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”
While there is no universally agreed-upon definition of AGI or ASI, key tech industry figures have over the past week suggested that the milestones are near.
Google DeepMind’s chief AGI scientist and cofounder, Shane Legg, said on Wednesday he believes there is a more than 50 percent chance that “minimal” AGI arrives before 2028.
“We’re getting close now,” Legg said on X.
On Sunday, Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, said ASI is “arriving”, pointing to the announcement that an Anthropic employee had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.
“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang said on X.

title: Kim Jong Un says North Korea should widen deployment of tactical nukes
text:
Kim Jong Un says North Korea should widen deployment of tactical nukes
Kim warns attempts to deny North Korea’s nuclear status will be seen as “an open declaration of war”.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has urged his country to focus on deploying tactical nuclear weapons “across multiple domains for different missions”.
Kim said North Korea’s nuclear material production capacity was being systematically expanded on Thursday, according to state media KCNA.
Maintaining North Korea’s status as a nuclear-weapons state was “absolutely inviolable”, Kim said during an inspection of nuclear material production and weapons research facilities. KCNA did not identify the facilities or their locations.
The country’s status would not change because of what he called “denuclearisation rhetoric from forces that ignore objective reality and failed to recognise the changed situation”.
“Our nuclear capability is now a reality,” he said, calling recent achievements in nuclear weapons production a major success in carrying out the country’s nuclear policy.
Any attempt to deny North Korea’s nuclear status, which it enshrined in its constitution in 2023, would be regarded as “an open declaration of war”, he said.
Kim said diversified use of tactical nuclear weapons was an “important and urgent task raised from tactical nukes’ military value in modern warfare and from the inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state”.
DMZ tensions
Kim’s statements come during a growing border dispute with South Korea over a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified territory between the two countries, on September 21.
Seoul demanded an apology from Pyongyang in October after a joint South Korea-United Nations investigation found that North Korea had planted the landmines more than a year ago.
Pyongyang sent a letter to the UN Security Council in response, accusing Seoul of fabricating the explosion, and fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast into the Sea of Japan less than a week later.
South Korea estimates that North Korea possesses between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads.

title: Photos: Storms and an El Nino-charged king tide batter California’s coast
text:
In Pictures
Photos: Storms and an El Nino-charged king tide batter California’s coast
Meteorologists have warned that the king tide could pair with high surf to bring historic surges to parts of the state.
California and other parts of the United States West Coast have experienced record-high water levels, causing flooding, destruction and dangerous waves.
On Wednesday, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced that the fishing community of Charleston, Oregon, notched its highest-ever coastal water level, roughly 1.12 metres above the mean high water level.
It was as high as 3.4 metres above the mean low water mark.
Other NOAA stations recorded some of their highest water levels on record, including San Diego, Los Angeles and Santa Barbara, all on the southern California coast.
Further north, the L-shaped municipal pier in Pacifica, a city south of San Francisco, crumbled into the surf after a wave as tall as its platform crashed into it.
In a video on social media, bystanders could be heard voicing astonishment at the sight. “Oh my god, it’s gone. Oh my god,” one person said.
The pier had faced multiple closures in recent years, as seawater weakened its concrete structure, but experts say this week’s conditions were more dangerous than normal.
The high coastal water levels were spurred by a combination of factors, including a phenomenon popularly known as king tides.
The term is applied to the highest tides of the year, created when both the sun and the moon are aligned to create a larger-than-normal tidal bulge, pulling the water with their combined gravitational force.
The king tides have been exacerbated by the El Nino weather pattern as well as human-fuelled climate change.
While El Nino is a regular occurrence, this year’s edition is projected to be stronger than normal, according to forecasters, leading to record-warm waters off the Pacific coast. That warming, in turn, helps churn up powerful storms that contribute to waves battering the shoreline.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie announced on Wednesday that his city had made it through the worst of this week’s surge with flooding and waves up to 9 metres, but he warned of more king tides to come.
“The last two weeks have been an important reminder to get prepared for the rest of El Nino season. We’re expecting more king tides in December and January,” he wrote on social media. “We need to take these events seriously, prepare ahead of future storms, and stay alert.”

title: Ukraine attacks Russian military base, says five planes struck
text:
Ukraine attacks Russian military base, says five planes struck
The Ukrainian General Staff says its forces struck an airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region east of Moscow.
Ukrainian forces have hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.
Ukraine struck the Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region, the General Staff said on Wednesday, adding that three MiG-31 jets were used to fire hypersonic missiles and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were damaged.
Russia did not immediately comment on the report by the General Staff, which said the Savasleyka airbase had been hit in the latest long-range attacks aimed at crippling Moscow’s war effort.
The operation followed a series of high-profile strikes by Ukrainian forces in recent days in which two Russian ships were hit in Libyan waters and a Russian vessel was struck in the Gulf of Finland.
Last week, Ukraine destroyed the road portion of Russia’s prized bridge to the Crimea peninsula after consecutive attacks.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and fighting has continued despite a renewed US-backed push to end what has become Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.
Kyiv is trying to dent Moscow’s military might as it struggles under a renewed campaign of attacks on its energy system and mounting Russian strikes on front-line cities.
Ukrainian forces are hunting Russian ballistic-missile launchers used to carry out many of those attacks, striking 16 over the past several months, Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said this week.
Renewed Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ processing volumes by 45 percent since late October, industry sources said this month. Kyiv has said it will stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow does the same.

title: Storms push Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City to Saturday
text:
Storms push Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City to Saturday
The parade, which marks its 100th edition, got a last-minute rain check ahead of heavy gusts on Thursday.
New York City is famous for its annual Thanksgiving Day Parade, a procession of towering helium balloons, elaborate floats and marching bands.
But on Wednesday, organisers in the United States announced that this year’s edition has been postponed because of an East Coast storm that threatens turbulent weather.
It was rescheduled for Saturday instead, right after Black Friday, a day when retailers traditionally offer holiday shopping and discount prices.
The annual parade is sponsored by Macy’s, a New York-based department store brand, and Saturday’s event will be its 100th Thanksgiving procession.
“While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our participants and spectators is and always will be our top priority,” Will Coss, Macy’s executive producer, said in a Wednesday news conference.
“ We’re saddened by the shift, but we’re optimistic about our opportunity to deliver the most spectacular 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the best and biggest parade in our history.”
The parade, founded in 1924, was cancelled three times during World War II, but this year marks the first time it was postponed.
The event’s signature balloons were already being inflated on Wednesday when Macy’s announced the delay.
The decision came amid warnings issued by the National Weather Service of lashing winds and possible coastal flooding for the New York City area.
Gusts are forecast to reach up to 97 km/h, and rainfall of 2.5 to 5cm is expected from Thursday into Friday. A high wind warning is also in effect from 10am local time (15:00 GMT) Thursday through 1am (6:00 GMT) Friday.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani described the decision as tough but necessary given the forecast.
“I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences. Yet safety has to come first,” he said at Wednesday’s news conference. “On Saturday, when balloons climb into the sky, every New Yorker and everyone visiting will be able to take in a show that is both truly spectacular and also safe.”
The holiday extravaganza typically draws more than 3.5 million spectators along its Manhattan route, according to New York City authorities. It is also broadcast nationwide.
For many Americans, the parade is a fixture of Thanksgiving, and the postponement marks a break with a familiar holiday ritual.
NBC, the television network that airs the annual parade, said it would instead broadcast a repeat of the 2025 edition on Thursday.
It remains unclear whether the full roster of performers scheduled for the parade will continue to perform on Saturday. According to Macy’s website, singers like Raye and Wyclef Jean were scheduled to headline, as were actors and Broadway stars like Leslie Odom Jr and Anthony Ramos.
New floats include a five-storey-tall balloon of the cartoon character Bluey wearing a crown, and a 17-meter-long version of the beagle Snoopy carrying his bird sidekick Woodstock.
There will also be a blue hippopotamus, a nod to the balloon that floated off from the 1931 parade and was lost.
Mamdani assured New Yorkers that the parade route would be safe once the storm passes on Saturday, thanks to a surge of law enforcement.
“ There will be an expanded police presence this Saturday along the route, and the [New York Police Department] is fully prepared for an event of this magnitude, just as they have been prepared for the 99 parades that preceded this,” Mamdani said.
“I want to make clear that there are no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time.”
The festivities are slated to begin at 8:30am local time (13:30 GMT).

title: ISIL blamed for multiple suicide attacks in Syria
