ISIL blamed for multiple suicide attacks in Syria
NewsFeed
ISIL blamed for multiple suicide attacks in Syria
Two members of Syria’s security forces have been killed in a suicide attack on a security post in Hasakah, in north-eastern Syria. Five others were injured. Authorities accuse ISIL for sending four attackers who used suicide vests and a motorcycle laden with explosives.
Published On 26 Nov 2026

title: Two Syrian security personnel killed in ISIL suicide attack
text:
Two Syrian security personnel killed in ISIL suicide attack
Syrian forces say the attack in northeastern Syria’s city of Hasakah involved four assailants who were all killed.
A suicide attack by the ISIL (ISIS) group has killed two security personnel and wounded five others in Syria’s northeastern city of Hasakah, according to local authorities.
Four gunmen targeted an Internal Security Forces (ISF) checkpoint on Wednesday in the Mushirfa neighbourhood of Hasakah, an official statement from the governorate’s media directorate said.
All four of the assailants died in the attack, two in clashes with security forces and the other two in suicide explosions, the ISF said.
One of the suicide attackers, Syrian media reported, was riding a booby-trapped motorcycle when he detonated himself at the entrance of the post.
The deputy governor of Hasakah, Ahmed al-Hilali, vowed “to uncover the circumstances of the attack and identify the perpetrators”.
“Ensuring the safety of citizens and the stability of the region is a responsibility from which we will not waver,” al-Hilali added.
The ISF shared photos from the site on their X page, including an image of the vest they say was worn by one of the two perpetrators who was “neutralised” by the forces.
Continued attacks
A report in February by the UN said that Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and two of his senior cabinet ministers were the targets of five foiled assassination attempts by ISIL over the past year.
The report did not provide specific dates as to when the foiled attacks took place, though it noted their locations in northern Aleppo, the country’s most populous province, and the southern province of Deraa.
In October, the Interior Ministry reported that two members of Syria’s internal security forces were killed and five wounded in clashes with a suspected ISIL cell during a raid on the outskirts of Damascus.

title: Zambia bans protest against push to remove presidential term limits
text:
Zambia bans protest against push to remove presidential term limits
Critics fear the campaign could undermine democratic safeguards as senior opposition figures remain behind bars.
Lusaka, Zambia – Zambian authorities have banned a planned protest against calls to remove presidential term limits, amid mounting concerns over political freedoms following President Hakainde Hichilema’s disputed re-election in August.
The demonstration, scheduled for November 25, was organised by civil society groups and human rights defenders opposed to proposals that could allow Hichilema to remain in power beyond 2031, when his second and final five-year term is due to end.
Police cited the risk of clashes after a pro-government youth group announced plans to hold a rival demonstration in support of removing presidential term limits.
Three organisations aligned with the governing United Party for National Development (UPND) have petitioned the National Assembly to remove constitutional restrictions on presidential terms, potentially paving the way for Hichilema to seek a third term.
The campaign has drawn opposition from civil society organisations, the influential Catholic Church and the Law Association of Zambia (LAZ), which have called for an end to the debate over extending presidential tenure.
Hichilema, who swept to power in 2021 on a promise of democratic reforms, had repeatedly criticised African leaders who sought to extend their rule through constitutional amendments.
His office has sought to reassure critics. In a statement on November 20, presidential communications official Clayson Hamasaka said Hichilema would respect the constitution “at all times”.
“The president also respects every citizen’s right to freedom of expression,” Hamasaka said.
But the campaign to remove term limits, coupled with the prolonged detention of senior opposition figures, has raised concerns among government critics about the future of one of Africa’s more established multiparty democracies.
‘We are being blocked from protesting’
On November 4, civil society organisations and human rights defenders notified police of their intention to march against the removal of presidential term limits.
A pro-government youth alliance subsequently announced plans to demonstrate in support of the proposals, prompting police to cite the risk of confrontations between the two groups.
Minister of Home Affairs and Internal Security Clement Andeleki defended the decision to cancel the demonstrations, dismissing suggestions that Hichilema was seeking a third term.
“We cancelled [the protests] because those are trying to go to the streets, they are going to do what? Because there is no third term that the president [Hichilema] wants,” Andeleki told Al Jazeera.
The decision came days after Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu pledged to protect citizens exercising their right to petition parliament for the removal of presidential term limits.
“We’ll not allow individuals threatening others who are exercising their rights to express themselves freely,” Mwiimbu told journalists in Lusaka on November 18, adding that Hichilema would respect any amendments to the constitution.
Linda Kasonde, a former president of the Law Association of Zambia and one of the organisers of the planned demonstration, said the group had appealed against the police decision.
“We have seen that we are being blocked from protesting and so, we have written to the police to give us an alternative date and we have also written to the minister of home affairs to appeal the decision of police,” Kasonde told Al Jazeera.
She said the organisers remained committed to peaceful protest and wanted to demonstrate public opposition to the removal of presidential term limits.
A disputed election and opposition crackdown
The controversy comes against the backdrop of a disputed general election and the detention of some of Hichilema’s most prominent political opponents.
Hichilema was re-elected in August with more than 61 percent of the vote in an election in which observers, including the European Union Election Observation Mission, reported irregularities.
A six-hour suspension of vote counting and the announcement of results, the deployment of soldiers at polling stations and tallying centres, and the removal of opposition and independent monitors raised questions about the credibility of the electoral process.
The closure of courts following the election also raised concerns over the opposition’s ability to challenge the results.
Brian Mundubile, who finished second in the presidential race and accused Hichilema of electoral fraud, was arrested alongside his running mate, Makebi Zulu, in a post-election crackdown.
Then, former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally wounded by security forces during a raid on a house in Lusaka where senior opposition figures were meeting.
Mundubile, Zulu and several other opposition figures have been detained for more than 100 days over allegations of attempting to overthrow Hichilema’s government and engaging in seditious activities.
The accused say the charges are politically motivated.
Their prolonged detention has drawn condemnation from local and international human rights defenders and prompted a legal challenge against the state.
A day before the High Court was due to rule on their continued detention, prosecutors produced a charge sheet alleging treason.
Sakwiba Sikota, a leading defence lawyer, told Al Jazeera that the trial was expected to begin in 2027.
Treason is a non-bailable offence in Zambia and carries a possible life sentence. Lengthy legal proceedings could keep some of the country’s most prominent opposition figures out of public life for monthsm or even years.
Muhabi Lungu, secretary-general of the Tonse Alliance, the opposition coalition led by Mundubile, alleged that the prosecutions were intended to weaken the opposition ahead of possible constitutional changes.
“This scheme was hatched a long time ago, and so, this treason issue is an attempt to try and denigrate the opposition so that somehow, they can justify why he must continue beyond the constitutional requirement,” Lungu told Al Jazeera.
He urged the authorities to expedite the trial and make public the evidence against the accused.
The battle over presidential term limits
Supporters of the proposed changes argue that presidential term limits restrict voters’ democratic right to choose their leaders.
Mark Simuuwe, the UPND’s head of media, rejected suggestions that the campaign was specifically intended to secure a third term for Hichilema.
“We are not talking about a third term bid here; instead we are talking about removal of the term limit restrictions because we feel the current constitution is undemocratic as it denies electorates a chance to elect a president of their choice when they want to,” Simuuwe said in an interview.
A constitutional amendment would require the support of at least two-thirds of parliamentarians, although additional constitutional procedures may apply to changes affecting presidential tenure.
The UPND does not command a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly but could seek support from independent legislators and other members of parliament.
For critics, however, removing presidential term limits would risk dismantling an important democratic safeguard in a country that has experienced several peaceful transfers of power since the introduction of multiparty democracy in 1991.
Among them was Hichilema’s own election victory in 2021, when he defeated incumbent President Edgar Lungu.
A wider regional trend
The debate in Zambia comes as constitutional changes elsewhere in Africa have renewed concerns over presidential tenure and democratic accountability.
In neighbouring Zimbabwe, President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed into law constitutional amendments in July that would allow him to remain in office two years beyond his previous term limit.
The amendments extend presidential terms from five to seven years and replace direct presidential elections with a system under which parliament selects the president.
In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, another of Zambia’s neighbours, President Felix Tshisekedi has approved legislation allowing constitutional changes to be put to a referendum, a development that critics fear could pave the way for a third presidential term.
In Zambia, the debate over term limits is unfolding as opposition leaders remain behind bars and civil society groups await a response from the authorities on whether they will be allowed to demonstrate.
For Kasonde, the campaign to remove term limits cannot be separated from the political tensions that followed the August election.
“This attempt to remove the term limits to consolidate power is not for ideological reasons but because of the [decline in] legitimacy following a controversial election,” she said.

title: A meeting with Democrats over healthcare? Trump says he’s open to it
text:
A meeting with Democrats over healthcare? Trump says he’s open to it
Experts tell Al Jazeera they are sceptical that Trump would back Medicare for All, a proposal for national healthcare.
Just weeks after attacking Abdul El-Sayed on the campaign trail, United States President Donald Trump says he will meet with the incoming Democratic senator to discuss Medicare for All, a proposal to establish a national healthcare programme.
Trump confirmed his willingness to sit down with El-Sayed in an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, calling the Democrat a “smart guy”.
“I know I’ll be meeting with him,” Trump said. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.”
A former public health official in Detroit, El-Sayed catapulted to national prominence in the 2026 midterm elections, when he won a hotly contested Senate seat in Michigan. A central part of his platform has been expanding access to healthcare.
In an interview with Zeteo this month, El-Sayed even floated renaming Medicare for All after Trump.
“If he wants to pass Trumpcare for All, I’m OK with it,” El-Sayed told host Mehdi Hasan. “He seems to like to put his name on things.”
Days later, he posted on social media a mockup of a gold-colored insurance card, bearing Trump’s signature and the name “Trumpcare”.
In an accompanying caption, El-Sayed asked the president to “guarantee health care for every American, from cradle to grave”.
The White House initially dismissed the proposal. Then, on Saturday, Trump shared El-Sayed’s image of the card on Truth Social. In his interview with the New York Post, Trump also called the “Trumpcare” branding “very smart”.
El-Sayed is pitching a government-run health insurance programme, which would cover “all necessary healthcare” and still allow private insurance.
Trump has not endorsed the proposal, and there is no set date for the meeting.
But with Democrats set to take control of the US Congress in January, healthcare advocates and political experts are closely watching what will come out of any potential meeting between the two politicians.
It remains unclear what Trump’s support could mean for the effort to get guaranteed healthcare for every American.
A long road for US healthcare
For more than a century, the US has weighed the possibility of offering universal healthcare access. But such proposals in recent decades have faced stiff opposition from the private sector.
During the Great Depression in the 1930s, for instance, President Franklin D Roosevelt appointed a Committee on Economic Security whose mission was to address the need for “all forms of social insurance”, including healthcare.
While a national health bill did not pass during Roosevelt’s administration, his successor, Harry Truman, became the first US president to propose a comprehensive national health insurance system in 1945. It failed amid fierce opposition from the American Medical Association, which called it “socialized medicine”.
Twenty years later, President Lyndon B Johnson signed two government insurance programmes, Medicare and Medicaid, into law. But their scope was limited to providing coverage for older Americans and some people in low-income brackets or with special needs.
Since then, a number of Democratic leaders have tried different paths to expand coverage.
In 1994, President Bill Clinton’s plan proposed giving everyone healthcare through private insurance, with employers required to help pay for it. Insurers ran advertisements warning the plan would limit people’s medical choices, and the plan died without a vote amid divisions in the US Congress.
The next Democratic president, Barack Obama, took up the fight to expand healthcare access again in the new millennium.
His name became associated with a sweeping overhaul of the US healthcare system — the Affordable Care Act, popularly known as “Obamacare” — that passed in 2010.
The Affordable Care Act expanded Medicaid, helped people pay for private insurance and made it illegal for insurers to turn people away because of pre-existing conditions. But a proposal to let people buy a government-run plan alongside private options failed in the US Senate.
During the 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns, Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, made Medicare for All a centrepiece of his platform, proposing a federal plan to replace most private insurance, including the coverage people get through work.
While the idea was embraced by progressives, Democrats as a whole were divided over whether to replace private coverage and who would bear the cost.
Sanders and his allies introduced another bill in 2025, but it has yet to pass through the US Congress.
Eagan Kemp, a healthcare policy expert at the consumer advocacy nonprofit Public Citizen, believes such proposals have struggled because of the economic heft the healthcare industry wields.
“I think the big reason is profit,” said Eagan Kemp. He described the country’s medical system as the “Wild West”.
In the 1980s, US healthcare costs were similar to those in other countries, according to Kemp.
But the American system became more corporatised and driven by profit, he explained, and it lacked the regulation many countries introduced as they moved towards universal healthcare.
Kemp argued that programmes like Medicare for All would rein in what companies can charge, how much care they can cut and how much profit they can take out of the system.
It would also cut out the insurance middlemen that drive up costs and make it harder for people to get the care they need, he said.
Sceptical but hopeful
Experts note that Trump’s flirtation with El-Sayed’s Medicare for All proposal isn’t drawing the amount of opposition that would be expected for what has historically been a very partisan issue.
Republican strategist Ashley Davis, who worked in President George W Bush’s administration, told Al Jazeera she was bullish that Trump could pick up some bipartisan support on healthcare, an area she says he’s been “focused on”.
“I’m actually happy they’re meeting because, maybe for once, Republicans and Democrats can get along and something productive will come out of this,” Davis told Al Jazeera.
However, she expressed doubt that a bill resembling Medicare for All will materialise from any meeting with El-Sayed, saying agreements to lower drug prices, provide more funds for rural healthcare or expand Medicare for children are much more likely.
In order to pass something like Medicare for All, Davis explained that “you would have to bring on some of the new [Democratic] senators in really red states”.
“It sounds great from a talking point perspective, but how it actually gets accomplished is a whole other thing,” she added.
Kemp was also sceptical that a policy like Medicare for All could cruise through the US Congress to Trump’s desk, citing the high number of political donations that lawmakers receive from healthcare and insurance providers.
“How much they’d be willing to do, or how quickly they’d be willing to move, is yet to be determined,” he said of the country’s Congress members. “I’m sceptical that there would be votes there.”
But Kemp noted that Trump has a tendency to break from Republican orthodoxy. The fact that he is not competing on the ballot in 2028 could also help pave the way for healthcare discussions with Democrats.
It may also be the last chance for Trump, who has described himself as a world-class dealmaker, to get a major piece of legislation passed during his final two years in the White House, according to Kemp.
“If it was any other Republican president in my lifetime, I wouldn’t hold much hope,” he said. “But I think this one will be interesting to see play out.”

Live updatesLive updates,

title: Houthis target Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports as strikes escalate
text:
Houthis target Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports as strikes escalate
Explosion reported in Sanaa after Saudi air defenses intercept ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh.
Yemen’s Houthi group has struck the port of Jizan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast as fighting intensifies near the Yemeni city of Taiz.
A Saudi-led military coalition said a Houthi attack on Jizan caused only minor damage and no civilian casualties on Wednesday, adding that “efforts are underway to determine the type of projectile” used.
The spokesman for the coalition, Turki al-Maliki, later said in a statement on X that its forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone over Jeddah’s port in Saudi Arabia.
No civilian injuries were reported from falling debris following the interception, he added.
After the coalition’s statement, an explosion was heard in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, according to Al Jazeera’s Nabil al-Yousfi.
The Saudi-led coalition then said its air defences intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh.
The attempted strike on the capital follows a Houthi drone attack on a skyscraper in Riyadh’s financial district on Tuesday, injuring at least 11 people.
The latest incidents mark a further escalation between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia, including strikes from both sides targeting airports, energy facilities and other civilian and economic infrastructure.
The strikes on Saudi Arabian ports come after the Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported new Saudi attacks on the port of Hodeidah in Yemen.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Houthis threatened to attack Saudi ports if Hodeidah came under attack.
“The port of Hodeidah handles 90 percent of imported goods into Yemen. If it is closed, it could bring the humanitarian situation to the brink of collapse”, said Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.
“Some of Saudi Arabia’s recent attacks at the Port of Hodeidah have targeted storage tanks and cranes used to load and unload shipments”, Mawry said.
Fighting in Yemen
Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have been battling the Houthis on several fronts, with the army’s spokesman saying 654 strikes have been carried out against the group on Wednesday.
Yemen’s western front has witnessed the heaviest concentration of recent strikes, according to Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz.
Government forces have said air strikes targeted Houthi positions west of Taiz.
“These strikes are part of an intense and sustained wave of air raids that have continued for approximately 72 hours”, Ali said.
“Particular attention is focused on the most significant mountain range overlooking central Taiz: Jabal Saber and its highest peak, Jabal al-Arus. The government says the Houthis want to seize this strategic peak”, she added.
The Houthis said there have been 105 air strikes and missile attacks by the Saudi-led coalition targeting civilian sites in Sanaa and 10 governorates on Wednesday.

title: Malen and Roma deny injury-hit PSG in Champions League draw
text:
Malen and Roma deny injury-hit PSG in Champions League draw
Champions League holders Paris Saint-Germain held to 2-2 draw by Roma as injury-ravaged squad struggle.
Donyell Malen’s penalty gave Roma a 2-2 draw away to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday, as the injury-hit reigning champions saw their perfect record in this season’s competition come to an end.
Malen stroked in from the spot in the 78th minute on a bitterly cold and wet night at the Parc des Princes, giving Roma a welcome point after their collapse from two goals up to lose 3-2 at Manchester United last time out.
Roma had earlier taken the lead through Mario Hermoso, only for Illia Zabarnyi to equalise before substitute Ousmane Dembele put PSG briefly in front with a penalty of his own.
The result ends PSG’s perfect record in this season’s league phase, and halts a run of 12 consecutive wins in all competitions for Luis Enrique’s team.
They fall two points behind Real Madrid, who are now clear at the top of the standings as the only side still with a 100 percent record after five matches.
It is only a minor setback for PSG in their quest to finish in the top eight of the 36-team table, and therefore qualify directly for the last 16 without having to go through the playoff round like in the last two campaigns.
But the Parisians could have done with the boost of a victory as they come to terms with the loss of the outstanding Desire Doue, who may not play again this season after rupturing the ACL in his right knee last weekend.
Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, another of their outstanding attacking players, recently succumbed to the same injury, while Dembele has been struggling for fitness, too, and PSG’s prospects of winning a third straight Champions League title are undoubtedly diminished as a result.
Dembele’s presence on the bench at kickoff meant that none of PSG’s five top scorers from last season was in their line-up here, with the others either injured or having departed in the case of Bradley Barcola and Goncalo Ramos.
Meanwhile, Roma coach Gian Piero Gasperini raised eyebrows by leaving Malen out of his starting XI. The Dutchman is running at an average of more than a goal a game this season and netted four against Parma last weekend.
However, Roma have been in prolific form in general, netting 26 goals in their last seven matches before arriving in the French capital.
They went ahead inside five minutes here as Matias Soule cut the ball back from the byline and Spanish defender Hermoso was on hand to convert.
Roma had blown even more promising leads already this season, though, losing 4-3 at home to Real Madrid after leading 3-1 with eight minutes left, and then going down 3-2 at Old Trafford despite being 2-0 ahead at half-time.
Ukrainian defender Zabarnyi levelled just after the half-hour mark as he found space at the near post to head in Senny Mayulu’s corner.
Evan Ndicka headed just off-target for Roma late in the first half, and Niccolo Pisilli forced a good stop from Matvei Safonov early in the second half.
Joao Neves then headed agonisingly wide for PSG as he arrived unmarked in the area to meet a Nuno Mendes cross, before Dembele was introduced for the hosts in place of the ineffective Ferran Torres.
Moments after that, PSG won a penalty when Achraf Hakimi stormed into the Roma box only to be pulled down by Wesley.
The French side had missed four penalties in the Champions League since the start of last season, but Dembele did score in the final against Arsenal in May.
He kept a cool head to convert his fifth goal of the campaign, but PSG could not make it five straight Champions League wins this season.
Malen entered the fray for Roma midway through the second half and looked on as Dembele was denied a brilliant solo goal by a Mile Svilar save.
Roma then won a penalty following a VAR check after Vitinha blocked a Soule shot with a raised hand in the box.
Up stepped Malen to score his 17th goal of a prolific campaign, boosting Roma’s hopes of reaching the knockout phase.

title: Man United denied at Sporting as referee overshadows Fernandes double
text:
Man United denied at Sporting as referee overshadows Fernandes double
Bruno Fernandes nets twice in Lisbon, but referee’s decisions in spotlight as Mauricio Pochettino denied first win.
Mauricio Pochettino must wait for his first win as Manchester United coach, after a wild 2-2 Champions League draw at Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday, with the hosts equalising thanks to a goalkeeping error from Senne Lammens.
The Belgian stopper’s poor handling allowed Luis Suarez to complete a brace for the hosts, cancelling out United playmaker Bruno Fernandes’s double against his former side.
United gave away two penalties in the first half, the second converted by Suarez, before Fernandes equalised from the spot early in the second half.
Fernandes sent United ahead with a lucky bounce taking his effort over the Sporting goalkeeper, before Suarez’s acrobatic effort levelled the game.
United midfielder Youri Tielemans was sent off in stoppage time for a second yellow card to end a compelling and often erratic match.
A crushing 4-0 defeat by rivals Liverpool in the Premier League at the weekend, leaving United 19th, was a disastrous first game at the helm for Pochettino after replacing Michael Carrick.
Pochettino brought Harry Maguire into the three-man defence as he shuffled his pack, as well as starting Joshua Zirkzee in place of the suspended Matheus Cunha.
Neither side took many risks in the opening stages, with few chances of note until the game burst into life midway through the first half as United lost control.
Lisandro Martinez brought down Geny Catamo in the area and Sporting were awarded a penalty.
The hosts blew their chance from the spot, with Suarez’s scuffed effort easily saved by Lammens, but the Red Devils gave away another spot kick just a couple of minutes later.
Goalkeeper Lammens came flying off his line and clattered Maxi Araujo, and this time Colombian striker Suarez made no mistake from the spot.
Manchester United unhappy with disallowed goals
United thought they had equalised when Amad Diallo hit the crossbar and then nodded home the rebound, but the goal was disallowed to their dismay.
Youri Tielemans was ruled to have fouled Goncalo Inacio, although he seemed to win the ball, upsetting United further after Leny Yoro’s controversial red card against Liverpool on Sunday that was later rescinded.
Fernandes pulled United level early in the second half from the spot after Eduardo Quaresma brought down Martinez.
The former Sporting playmaker calmly stroked his penalty beyond the dive of Kaique Pereira into the bottom left corner.
Fernandes said on the eve of the game he had stopped contract talks because he wanted to focus on helping United improve their form after a dire start to the season.
The midfielder soon had his second goal, with the help of a bizarre bounce off a divot on the pitch.
Fernandes’s low effort from distance seemed bound for Pereira’s hands, but suddenly bounced up off a patch of uneven turf and fortuitously over the goalkeeper’s head.
The Portugal international bent a free-kick narrowly off target as he looked to complete his hat-trick.
Lammens saved well from Sergi Altimira to protect United’s lead as Sporting battled to find an equaliser.
It eventually came from a howler from Lammens, who failed to claim a cross dropping out of the sky, spilling the ball in front of Suarez, who produced a hooked acrobatic effort to score.
Moments later United had the ball in the net at the other end after another goalkeeping error by Pereira, who mishandled Fernandes’s corner, pushing the ball into his own net.
However, what would have been the winner was disallowed for an elbow by Patrick Dorgu on the goalkeeper, a decision the visitors were also unhappy about.

title: Winter rains threaten 1,000 Gaza shelter sites, councils warn
text:
Winter rains threaten 1,000 Gaza shelter sites, councils warn
About 200,000 tents need replacing, Gaza’s municipalities say, as the European Union urges Israel to reopen all crossings into the territory to aid.
Gaza’s municipalities have warned that winter rains could flood about 1,000 camps and other sites hosting displaced Palestinians in the war-torn enclave, adding that damage to drains and sewers, and a shortage of pumps, have left their crews with little means to clear the water.
After a meeting in Gaza City on Wednesday, the Union of Gaza Strip Municipalities singled out al-Mughraqa and al-Zahra in central Gaza, where water levels in Wadi Gaza could rise suddenly. Across the territory, about 200,000 tents need replacing, and more than 2,000 damaged buildings are at risk of collapse, the union said. Gaza’s Government Media Office had warned on Tuesday that it expected another storm within days.
This is Gaza’s fourth winter since Israel launched its war in October 2023. The union said storms in early November flooded about 70,000 tents and affected more than 350,000 displaced people. During a winter storm this November, families piled sand at tent entrances to keep out the rain. Others carried their children out and salvaged what belongings they could.
One displaced mother said she had cut up the burial shroud she had bought for her son and used it to patch her tent. She wanted to keep the family’s bedding and clothes dry. “I couldn’t get a tarpaulin,” she said.
When the first rains hit, Gaza’s civil defence crews reached only a minority of those who called for help. Most of the other callers received advice by phone, Al Jazeera reported.
Tents waiting at the border
In Brussels on Wednesday, the European Commission called on Israel to reopen all Gaza crossings to humanitarian aid. Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova said tents were waiting on trucks outside Gaza because Israel had not allowed them or the equipment needed to put them up to enter.
The UN said earlier this month that more than 150,000 tents were awaiting entry into Gaza.
Al Jazeera’s open-source unit (Ar.) measured a queue of trucks stretching about 1.1km (0.7 miles) along the Egyptian road to the Rafah crossing in a November 17 satellite image, up from about 460 metres (1,510 feet) on October 6. The images do not establish what the trucks carried. Freight from Egypt is routed through the Karem Abu Salem crossing, known as Kerem Shalom in Israel, for inspection rather than entering Gaza through Rafah.
COGAT, the Israeli military body that coordinates aid, said that nearly 100,000 tents had entered Gaza since the start of a winter aid programme. It said Israel would allow reconstruction equipment into Gaza only after Hamas had fully disarmed.
Inside Gaza, aid workers have cleared drains, installed flood barriers and reinforced shelters. The UN’s humanitarian affairs office reported on November 20 that teams had recorded such work at 162 of the 356 flood-prone locations they had identified. Gaza’s municipalities are asking for pumps, backup generators and fuel before the next storm, as well as 10,000 tonnes of cement for emergency repairs and mobile homes that can withstand wind and rain.

title: US Education Department probes Virginia schools after sexual abuse scandal
text:
US Education Department probes Virginia schools after sexual abuse scandal
Virginia schools face scrutiny after revelations of abuse and widespread failures in mandatory staff background checks.
The United States Department of Education says it is launching an investigation and withholding funding from a district in the state of Virginia after local officials shut down all of its schools in the wake of a child sexual abuse scandal involving its employees.
“Parents should never have to question whether their child’s school is aiding and abetting child predators,” US Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said in a statement on Tuesday. “The Trump Administration is taking decisive enforcement action to hold those responsible accountable and ensure Virginia schools are safe places for children to learn.”
Officials in Albemarle County, Virginia, announced they were closing all 29 schools in the district last week, after learning that more than 500 staff had not been subjected to a routine background screening for a history of child sexual abuse. The school system has about 2,800 employees, and only a fraction of its $284m budget comes from the federal government.
Local officials emphasised that none of the 524 employees is suspected of abuse.
Approximately 14,000 students attend the schools, and parents have scrambled to find childcare, while many who depend on free school meals for their children have had to look for other sources of food.
Bob Beard, a member of the Albemarle school board, told Al Jazeera that families were struggling to deal with the shutdown, but schools would reopen on Monday.
The child abuse allegations have shaken the county and caught the attention of the Trump administration.
A former elementary school teacher was arrested for possession of child sexual abuse material earlier this year, while a counsellor at another school was put on leave and later indicted on 20 counts of sexual crimes involving seven different children, according to the Albemarle County Police Department.
Two county school officials and a school principal were later charged with failure to report child abuse, and the county’s superintendent of schools resigned.
‘Processes not followed’
Jason Grant, a spokesman for Albemarle County Public Schools, told Al Jazeera that none of the individuals implicated in those cases was among the 524 employees who were hired without the proper screening required to check for a history of child sexual abuse.
“This was not about having the policies in place, this was about processes that were not followed,” Grant said. He said officials were working with the state to “make sure the processes are in place to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”
Grant said all employees in the district undergo several stages of vetting, including a criminal background check and an attestation that they have no history of child abuse or neglect. Then the school system submits their information to the Virginia Department of Social Services to verify that they are not part of the agency’s abuse and neglect database.
For three years, it appears that vetting procedures were not consistently applied. Putting employees hired over that period on leave to carry out background checks meant schools would not be able to run, so officials decided to close them until next week.
“Those were for every range of employee, from teachers to bus drivers to substitutes and across the division, so we couldn’t get coverage for that amount of people,” Grant said.
All but three of the 524 employees have now been properly vetted, and none had background issues, Grant said, adding that the county will reopen schools on Monday.
The Trump administration has long called for the dismantling of the Department of Education. The US president signed an executive order last year that tried to set that in motion.
The department, which distributes federal funding to states for use in schools, also traditionally investigates whether local officials are complying with civil rights laws banning discrimination against minorities and marginalised groups.
Since returning to office in 2025, the Trump administration has cut more than half of the department’s staff and subjected it to wider changes it says are aimed at rooting out “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) policies.

title: Judge permanently blocks part of Trump’s ICC sanctions order, protects speech-based advocacy nationwide
text:
A federal judge has permanently barred the Trump administration from using part of its sanctions order against the International Criminal Court (ICC) to punish Americans for providing speech-based services to sanctioned individuals and organisations, extending the protection nationwide.
The ruling, issued by US District Judge Jesse M Furman of the Southern District of New York on November 23, 2026, marks a significant First Amendment challenge to President Donald Trump’s sanctions policy against the ICC. It protects Americans who submit evidence to the court, conduct research, publish material or provide other speech-related assistance to sanctioned groups and individuals. The plaintiffs are DAWN, the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG), and two individuals, Tarik Kanaana and William Doares. The case is Democracy for the Arab World Now, Inc. v. Trump, No. 26-cv-5957.
The lawsuit challenged Executive Order 14203, signed by Trump in February 2025, which authorised sanctions against people connected to the ICC. The order was issued after the court pursued investigations and actions involving individuals from the US and Israel. It declared a national emergency over what the administration described as the ICC’s improper actions and sought to restrict assistance to those targeted by the sanctions.
A key provision of the order prohibits providing or receiving “services” by, to or for the benefit of anyone designated under the sanctions programme. Violations of the sanctions framework can carry civil and criminal penalties under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). The plaintiffs argued that the services prohibition could prevent them from carrying out research, submitting evidence, publishing material and collaborating with others on matters related to the ICC.
In his November 23 opinion, Furman held that the prohibition, when applied to speech-based services, amounted to a content-based restriction on speech. Such restrictions are subject to strict scrutiny, a demanding legal standard under which the government must demonstrate that a restriction is narrowly tailored to serve a compelling interest. The judge found that the administration had not shown that penalising all speech-based services was necessary to achieve its stated national security and foreign policy objectives. The government’s arguments, he said, did not establish why every form of speech-related assistance to sanctioned individuals needed to be prohibited.
The ruling follows an earlier preliminary injunction issued on October 13, which had protected the plaintiffs themselves. The November decision went further with Furman concluding that the services prohibition was facially invalid to the extent that it covered speech-based services and that the injunction should extend to anyone providing or receiving such services.
The judge reasoned that restricting speech-related assistance could deter people from participating in public debate or supporting legal and human rights work, even if they were not directly involved in the lawsuit. The broader protection, he said, was necessary to address the chilling effect created by the threat of penalties.
However, the decision does not overturn Trump’s sanctions order in its entirety. The government retains the authority to designate individuals under the executive order and to enforce restrictions on the provision of funds, goods and non-expressive services. The court specifically noted that financial services, such as banking, brokerage and insurance, could remain subject to the prohibition where they do not involve protected speech.
The ruling also does not remove sanctions already imposed on ICC officials or other designated individuals. Instead, it limits the government’s ability to use the services prohibition to penalise constitutionally protected speech and advocacy connected with those individuals or organisations. Trump himself is excluded from the injunction, according to the court order. The judge directed the parties to submit an agreed proposed judgment, or competing versions if they could not agree, by December 1.
The case adds to a series of legal challenges against the administration’s sanctions policy targeting the ICC. In an earlier case, Rona v. Trump, another federal judge in the Southern District of New York blocked enforcement of the services prohibition against two law professors whose work involved speech and advocacy related to the court. 
Furman relied in part on that ruling in reaching his decision.
For DAWN and TAAG, the permanent injunction is a victory for their ability to continue working with the ICC and other sanctioned entities without facing penalties for speech-based activities. The ruling also establishes a broader nationwide safeguard for Americans engaging in similar forms of advocacy, research and evidence-sharing.

title: Watch: Zelenskyy, Hungary PM Magyar play volleyball during Ukraine visit
text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar took to the volleyball court with students during a visit to the Lajos Kossuth Lyceum in Ukraine's Zakarpattia on Wednesday.
The two leaders interacted with students and teachers at the Hungarian-language secondary school, which has more than 500 students. Zelenskyy said the school also offers classes in Ukrainian and English and has continued to develop despite Russia's ongoing war, with classrooms undergoing renovation.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy highlighted the importance of providing Ukrainian-language education to children in Budapest, saying mutual respect for the languages of both communities should form the basis of cooperation between the two countries.
The visit was part of Magyar's trip to Ukraine, during which the two leaders also discussed bilateral cooperation in energy, transport infrastructure and security.
Zelenskyy said the discussions covered supplies of diesel fuel and other petroleum products to Ukraine, expanding rail connections between Kyiv and Budapest, electrifying railway lines and improving border infrastructure.
He also briefed Magyar on the situation at the front and Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities and villages. 
Zelenskyy said Ukraine wanted relations with Hungary based on equality and mutual respect.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine's defence was important for the whole of Europe and called for Europe, the US and other countries seeking peace to stand in solidarity with Kyiv.
"This war can truly be stopped only if Europe, America, and everyone who genuinely wants a real peace stand in full solidarity with Ukraine," he said, thanking Magyar for his support for Ukraine's defence.

title: 12-year-old UK station cat falls ill; $60,000 raised, surplus to help cats
text:
A 12-year-old cat who became a familiar face at a railway station in England has received an extraordinary show of support after suddenly falling ill. George, popularly known as the Stourbridge Station Cat, was taken to a veterinary clinic on November 23 after his family noticed that he was eating less and sleeping more than usual. News of his condition prompted his admirers to contribute to two online fundraising campaigns, with donations crossing $60,000. As veterinarians continued investigating his illness, his adopted family said the money remaining after his medical expenses would be used to support other cats in need. George's story has attracted attention well beyond the station he has called home for years.
George's sudden illness prompts fundraising effort
George's health began deteriorating over the weekend of November 21 and 22. His family became concerned when they noticed changes in his eating and sleeping habits and decided to seek veterinary attention.
He was admitted to a veterinary clinic on November 23, where he received treatment and was placed on a drip. He also remained under observation overnight while doctors investigated the cause of his condition.
Updates shared by his social media manager, Simone Carter, indicated that his kidney and liver functions were normal, although his thyroid levels were slightly elevated. 
Vets were also concerned about his persistently high temperature and planned a CT scan to investigate the underlying problem.
By November 25, his family reported some encouraging developments. George was no longer dehydrated, and his temperature had come down slightly. However, he was still receiving assistance with feeding, while veterinarians continued investigating the cause of his illness.
More than $60,000 raised through two campaigns
The news of George's illness prompted an overwhelming response from people who had followed his adventures at the railway station and on social media.
Two separate fundraising campaigns were launched to help cover his veterinary expenses. According to figures reported by local newspaper Express & Star on November 25, the GoFundMe campaign had collected £46,578, while the JustGiving campaign had raised £14,468.
Together, the campaigns had generated £61,046, equivalent to approximately $80,000 at the time.
The initial veterinary expenses had already reached £1,500, with further diagnostic tests and treatment potentially adding to the bill. The fundraising was organised to help ensure George could receive the medical attention he needed.
His adopted family promises to support other cats
The fundraising campaign was organised by Simone Carter, who manages George's social media accounts, after his adopted owner, Ian Tomlinson, asked her to arrange financial assistance for his veterinary care.
The family has made it clear that the donations will first be used to cover George's medical expenses. However, any amount remaining after his treatment and care have been paid for will go towards helping other cats in need.
Carter told BBC Radio WM that she had opened a separate bank account to manage the funds collected for George. Once his veterinary bills are settled, the money could be used to assist animal charities and cat rescue organisations, both locally and further afield.
The decision means the generosity shown towards George could also benefit other animals requiring care and support.
How George became a familiar face at a UK railway station
George first started visiting Stourbridge Junction railway station in the West Midlands in 2017. The ginger-and-white cat gradually became a familiar presence among commuters, railway employees and visitors.
When his original owner moved to Spain, railway supervisor Ian Tomlinson adopted him, allowing George to remain at the station he had come to frequent.
His popularity eventually extended far beyond the railway community. He attracted more than 260,000 followers across social media platforms, with admirers travelling from countries including the United States, Canada and parts of Asia to see him.
He also received his own Google Maps marker, while his photographs and merchandise helped establish him as a recognisable local personality.
A train was named after the famous feline
George's popularity has also earned him recognition within the railway network. In August 2025, a Stourbridge Shuttle train was named George the Station Cat in his honour.
The train, numbered 139002, operates between Stourbridge Junction and Stourbridge Town. The naming recognised the cat's connection with the station and the affection he had earned from railway staff and passengers.
George's life has also been documented in a book titled Just George: The Autopawography of a Station Cat, written by Simone Carter. It recounts his journey from a rescue cat to a much-loved railway station resident.
His followers continue to wait for updates
As George remained under veterinary care, his family continued sharing updates with supporters who had contributed to the fundraising campaigns. The November 25 update brought some encouragement, with his dehydration resolved and his temperature showing signs of improvement.
His diagnosis was still being investigated, and his family remained hopeful that further veterinary care would help establish what had made him unwell.
For the people who regularly encounter him at Stourbridge Junction, George has become more than just a station cat. His story has connected railway commuters, animal lovers and social media followers, whose contributions have also created an opportunity to support other cats through the surplus donations.

title: Watch: FedEx aircraft runs off runway at Miami airport on eve of Thanksgiving
text:
A FedEx cargo aircraft overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, forcing the temporary closure of all but one runway and disrupting flight operations on the eve of Thanksgiving.
There were no immediate reports of injuries in the incident, which occurred around 8:40 pm, the airport said. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the scene.
The McDonnell Douglas MD-11 was arriving from Memphis when it ran off the runway. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said flights were expected to resume shortly and that it would investigate the incident.
The airport urged passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night to check with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.
"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," the airport said in a statement.
The incident comes nearly three months after an Amazon cargo aircraft overran another runway at the airport in September, killing five people on the ground. Although Wednesday's incident involved a different runway, three of Miami International Airport's runways converge at the western end, leaving the FedEx aircraft close to the site of the earlier crash.
In the September incident, the Amazon plane veered across a road and struck a van carrying an aircraft cleaning crew.
The FedEx aircraft was an MD-11, the same model involved in a deadly UPS cargo plane crash in Kentucky last year. In that incident, an engine detached from the aircraft during takeoff, killing three pilots and 12 people on the ground.
The FAA subsequently approved Boeing's proposed fix for the aircraft, and FedEx resumed operating its MD-11 fleet in May.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said it had no information about Wednesday's incident.

title: Storm hits New York: Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving parade postponed for first time
text:
Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for the first time in its history. New York City officials are moving the annual spectacle to Saturday as powerful winds and heavy rain threaten to make Thursday’s celebrations unsafe.
The parade, which was scheduled to take place on Thanksgiving Day, November 26, will now begin at 8.30 am local time on November 28. The decision was taken by Macy’s in consultation with city officials and the New York Police Department (NYPD), with organisers saying the safety of participants and spectators was the priority.
Macy’s had planned to mark the centenary with a record 100 inflatables, including its iconic giant character balloons. But a powerful 
storm
 approaching the US East Coast was expected to bring sustained winds, strong gusts and heavy rain to the city, threatening to ground the balloons and drench spectators.
“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority,” Macy’s said in a statement, announcing the postponement.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the city had been looking forward to celebrating the parade’s 100th edition but had to reschedule because of extreme weather.
Stating that the decision to postpone the parade was taken in coordination with Macy’s, the NYPD and other city agencies as the storm forecast developed.
“Out of an abundance of caution, together, we’ve made the decision to postpone the Thanksgiving Day parade until Saturday,” Mamdani said, warning that the city could face wind gusts of up to 65 mph, coastal flooding and heavy rain from Thursday afternoon into the evening.
Urging residents to avoid flooded roads and basements, he said the winds could bring down tree limbs and power lines. New Yorkers living in flood-prone basement apartments were advised to make plans to move to higher ground before flooding began.
“We know how much this holiday means to New Yorkers. But the most important thing is getting everyone through this storm safely and back with the people they love,” Mamdani said, adding that the city was looking forward to celebrating the parade on Saturday.
New York governor Kathy Hochul warned that gusts could reach 60 mph in parts of New York City, Long Island and the lower Hudson Valley.
The winds posed a particular risk to the parade’s giant balloons. Under safety rules introduced in 1998, balloons cannot fly when sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts exceed 34 mph. The NYPD has the final authority on whether the balloons can take to the streets.
The parade’s balloons had begun inflating on Wednesday, a day before the scheduled event. A city official said they would be deflated from 7 pm and reinflated on Friday afternoon. Organisers, however, said there would be no public viewing of the second inflation session.
Thousands of police officers are expected to be deployed for the rescheduled parade, with specialised units including mounted officers, K-9 teams, Harbour Aviation and the Emergency Service Unit assisting with security. The NYPD said there were no known, specific or credible threats to the event.
The postponement is unprecedented for the parade itself. It was cancelled in 1942, 1943 and 1944 because of wartime restrictions on helium and rubber, while high winds grounded its giant balloons in 1971. In 2006 and 2019, poor weather forced balloons to fly at lower heights.
The safety rules were tightened after a 1997 incident in which strong winds pushed a Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost, critically injuring a spectator.
The weather is also disrupting other Thanksgiving celebrations. Organisers of Philadelphia’s parade have decided against a street procession, switching instead to a televised programme featuring several planned performers and guests.
The storm is expected to affect holiday travel across the US, with more than 80 million people projected to travel during the Thanksgiving period. Officials have warned of damaging winds, coastal flooding and possible power outages across parts of the East Coast.
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a statewide state of emergency ahead of the storm, urging residents with holiday travel plans to reach their destinations before the worst conditions arrive.
Despite the postponement, the parade is expected to retain its full spectacle on Saturday, when weather conditions are forecast to be more favourable. The event drew an estimated 34.3 million viewers across NBC and Peacock in 2025, setting a viewership record.

title: Phil Knight and wife pledged biggest-ever $2 billion cancer gift in 2025
text:
A cancer diagnosis can set off a difficult journey that extends well beyond medical treatment. Patients and their families often have to navigate unfamiliar healthcare systems, seek access to specialised care and make decisions about treatment options while dealing with considerable uncertainty. At Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU), a new philanthropic commitment is intended to address some of these challenges. Nike co-founder Phil Knight and his wife, Penny Knight, pledged $2 billion to the university's cancer research institute, a contribution that could reshape its approach to early detection, clinical research and patient care. The couple's latest commitment also marks a significant expansion of their longstanding involvement in cancer research in Oregon.
Phil Knight and wife make record $2 billion cancer research pledge in 2025
Announced in August 2025, the pledge is directed towards the Knight Cancer Institute at OHSU in Portland, Oregon. The university described it as the largest single donation ever made to a higher-learning institution in the United States.
The funding is intended to help the institute advance its diagnostic capabilities, widen access to innovative clinical trials and make the experience of receiving cancer care less complicated for patients and their families. 
Rather than concentrating exclusively on laboratory research, the proposed work also addresses the difficulties people encounter while moving through the healthcare system after a diagnosis.
For OHSU, the commitment represents an opportunity to expand work across several areas of cancer research and treatment. The institute has indicated that it wants to improve how cancers are identified, develop more targeted approaches to treatment and make promising medical advances more accessible to patients.
Phil and Penny Knight said they were encouraged by what the institute could achieve through the initiative, describing its potential impact as extending beyond the university and benefiting humanity.
How earlier donations shaped OHSU's cancer research programme
The couple's relationship with OHSU goes back well before the latest announcement. In 2008, the university named its cancer institute after Phil and Penny Knight following their $100 million contribution. That donation helped establish the foundation for their continuing involvement in the institution's cancer research programme. Five years later, they announced another substantial commitment. The Knights offered $500 million through a fundraising challenge, on the condition that the university raise an equivalent amount within two years. OHSU met the target, allowing the institution to move forward with an expanded cancer research programme.
The earlier contributions also helped support developments in early detection. According to Dr Brian Druker, chairman of leukemia research at the Knight Cancer Institute, the funding contributed to the creation of a large-scale programme focused on identifying cancer at an earlier stage.
Druker has also credited the cancer challenge with encouraging the development of blood tests designed to detect cancer before it progresses. The institute subsequently expanded its work in precision medicine and targeted therapies, approaches that seek to identify treatments based on the characteristics of a particular cancer.
How the institute plans to make cancer care easier for patients
For someone diagnosed with cancer, getting the right treatment can involve more than finding a specialist or identifying an appropriate therapy. Patients may need to understand complicated medical information, explore clinical trial opportunities and navigate different parts of the healthcare system. This is one of the problems the Knight Cancer Institute has identified as part of its future work. Druker has acknowledged that navigating healthcare after a cancer diagnosis can be particularly difficult, and said the institute intends to change how patients encounter the system.
The proposed investment is expected to support improvements in diagnostic technology and access to clinical trials, alongside efforts to simplify the process for patients and their families. Clinical trials are an important part of cancer research because they allow investigators to assess emerging treatments and examine whether new approaches can improve outcomes.
The institute's existing work in precision medicine also provides a foundation for its plans. Instead of relying on a single treatment approach for every patient, precision medicine uses information about an individual's cancer to help guide decisions about care.
Phil Knight's philanthropy extends beyond cancer research
The $2 billion commitment is among the largest philanthropic contributions associated with Phil Knight, whose fortune was estimated at $35.4 billion by Forbes at the time of the announcement. Knight, 87 at the time, built his wealth through Nike, the sportswear company he co-founded. He stepped down as its president and chief executive in 2004 before retiring as chairman in 2016. His charitable contributions have frequently supported education, research and institutions connected to his own academic background.
The University of Oregon, where Knight studied and competed as a track athlete, has been a major recipient of his philanthropy. Several facilities at the university carry the Knight family name. These include the Knight Library, while its basketball arena honours his son Matthew Knight, who died in a scuba diving accident in 2004.
Knight has also supported Stanford University, where he completed his business education. In 2016, he pledged $400 million towards a programme intended to bring graduate students from around the world to Stanford to work on major societal challenges, including poverty and climate change.
How the donation compares with other major gifts to US institutions
Large donations to universities and medical institutions have become an important part of American philanthropy, particularly when wealthy individuals direct substantial portions of their resources towards education and research. In 2018, businessman and former New York mayor Michael Bloomberg pledged $1.8 billion to Johns Hopkins University. The contribution was intended to strengthen financial aid and help students from low- and middle-income backgrounds attend without having to shoulder the full cost of their education. In February 2024, Ruth Gottesman, the widow of financier David Gottesman, donated $1 billion to the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in the Bronx, New York. The gift was intended to fund free tuition for students at the medical school.

title: Nasa's asteroid crash test left stadium-sized crater; first images reveal
text:
The first images of an asteroid deliberately struck by a 
Nasa
 spacecraft in 2022 have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface, offering a closer look at the impact of the planetary defence test.
The European Space Agency (ESA) on Wednesday released the first images captured by its Hera spacecraft, which was sent to examine the aftermath of the collision on the target asteroid, Dimorphos. The images show Dimorphos orbiting its larger companion, Didymos, with the impact site coming into view before the smaller asteroid disappears into Didymos's shadow.
Nasa's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (Dart) mission deliberately crashed a car-sized spacecraft into Dimorphos at around 14,000 miles per hour in 2022. The impact changed the asteroid's orbit by 33 minutes, demonstrating that a spacecraft could alter the trajectory of a space rock.
Dimorphos posed no threat to Earth, and the mission was designed to test whether an asteroid could be deflected to prevent a potential collision with the planet.
However, Dart's impact left scientists with questions about the extent of the damage and how the asteroid responded to the collision. 
The Hera mission is examining the site to gather more detailed information about the impact and assess how effective such a deflection strategy could be.
Announcing the release of the images, ESA said Hera had captured Dimorphos completing a full orbit around Didymos, allowing the impact site to be observed.
The agency said the mission would investigate the collision up close and help scientists understand how asteroid deflection could be used to protect Earth in the future.

title: 4 from Keralam among 11 Indians killed in UAE bus accident
text: Four people from Keralam are among 11 Indians who were killed when a bus rammed into a truck parked along a road in the UAE’s Ras Al Khaimah early Tuesday. The other deceased Indians were from Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Gujarat. The bus, owned by a Keralam-based travel company, was carrying 41 passengers, who were returning after travelling to Oman to complete their visa change process.

title: 44 Nvidia trades put Trump’s financial interests under spotlight after CEO’s return
text:
US president 
Donald Trump
’s investment portfolios traded shares of chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times between January and September, with the value of his holdings potentially rising by as much as $15 million after the company’s stock surged following the return of chief executive Jensen Huang.
A review of Trump’s financial disclosures by BBC Verify found that his portfolios bought between $5.2 million and $17 million worth of Nvidia shares during the first nine months of the year, while selling between $4.4 million and $12 million worth.
The filings, submitted to the US Office of Government Ethics, report transactions in broad value ranges rather than exact amounts, making it impossible to establish precisely how much Nvidia stock Trump traded or how many shares he held.
Trump’s latest disclosure, submitted on November 5, indicated that he could have held as many as 370,000 Nvidia shares as of September 30.
Nvidia shares surged more than 30% on Monday after the company’s board reinstated Huang as CEO, potentially increasing the value of Trump’s investment by $15 million.
The rally followed Trump’s public involvement in Huang’s reinstatement. The president told CNBC he had spoken to Nvidia’s board and “made the deal” to bring the executive back. 
Nvidia said it had received input from senior US government officials before deciding Huang’s return posed no national security risk.
Trump’s portfolios also held between $12.5 million and $58 million worth of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025, according to the disclosures.
The White House has said Trump’s stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties, and that neither the president nor his family can direct or influence investment decisions.
The frequent trading of Nvidia shares has nevertheless raised questions about potential conflicts of interest, particularly given Trump’s role in the company’s leadership decision and the administration’s oversight of advanced chip exports to China.
Nvidia has become one of the world’s most valuable companies amid the boom in artificial intelligence. Its shares account for more than 6% of the S&P 500, making it one of the most influential stocks in the index.

title: Malaysia sues Google over ‘harmful’ content
text:
Malaysia’s communications regulator said Wednesday it has filed lawsuits against 
Google
 seeking a combined 600 million ringgit ($145.8 million) in damages, alleging it had failed to take adequate action against harmful content.
The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission said Google, a major investor in the country, had not taken adequate action to address content related to online gambling, scams and fraud on its YouTube platform, or take proactive measures in relation to “various volatile content” by a well-known blogger. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Eisenkot bags 1st coalition pact in govt formation talks
text:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot secured his first coalition deal with bloc ally Avigdor Liberman, a milestone in his efforts to form a govt with 10 days left on his initial mandate.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party said the two leaders met Sunday and agreed to sign a coalition agreement. Their parties hold 28 of the opposition bloc’s 48 seats after the Oct 27 election, short of the 61 required for a majority. The left-wing Democrats ended talks with Yashar, citing its negotiations on a unity govt with Benjamin Netanyahu and a committee to seek agreement on a judicial overhaul.
Liberman is trying to draw at least one ultra-Orthodox ally away from Netanyahu’s 53-seat bloc without relying on Israeli Arab parties. He said talks with United Torah Judaism had its rabbis’ approval. Its support would give the opposition 55 seats but require concessions on drafting ultra-Orthodox men.
Israel’s parliament Wednesday gave preliminary approval to a bill establishing the inquiry. It forms part of an opposition legislative drive to reverse Netanyahu’s policies while Eisenkot retains the mandate.

title: Trouble for Netanyahu? Israeli judges question key charges in corruption trial
text:
Israeli judges on Wednesday urged prosecutors to reconsider three corruption cases against prime minister 
Benjamin Netanyahu
. The judge stated that the chances of convicting him in one bribery case were low and questioned whether an offence had been committed in another, in a major setback for the long-running prosecution.
The judges at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who has the authority to decide whether the cases should proceed, and asked her to consider dropping one of the charges and reassessing the others.
The panel said there was little likelihood of a conviction in Case 4,000, which alleges that Netanyahu granted regulatory favours to a telecommunications mogul in exchange for favourable coverage on a news website. The judges also expressed serious doubts over whether the alleged conduct in Case 2,000, involving a proposed deal with a newspaper publisher, amounted to a criminal offence.
They left open the possibility of a conviction in Case 1,000, in which Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust for accepting gifts from wealthy businessmen in return for helping them with their interests.
Baharav-Miara told the court that she and her team would consider the judges’ recommendations and remain open to all options based on the evidence, according to a transcript provided by a Justice Ministry spokeswoman to New York Times.
The judges stressed that their remarks reflected their assessment of the evidence at this stage and did not amount to a verdict.
Netanyahu, who has denied all wrongdoing and described the prosecution as a political witch hunt, said the trial had collapsed and called for it to end immediately.
“Today, the trial has fallen,” he said in a televised statement, describing the judges’ comments as “a ray of truth and justice”.
The prime minister said it had taken 10 years for the truth to emerge, referring to the investigations into his conduct that began about a decade ago. He also spoke of the “terrible suffering” endured by him and his family.
Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate but interlocking cases. Prosecutors allege that he granted government and regulatory benefits to business figures in exchange for gifts and favourable media coverage for him and his family.
Three cases at the centre of trial
In Case 4,000, Netanyahu is accused of helping the controlling shareholder of Israel’s largest telecommunications company, Bezeq, in return for positive coverage on the news website Walla, which the businessman owned. The judges said the chances of conviction in the bribery case were low enough to warrant reconsideration.
Case 2,000 concerns an alleged backroom arrangement between Netanyahu and the owner of a popular daily newspaper. The proposed deal, which never came to fruition, would have involved favourable coverage of Netanyahu in exchange for measures against a rival publication. The judges said they had serious doubts that the evidence established a criminal offence.
Case 1,000 involves allegations that Netanyahu accepted nearly $300,000 in gifts, including cigars and champagne, from Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian billionaire James Packer between 2007 and 2016.
Prosecutors allege that Netanyahu sought to help Milchan extend a tax exemption and used his influence to assist him in renewing his US visa. The attorney general said the options in this case were either a verdict or a plea deal.
Netanyahu completed his testimony in June, prompting the judges to take stock of the proceedings, which have been delayed over the years, including by the war in Gaza.
Political future in the balance
The development comes at a crucial moment for Netanyahu, whose political future has been thrown into uncertainty after last month’s election failed to produce a clear parliamentary majority.
His rival, former military chief and centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has been given the first opportunity by Israel’s president to form a new government. Netanyahu and his allies won more seats than Eisenkot’s bloc but fell short of securing an outright majority.
Netanyahu’s indictment and trial have contributed to years of political instability in Israel, with several mainstream parties refusing to join coalitions led by him, arguing that he is unfit to govern while facing criminal charges.
The judges’ intervention could now give Netanyahu a significant political boost, though the cases remain before the court and no final decision has been made on whether they will be dropped or proceed to judgment.

title: Black nurses faced alleged racial abuse at Vermont home; Elderwood agrees to $450,000 settlement
text:
They travelled away from their homes and families during a global health emergency to help care for vulnerable residents, but some Black nurses and nursing assistants allegedly faced racial slurs, threats and physical attacks at the facility where they worked. Four years after a federal discrimination lawsuit was filed over the alleged treatment, a Vermont nursing home operator has agreed to pay $450,000 to settle the case and introduce measures to prevent further harassment.
According to the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), which announced the settlement on November 24, 2026, 98 Starr Farm Road Operating Co., doing business as Elderwood at Burlington, and Elderwood Administrative Services LLC agreed to the financial settlement and additional workplace protections. The agreement resolves a federal lawsuit alleging that the companies failed to respond adequately to repeated racial harassment of Black employees by nursing-home residents.
Black nurses faced racial harassment while working during the pandemic
The allegations concern employees at Elderwood at Burlington, a skilled nursing facility in Burlington, Vermont. According to the EEOC, the harassment began in 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, when the facility was dealing with staffing shortages. 
Most of the affected Black employees were travelling nurses who had left their homes and families to help the nursing home maintain its services during a difficult period. Instead of finding a supportive working environment, they allegedly encountered repeated racial abuse from some of the residents.
The EEOC's lawsuit described incidents involving racial slurs, threats and physical attacks. One resident allegedly repeatedly told Black employees to return to Africa, followed them around the facility while directing racial abuse at them and physically assaulted several workers. Other incidents involved residents making threats of violence and expressing preferences against receiving care from Black employees.
The agency alleged that nursing-home managers and supervisors knew about the incidents, either because they witnessed the behaviour or because employees reported it to them. However, the company allegedly failed to take sufficiently prompt and effective action to stop the harassment.
How the federal discrimination lawsuit began
The EEOC filed its lawsuit on September 6, 2022, in the US District Court for the District of Vermont. The case, EEOC v. 98 Starr Farm Road Operating Co., LLC, also named Elderwood Administrative Services LLC as a defendant. The agency argued that the alleged conduct created a racially hostile work environment in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The federal law prohibits employment discrimination based on race and requires employers to take appropriate action when they become aware of workplace harassment.
An important issue in the case was that the alleged harassment came from nursing-home residents rather than supervisors or fellow employees. The EEOC maintained that employers still have responsibilities to protect workers from racial harassment by people they encounter while performing their jobs, including patients and residents.
The defendants sought summary judgment, asking the court to resolve the case in their favour without a trial. However, on March 26, 2026, the federal district court denied that request. The court concluded that a reasonable jury could find that the workplace had been affected by severe or pervasive racial discrimination and that the defendants had failed to take sufficiently effective corrective action. This allowed the EEOC's hostile-work-environment claim to proceed towards trial.
What the $450,000 settlement requires
The settlement was reached before trial and is governed by a two-and-a-half-year consent decree. Under the agreement, the defendants will pay a total of $450,000 in monetary relief to the affected employees. The defendants denied the allegations and made no admission of liability under the consent decree. The financial payment is accompanied by several requirements aimed at preventing similar incidents. Elderwood must revise and distribute its anti-discrimination policy, establishing procedures for reporting, investigating and responding to racial harassment by residents and other people who are not employees.
The company must also provide annual interactive anti-discrimination training to employees at the Burlington facility and its corporate office. Managers and supervisors will receive additional training on their responsibilities. Another significant requirement is a resident code of conduct that prohibits discrimination and harassment against employees. It will make clear that the facility will not accommodate requests to assign or exclude caregivers based on their race.
The agreement also requires an independent hotline for discrimination complaints, notices to employees, an annual message from the Elderwood administrator reaffirming the company's commitment to a harassment-free workplace and periodic compliance reports. The EEOC will monitor the defendants' compliance throughout the decree's term.
