EEOC officials said the settlement reinforces the responsibility of healthcare and long-term care employers to respond to racial harassment, regardless of whether the alleged perpetrators are employees, patients or residents. The agreement brings the four-year federal lawsuit to a resolution without a trial verdict on the discrimination allegations, while requiring Elderwood to compensate the affected workers and strengthen its policies for protecting employees.

title: Elise Stefanik family’s DC home sells for $2.9m cash after failing to fetch $1.99m, flagged as unusual
text:
A Washington home owned by US Congresswoman Elise Stefanik’s family sold for $2.9 million in cash months after leaving the market, even though it did not sell at a lower asking price of $1.99 million. City tax officials have now marked the sale as unusual, saying the price was high compared with past listings and that some deal details could not be fully checked. The three-bedroom home on Independence Avenue SE sits about six blocks from the US Capitol and was sold in June to a new Delaware company called AFS Real Estate Holdings, whose backers are not publicly known. The Washington Post first looked into the sale, reporting on the price jump and the buyer's scarce public records, and in a follow-up story on 25 November reported that Washington, DC, property records gave the deal a special label called "Sale Code 4". That label has put new focus on the sale, which involved a home held by a company where Stefanik and her family members owned shares, while Stefanik’s office called the deal commercially reasonable and said it would appear in her required financial report.
A property that failed to sell
EMS DC Properties, a limited liability company tied to Stefanik and her family, bought the townhouse in August 2010 for a little more than $1.2 million, according to The Washington Post. 
Stefanik bought it with her parents and brother, and later reported an ownership stake in Washington residential rental property through EMS DC Properties. The home went on the market in September 2025 for $2.195 million, dropped to $1.99 million in November after failing to sell, and came off the market in February 2026 after more months with no buyer. The sale happened in June while the home was no longer listed for sale, changing hands for $2.9 million in all cash, which was $910,000 above its last asking price, with The Washington Post reporting that only two homes on Capitol Hill had public records showing a higher sale price over the prior year. The newspaper said it found no records or work permits showing renovations done in the four months between taking the home off the market and selling it, and records also showed no mortgage tied to the sale.
Why the sale was flagged
The D.C. Office of Tax and Revenue gave the deal "Sale Code 4", a label covering sales with unusual buyer-seller deals where the price does not seem to match market value. Office spokeswoman Brianna Jordan told The Washington Post that officials used the code because "the sale price was elevated relative to its prior listing prices, and the circumstances surrounding the transaction could not be fully verified." Jordan said off-market sales sometimes get this label depending on the facts of each deal, and the newspaper's check of city records found that under 500 property sales, or about 6 per cent of roughly 8,000 home and business sales recorded from January through October 2026, got Code 4, while most sales were logged as normal market-rate deals.
Stefanik’s office pushed back on claims that the label was rare, initially saying about 6,000 property sales had been flagged as unusual that year. The Washington Post reported that number seemed to cover a much broader group of deals marked "unqualified", which uses many codes and does not mean every sale got Code 4, and after being asked to clarify, the office said 480 deals got a code similar to the one on the Stefanik home.
Questions over the buyer and the price
The buyer, AFS Real Estate Holdings, registered in Delaware roughly a month before the June sale, has no known online presence, and public record searches did not show who owns or runs it. Lawyer Janis M. Penman, a partner at the Washington office of Cleveland-based law firm BakerHostetler who filed the papers to set up the company, did not reply to a request for comment from The Washington Post. Stefanik did not answer written questions from the newspaper asking if she knew who owned or ran AFS, while her office said the home was listed during a government shutdown and "a slow holiday season", called the final sale a "commercially reasonable transaction", and said Stefanik held a minority share in the home. The office also said the price fit other historic townhouses nearby, stating: "The offer to buy the investment property was made and accepted within the range of prices for comparable historic townhouse sales in the neighborhood that range from $2-$4 million," according to its statement to the newspaper.
The Washington Post asked six local estate agents and property lawyers with decades of Capitol Hill experience to review the sale, and none could recall another case where a buyer paid so much above a recent asking price. Settlement lawyer Patrick Tangney, who has 20 years of experience in the Washington area, said the price looked unusual based on listing and property records, while Capitol Hill estate agent Tom Faison, who has over 30 years of experience, told the newspaper: "A reasonable appraiser looking at six months of sales in my opinion would not be able to justify $2.9 million for this house," adding a question over whether buyers would overlook the home's recent failure to sell for less. The newspaper also reviewed 34 homes given by Stefanik’s office as examples of similar sales, finding that 13 sold for more than the family’s home, though most had more bedrooms or more living space, and some had features the Independence Avenue home lacked, such as a swimming pool, a garage or private parking. The townhouse itself was listed with three bedrooms, 3.5 bathrooms, three fireplaces and about 2,700 square feet of space.
Family company bought a Virginia home
The June 24 sale went through EMS DC Properties, the limited liability company in which Stefanik and her relatives held shares, and after selling the Washington townhouse, EMS bought a newly built home in McLean, Virginia, for $3.3 million. A paper tied to that purchase listed a $434,425 mortgage signed by Stefanik, who was named the company’s managing member. In a statement reported by The Washington Post, Stefanik’s office said she had shared required details in her yearly personal financial reports while in Congress, and added that the sale followed the law and House ethics rules and would go into her next yearly financial report.
 North Country Public Radio also covered the sale on 24 November, noting that the buyer's identity stayed unclear, the sale price was well above the last asking price, and the family bought the home in 2010 for about $1.2 million. Stefanik, who represents New York’s 21st Congressional District, is set to leave Congress when her current term ends in January, with her office saying the property sale would be properly reported in her next yearly report while who owns the company that paid $2.9 million for the townhouse remains unknown.

title: Lululemon founder Chip Wilson says Canadian women aren't having as many babies as men want; some men may need to import brides from Thailand
text:
Lululemon founder Chip Wilson has triggered a backlash after making controversial remarks about women's reproductive choices, birth control and workplace opportunities during a leadership conference attended predominantly by women in Calgary, Canada. Wilson, who founded the popular athleisure brand in 1998, was invited to speak at the Axis Connects Leadership Forum on Monday at the BMO Centre. The event brought together around 720 attendees, most of them women, to discuss leadership and barriers faced by women in business.
Wilson said women in Canada often do not agree to have as many children as men want. And then he suggested that men seeking to have multiple children might need to import brides from Thailand.
Axis Connects, the non-profit organisation behind the conference, acknowledged that Wilson's remarks had upset attendees. In an email to The Globe and Mail, CEO Nuvyn Peters said several of his comments were offensive and inconsistent with the organisation's values and mission. "We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community," Peters said.
"Challenging those attitudes is central to the work and ethos of Axis Connects," she said.
Wilson's session was scheduled to last an hour but was reportedly cut short by Peters.
A spokesperson for Wilson highlighted how Wilson encouraged women's leadership. "This is an effort to discount Chip Wilson's record of mentoring women who have become executives and entrepreneurs in their own right to drive revenue with a clickbait headline," the spokesperson said.
This is not the first time Wilson has faced criticism over comments about women's bodies. In 2013, he stepped down as chairman of Lululemon's board following controversy over remarks he made during a television interview about complaints that some of the company's yoga pants were see-through. At the time, Wilson suggested that the problem was not necessarily the quality of the clothing but that "some women's bodies just actually don't work for" the garments.
During Monday's conference, Peters reportedly asked him whether he regretted those remarks. Wilson responded that they had been taken out of context.

title: Bournemouth residents oppose two new padel courts, citing noise and swearing from existing courts
text:
Residents living near a prestigious tennis club in Bournemouth are fighting a proposal to build new padel courts, saying the existing facilities already create constant noise and shouting that disturb their daily lives. Homeowners living next to the exclusive West Hants Club in the wealthy Talbots Woods area have made dozens of formal complaints to BCP Council. Their main concern is the "constant thudding" and "aggressive language" coming from the club's four outdoor padel courts. They say the noise makes it difficult to enjoy their gardens. The dispute has grown following the club's latest planning application to build two more floodlit padel courts. Residents fear the expansion will make the noise even worse, bringing the activity closer to their property boundaries and private outdoor spaces. The disagreement has set the private members' club against the people living nearby. It has also raised questions about planning rules, noise in residential areas and the growing popularity of padel, a sport similar to tennis but played on an enclosed court.
The sound of contention
Residents say padel naturally creates more noise than traditional tennis. 
The game uses a solid bat and a pressurised ball, which make a louder "pock" sound when they hit each other than a tennis ball hitting the strings of a racket. The courts are also surrounded by glass walls and wire mesh, which residents say make the sound louder and send it upwards towards nearby homes. Homeowners have described the noise as constant, comparing it to the repeated sound of a mechanical hammer. But the noise of the game is not their only concern. Residents have also reported hearing frequent shouting, swearing and angry outbursts from players during matches. They say these sounds carry easily into their homes.
In complaints submitted to the council during the planning consultation, one resident living on nearby Rothesay Road said the noise from the existing courts was "already unbearable". They described their garden as a "noisy, stressful environment". Another resident, whose home backs directly onto the club, said they can no longer leave their windows open during the summer because of the noise. They also complained that players frequently use inappropriate and offensive language in what they consider a family neighbourhood.
Proximity to premium properties
The West Hants Club is in a highly sought-after part of Bournemouth, where many nearby homes are worth more than £1 million. Residents have spent large amounts on their properties and say they expected to enjoy a quiet suburban setting. The proposed sites for the two new floodlit courts have become a major concern because they would be close to existing homes. Residents say the courts would be only a few metres from their back gardens, making the current noise problems even worse.
The planned floodlights have also raised concerns about light pollution. Residents fear they could extend the disturbance into the evening, seven days a week. They believe the club is putting its expansion plans and the growing demand for padel ahead of the quality of life of people living nearby. The local residents' association has gathered support against the proposal and urged BCP Council to reject the application. It says the new courts could have a negative effect on the daily lives of nearby homeowners.
Club insists on strict management
The West Hants Club has defended its plans, saying padel is a rapidly growing sport and that more courts are needed to meet demand from members. The club says it acts responsibly towards its neighbours and has already introduced measures to control noise. In its planning statement submitted to the council, the club said court use is limited to reasonable hours and that staff actively monitor players' behaviour. It also said the proposed courts would include modern features designed to reduce noise if the application is approved.
 A separate management plan would also be introduced to limit any disturbance to nearby residents.
The club has also pointed to the health and social benefits it offers to the wider Bournemouth community. It argues that continued investment and development are important to its future and will help it provide more opportunities for people to take part in sport. Club representatives have also said that independent noise surveys commissioned by the club found that sound levels were within acceptable limits set by the local authority. However, residents have strongly challenged these findings, saying the reports do not reflect the experience of living beside the courts every day. BCP Council is still considering the planning application, with a decision expected in the coming months. The dispute highlights the growing tension between sports clubs looking to expand and residents who want to protect the peace and quiet of their homes.

title: Egypt highway inferno kills 30 after fuel tanker overturns
text:
At least 31 people were killed and 21 injured after a crash involving a fuel tanker triggered a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo in Egypt on Wednesday, authorities said. The blaze broke out on the Ring Road in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo region. More than two dozen cars and motorcycles were charred in the fire.
The fire spread among vehicles following the crash, trapping people inside burning cars. Rescue workers were seen pulling victims out of the vehicles as firefighters worked to bring the blaze under control, according to an Associated Press video. Hundreds of people gathered near the accident site in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.
Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic after the road was blocked, said he saw the fuel tanker and several cars engulfed in flames. He also witnessed at least eight bodies being removed from burned vehicles.
“It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire," Associated Press reported quoting him as he described the fear and panic that followed, "It was a shocking scene.”
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his condolences to the victims. The Public Prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were underway to identify those killed.
Egypt health minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured had been taken to nearby hospitals. He also said he would visit the accident site. The death toll was preliminary and could rise further, he added.
The Ring Road is a major transport artery connecting key highways across Greater Cairo and linking the governorates of Cairo, Giza and Qalyubia.
Road accidents are common in Egypt due to factors such as speeding, poor road conditions and weak enforcement of traffic regulations. Thousands of people die in traffic accidents across the country every year.
In January, 21 people were killed and 16 injured in a massive multi-vehicle pile-up on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

title: Chinese scientist, Arizona State University assistant professor, says he does not know why he was arrested by ICE: 'I still have nightmares'
text:
A Chinese-born scientist working in the United States has described the fear and uncertainty he experienced after being arrested by ICE agents despite having what he believed was a clean immigration record and having followed the rules for years. Di Liu, an assistant professor of chemistry at Arizona State University, was arrested by plainclothes ICE agents at an airport in July while preparing to board a domestic flight from Phoenix to Nashville, Tennessee, to attend an academic conference.
Liu told 
Science
 he was in an airport bathroom when three men suddenly appeared and blocked his way. The agents identified themselves as immigration officers and arrested him over alleged immigration violations.
The scientist initially thought the encounter was a prank. Having moved to the United States from China in 2011 to pursue his PhD, he said he had carefully followed immigration requirements and never expected to be detained.
Liu was released on July 28, but said the experience continued to haunt him. "They didn't tell me why. No explanation," he recalled.
He said he still experiences nightmares about the arrest and described the incident as a deeply frightening experience.
'I was certain they made a mistake'
Liu said when he was being handcuffed and taken to a holding room at ICE’s field office in Phoenix, he continued to hope against hope that agents would soon realize they’d made a mistake and let him go. Only when he was transferred to ICE’s immigration jail in the early morning of July 21, two days after his arrest, did he start to panic. “I was wrapped in enormous fear,” he said. “I didn’t know what would happen next and how I ended up here.”
Liu’s wife, a physicist at ASU, later told him that when she picked up his call from a jail payphone number, she was suspicious, wondering whether a scammer was using artificial intelligence to mimic his voice.
On July 28, Liu was released as mysteriously as he was arrested.
Liu’s university had filed a renewal application four months before his visa was set to expire, which used to be enough time for the application to be renewed, but now the waiting time is long and such cases eventually become "visa overstay".
Liu said he could not attend the important conference that day where he was scheduled to present his lab's new research. As he was arrested, he also missed some deadlines for grant proposals. The three papers he aimed to publish during the summer were deferred. In the third year of his position, these delays could mean the difference between earning tenure or not, he said.

title: Michigan widow's $78m truck crash award cut by $24m as court orders retrial on $19m claim
text:
A Michigan appeals court has overturned $24 million awarded to a widow for the fear her husband and son may have felt moments before a fatal lorry crash, ruling that state wrongful-death law does not allow compensation for pre-impact fright and shock. The court has also ordered a new trial over $19 million awarded for the pair’s conscious pain and suffering, leaving other parts of a judgment worth more than $78 million intact. The ruling was issued on 20 November 2026 by the Michigan Court of Appeals in a case brought by Natalie Attianese, whose husband, Jude, and 20-year-old son, Zachary, died in the crash on Interstate 75 in June 2018. The original jury award, including interest, was $78,517,580.94.
How the fatal crash happened
The collision happened on the night of 15 June 2018, as the family travelled from New Jersey to Michigan for a funeral in Sterling Heights. Jude Attianese, 56, was driving north on I-75 with Zachary in the passenger seat. They were moving at about three miles per hour in slow traffic caused by roadworks. Jose Angel Nogueras, who was driving an 18-wheel lorry for Canadian trucking company Challenger Motor Freight, approached from behind.
 He failed to stop and struck their car at more than 50 miles per hour. The impact pushed their vehicle forward into the car in front, causing a second collision.
The court's opinion said Nogueras had Parkinson's disease and was taking medication that made him drowsy at the time. There was no evidence that he applied the brakes before hitting the Attianeses' vehicle. Both men suffered fatal injuries, including internal decapitation and bleeding around the brain. An eyewitness who reached the car after the crash said neither man was moving or appeared to be breathing. Police officers also found them unresponsive. Natalie filed a lawsuit against Nogueras and Challenger in November 2019. The defendants admitted that Nogueras had been negligent and that Challenger was responsible for the deaths. They later admitted liability for all claims, leaving the trial to focus on the amount of compensation.
Jury awarded more than $78 million
The trial took place in April 2023 and focused on damages. The jury heard evidence about whether Jude and Zachary had been aware of the approaching lorry, whether they suffered before dying and how their deaths affected Natalie. The court heard testimony from witnesses who said the lorry could be seen and heard approaching. One driver, Lawrence Chockley, said he saw it coming in his rear-view mirror and feared it would not stop before reaching the traffic queue.
The jury awarded $12 million each for Jude and Zachary's fear and shock before the collision, making a combined $24 million. It also awarded $8 million for Jude's conscious pain and suffering and $11 million for Zachary's. Natalie received a further $9 million for the loss of society and companionship for each man from the date of the crash until the trial. The jury also awarded future damages for the loss of their company, including payments calculated over periods extending to 2039 for Jude and 2076 for Zachary. After adjustments for future payments and interest, the trial court entered a judgment of $78,517,580.94. That included about $71.2 million in past non-economic damages and $7.28 million in future non-economic damages. The defendants challenged the verdict, arguing that some of the damages were not permitted under Michigan law and that the trial had included evidence and testimony that unfairly affected the jury's decision.
Why the appeals court removed $24 million
The appeals court said the $24 million award for pre-impact fright and shock could not stand under Michigan's wrongful-death law. Its decision relied on a Michigan Supreme Court ruling in Daher v Prime Healthcare Services-Garden City, issued in July 2024, after the original trial court had rejected the defendants' post-trial challenge. The law allows certain types of compensation in wrongful-death cases, including reasonable payment for pain and suffering experienced while the person was conscious between the time of injury and death. The appeals court said the law does not allow a separate award for fear experienced before the injury itself. Natalie had argued that the fear Jude and Zachary experienced when they realised the lorry was about to hit them should count as part of their injury. The appeals court rejected that argument, saying there was no evidence of physical consequences before the collision. It therefore ruled that the jury had no legal basis to award separate damages for pre-impact fright and shock. The full $24 million award was set aside.
$19 million pain and suffering award faces retrial
The court also ordered a new trial over the $19 million awarded for conscious pain and suffering. It did not rule that the claim itself was invalid. Instead, it found that the trial judge had made a mistake by allowing a replacement medical expert to testify without giving the defence enough notice or a fair chance to examine his opinions. Natalie's original medical expert, Dr Lawrence Shields, was unable to testify on the revised trial schedule. Dr Kenneth Mankowski was brought in to replace him. The appeals court said the defence had not received the required details of Mankowski's opinions and was not allowed to question him before he gave evidence.
Mankowski told the jury that Jude may have remained conscious for about 65 to 70 seconds after the crash, while Zachary may have been conscious for around three minutes. He said they could have realised they were unable to breathe. The jury's awards of $8 million and $11 million were based on this testimony. The defence's medical expert, Dr Ljubisa Dragovic, disagreed. He said the injuries caused by the collision led to immediate unconsciousness and death. The appeals court said the question of whether the two men experienced conscious pain and suffering could properly be decided by a jury, but the replacement expert's testimony had been admitted unfairly. It sent the issue back for a new trial, giving the defence an opportunity to examine the evidence properly.
Other parts of the judgment remain in place
The appeals court rejected the defendants' request for a new trial on all issues. It found that some evidence about liability should not have been presented, but said this did not justify reopening the entire case. It also upheld the awards for loss of society and companionship. The defendants had argued that the verdict was excessive, but the court noted that their own lawyer had suggested a similar annual figure for future damages during the original trial.
 The final ruling therefore leaves the compensation for the family's loss in place while removing the $24 million pre-impact award and sending the $19 million pain and suffering claim back to a jury. The case, Estate of Zachary Attianese v Jose Angel Nogueras, was decided by the Michigan Court of Appeals on 20 November 2026.

title: Alberta family donates 160 acres of native prairie for conservation while allowing cattle grazing
text:
A ranching family in southern Alberta has donated 160 acres of untouched native prairie for permanent protection, more than 100 years after first settling in the region. The land will remain open for cattle grazing, allowing the family’s farming tradition to continue while protecting the natural grassland. The Nature Conservancy of Canada (NCC) announced on 24 November 2026 that the Coppieters family had donated the 65-hectare property, known as Coppieters Acres, along Alberta's Milk River Ridge. The land is located 17 kilometres southeast of Magrath in Warner County. It will remain protected as native fescue grassland while continuing to support local ranching.
"Peter and I have always really appreciated and looked up to people who chose to conserve their land. When we talked about it, we thought this was the best thing we could do with the quarter pasture. We're happy that it will stay the way it's always been," land donor Donna Coppieters said in the Nature Conservancy of Canada announcement.
A century of family stewardship
The family has long referred to the property as the "quarter pasture". Peter Coppieters Sr. and his wife, Mary, first settled in the region in 1925. They bought land and started the family farm. 
Their son, Peter, later bought the quarter pasture with his wife, Donna, continuing the family's care for the property. The land has never been ploughed or used for crops. It has remained natural prairie, where cattle graze and generations of the family have made memories. Donna Coppieters said the property is home to a wide range of wildlife, including elk, deer, pronghorn and many types of birds. Protecting the land will preserve both an important part of the family's history and an area of native prairie for future generations.
Milk River Ridge and threatened grasslands
Coppieters Acres lies along the Milk River Ridge, which follows Alberta's southern border between Magrath and Milk River. The area is an important refuge for foothills rough fescue grassland, one of Alberta's most threatened natural ecosystems. Around 80 per cent of the remaining foothills rough fescue ecosystem is on privately owned land. This makes voluntary conservation efforts by landowners especially important. According to the Nature Conservancy of Canada, the donation builds on earlier conservation work in the region supported by its donors, including McIntyre Ranch and Sandstone Ranch. Water collected along the Milk River Ridge supplies communities and farms across central North America. Water flowing north enters the Oldman watershed and moves across the Prairies towards Hudson Bay. Water flowing south enters the Milk River watershed before travelling through the Missouri and Mississippi rivers to the Gulf of Mexico.
Wildlife and carbon storage on the land
About 87 per cent of the 65-hectare property is covered by native fescue grassland. The remaining area consists of wetlands and areas beside rivers and streams. These natural areas help store and filter water before it reaches downstream watersheds. Field surveys conducted in 2026 recorded bobolinks on the property. The bird is listed as a species of special concern in Canada, and its Canadian population has fallen by about 80 per cent since 1970, according to the Nature Conservancy of Canada. Survey teams also confirmed the presence of hoary bats and silver-haired bats. Both are listed as sensitive in Alberta and have been recommended for Endangered status by the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC). Five other species of concern, all listed as sensitive in Alberta, were also recorded in the project area. They are Brewer's sparrow, eastern kingbird, plains garter snake, sharp-tailed grouse and upland sandpiper.
The protected prairie also provides benefits beyond wildlife habitat. Natural grasslands help filter water and support pollinating insects. These insects contribute an estimated $3 billion each year in ecosystem service value to prairie crop production, according to the Nature Conservancy of Canada. Alberta's native fescue grasslands also store large amounts of carbon. They can hold up to 200 tonnes of carbon per hectare in the top metre of soil. The Nature Conservancy of Canada estimates that about 11,400 tonnes of carbon are stored beneath Coppieters Acres. This is similar to the annual emissions produced by nearly 14,000 cars. The wider loss of prairie grasslands has also been significant. Figures from the Nature Conservancy of Canada show that Canada has lost more than 80 per cent of its prairie grasslands since European settlement. Around 60,000 hectares are still lost each year, while less than 6 per cent of the remaining grasslands are formally protected.
Grazing stays part of the plan
The donation combines permanent protection of the natural habitat with continued ranching. Carefully managed cattle grazing helps keep prairie landscapes open, supports a variety of native plants and contributes to the rural economy.
"Milk River Ridge is one of the most intact grassland landscapes left in Alberta, and every hectare that stays whole matters. The Coppieters family's gift is exactly the kind of local stewardship that keeps these grasslands healthy, working and connected for the ranchers, wildlife and communities who depend on them," said Tom Lynch-Staunton, regional vice president for the Nature Conservancy of Canada.
The organisation's stewardship staff will assess the property and prepare a management plan to guide future grazing. This will include checking the health of the grassland and managing invasive species. The Nature Conservancy of Canada said the project was made possible by the Coppieters family, with support from Cenovus through the Conserving Critical Wetlands Program.
